title: 1 HENRY IV
author: Shakespeare
summary: A history play of rebellion against Henry IV, balancing the court and battlefield against the Eastcheap tavern world of Falstaff; it traces Prince Hal's education toward kingship, climaxing at Shrewsbury with the defeat of Hotspur.

title: 1. Awake ye muses nine, sing me a strain divine
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: An early comic valentine cataloguing how all things in nature pair off in courtship and marriage; a lyric on love, union and the loneliness of the single soul.

title: 10. My wheel is in the dark!
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of faith amid obscurity: the unseen turning wheel and unfrequented road of life leading through the 'busy tomb' to a clearing at the end.

title: 100. A science — so the Savants say,
author: Dickinson
summary: Comparative anatomy, which reconstructs a creature from one bone, becomes an emblem: a single winter flower stands representative of all roses, lilies, and butterflies to come — promise of renewal.

title: 1000. The Fingers of the Light
author: Dickinson
summary: A dialogue lyric personifying dawn-light as an imperious guest tapping at a sleeping town and rousing all nature to obeisance; a playful aubade of sunrise and nature.

title: 1009. I was a Phoebe — nothing more —
author: Dickinson
summary: A self-deprecating lyric in which the speaker identifies as a humble phoebe-bird, dwelling low and shy yet leaving a small print upon the floors of fame; themes of humility, identity, and modest art.

title: 101. Will there really be a "Morning"?
author: Dickinson
summary: A child-pilgrim's questioning lyric asking whether 'Morning' truly exists; faith and doubt about a promised dawn (heaven/immortality) addressed to scholars and wise men.

title: 1010. Up Life's Hill with my little Bundle
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the uphill pilgrimage of life carrying a little bundle, the heart having accepted homelessness for home; themes of life's journey, endurance, and exile.

title: 1012. Which is best? Heaven —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric weighing present Heaven against a deferred Heaven shadowed by doubt, preferring the bird in the hand; themes of faith, doubt, and immortality.

title: 1013. Too scanty 'twas to die for you,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A love lyric arguing that to live for the beloved is costlier than to die, since living includes dying multifold without the respite of death; merges love, sacrifice, and mortality.

title: 1018. Who saw no Sunrise cannot say
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the deprivation of light: only one who saw sunrise can grieve its loss, the emigrant of light afflicted, blindness that beheld and blest yet cannot find its eye. Themes of loss, vision, and grief.

title: 1020. Trudging to Eden, looking backward,
author: Dickinson
summary: A tender consolatory lyric in which the speaker, journeying toward Eden, meets a dead mother's little boy unafraid and smiling among new acquaintance in heaven; themes of death of a child, consolation, and immortality.

title: 1021. Far from Love the Heavenly Father
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on divine providence: God leads the elect child through briar and the dragon's claw rather than mild meadows, framing suffering as predestined guidance toward heaven.

title: 1024. So large my Will
author: Dickinson
cluster: Vanitas · Contemptus Mundi · Vanity of Worldly Things
summary: A meditation on the smallness of earthly gifts against eternity: human will is large but its offerings are a scanty toy, an affront to the God who possesses all.

title: 1025. The Products of my Farm are these
author: Dickinson
summary: A wry agrarian conceit casting the poet's inner produce as a perpetual harvest, reversing the zodiac when frost comes to gather the acres in.

title: 1026. The Dying need but little, Dear,
author: Dickinson
summary: A tender deathbed lyric enumerating the small needs of the dying — water, a flower, a friend's regret — and the certainty of being mourned.

title: 103. I have a King, who does not speak —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a silent King (God) glimpsed in dreams; alternating joy and the failure to pray 'thy will be done,' dramatizing faith, doubt, and self-will.

title: 1031. Fate slew Him, but He did not drop —
author: Dickinson
summary: A heroic lyric in which a man withstands all that personified Fate inflicts, his unmoved endurance forcing Fate to acknowledge him a Man.

title: 1033. Said Death to Passion
author: Dickinson
summary: An allegorical debate between personified Death and Passion; Passion, sovereign as the sun, refuses Death and merely resets in the West, ending the contest.

title: 1035. Bee! I'm expecting you!
author: Dickinson
summary: A playful epistolary lyric written as a Fly's letter to a Bee, reporting the return of spring creatures and inviting the bee home.

title: 1037. Here, where the Daisies fit my Head
author: Dickinson
summary: A grave-bed lyric in which the speaker, lying among daisies, entrusts a flower to the earth and imagines union beyond death as a single bloom.

title: 1038. Her little Parasol to lift
author: Dickinson
summary: A flower-conceit lyric: the speaker would imitate a flower's small duty, hoping to be preserved blemishless from the sepulchral crease of decay.

title: 1039. I heard, as if I had no Ear
author: Dickinson
summary: A visionary lyric of awakening perception culminating in the soul's recognition by the dust and Time meeting Eternity.

title: 104. Where I have lost, I softer tread —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: An elegiac lyric of mourning: the speaker treads softly and guards the lost dead, sowing flowers on the grave; grief, loss, and the hope of reunion in bliss.

title: 1044. A Sickness of this World it most occasions
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A reflection on grief and longing when the best men die, leaving the living world a foreign, sickening place as the dead are content with Deity.

title: 1046. I've dropped my Brain — My Soul is numb —
author: Dickinson
summary: A poem of psychic paralysis and numbness imaged as marble and Carrara stone, holding a wager that being and breath may yet return beyond the centuries.

title: 1048. Reportless Subjects, to the Quick
author: Dickinson
summary: A meditation on the inexpressible: inner subjects vivid to the sensitive but foreign as a Danish dialect or Oriental tale to others.

title: 1049. Pain has but one Acquaintance
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric personifying Pain and Death as intimate companions, Death tenderly assisting the junior Pain before absconding.

title: 105. To hang our head — ostensibly —
author: Dickinson
summary: A witty, gnomic lyric on the immortal mind's true posture beneath a feigned humility; appearance versus the gauzy reality of soul and self.

title: 1051. I cannot meet the Spring unmoved —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on spring's emotional pull and a competitive desire, ending in remorse as the season vanishes hiding something unattained.

title: 1052. I never saw a Moor —
author: Dickinson
summary: A famous lyric of faith without sight: never having seen moor, sea, God, or Heaven, the speaker is yet certain of them as if given the checks.

title: 1053. It was a quiet way —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: An ecstatic lyric of being borne away by a beloved in chariot-swift transport beyond the mortal world into an eternal dawn.

title: 1054. Not to discover weakness is
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric on strength as the artifice of concealing weakness, impregnability resting on faith and pyramidal nerve like a hidden clockwork.

title: 1055. The Soul should always stand ajar
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric urging spiritual readiness: the soul should stand ajar, like an open door, so Heaven's visitor need not wait or depart unwelcomed.

title: 1056. There is a Zone whose even Years
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric envisioning an eternal timeless zone of perpetual noon and endless summer where consciousness itself becomes Noon.

title: 1057. I had a daily Bliss
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the paradox of value: a bliss half-ignored grows as it is pursued and only when lost beyond reach is learned to be estimated.

title: 1058. Bloom — is Result — to meet a Flower
author: Dickinson
summary: A nature lyric exalting the hidden labor behind a flower's bloom — opposing worm, wind, and bee — making it a profound responsibility.

title: 1059. Sang from the Heart, Sire,
author: Dickinson
summary: A poet-bird's apology and ballad: the song bleeds cochineal and vermillion because Death twists the strings, repeating the hallowed name of the Lord.

title: 106. The Daisy follows soft the Sun —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: An allegory of devotion: the daisy follows the sun as the soul/lover follows the beloved or the divine, stealing nearer at the parting west; love as religious longing.

title: 1060. Air has no Residence, no Neighbor,
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on air as a free, neighborless, ethereal guest and host at the dying outcast's pillow, attending the soul as it departs.

title: 1061. Three Weeks passed since I had seen Her —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: An elegiac lyric recounting a final encounter with a dying woman amid text and village singing, ending in a riddling question about who is now out of sight.

title: 1062. He scanned it — staggered —
author: Dickinson
summary: A stark narrative of a man's mental collapse and suicide: groping for God and himself, he caresses a trigger and wanders out of life.

title: 1063. Ashes denote that Fire was —
author: Dickinson
summary: An emblematic lyric reading ashes as evidence of a departed fire, reverencing the gray pile for the vanished creature that once burned there.

title: 1065. Let down the Bars, Oh Death —
author: Dickinson
summary: A pastoral elegy addressing Death as a gentle shepherd whose fold receives the tired flocks into the stillest, securest night.

title: 1068. Further in Summer than the Birds
author: Dickinson
summary: A late-summer meditation on the crickets' unobtrusive Mass and Grace, an enlarging loneliness and elegy that is Nature's own liturgy at dusk.

title: 107. 'Twas such a little — little boat
author: Dickinson
summary: A miniature allegory of a little boat swallowed by a greedy sea — the fragile soul or life lost on the vast deep; transience and the indifferent grandeur of the sea.

title: 1070. To undertake is to achieve
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric on resolve: to undertake with fortitude against obstacle is itself achievement, revering departed standards and few true criterion sources.

title: 1071. Perception of an object costs
author: Dickinson
summary: An epistemological lyric: perceiving an object costs its loss, perception itself a gain that idealizes and then upbraids a perfectness set far off.

title: 1072. Title divine — is mine!
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A lyric of spiritual marriage: the speaker claims the divine title of Wife without the sign, Empress of Calvary, born-bridalled-shrouded in a day.

title: 1075. The Sky is low — the Clouds are mean.
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A wintry weather lyric personifying a complaining wind and a hesitant snowflake, finding Nature, like us, sometimes caught without her diadem.

title: 1076. Just Once! Oh least Request!
author: Dickinson
summary: A prayer-plea lyric pressing a small request on an adamantine God of Flint, wondering if even He could refuse so scanty a grace.

title: 1077. These are the Signs to Nature's Inns —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A lyric reading the sky's signs as Nature's open inn offering mystic bread and equal hospitality to beggar and bee alike.

title: 1079. The Sun went down — no Man looked on —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on sunset and sunrise witnessed only by the earth, the speaker, and a nameless bird — solitary witnesses to the sun's majesty and crown.

title: 1080. When they come back — if Blossoms do —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of doubt about renewal: whether blossoms, robins, and May can return, and whether the speaker will be present to see them again.

title: 1082. Revolution is the Pod
author: Dickinson
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · Common Man
summary: A political-botanical conceit: revolution is the pod from which systems rattle, and shaking liberty tests whether it is still alive or dead on the stalk.

title: 1084. At Half past Three, a single Bird
author: Dickinson
summary: A timed lyric tracing a bird's dawn song from a cautious term to full silver principle to vanished presence, leaving only circumference between.

title: 1086. What Twigs We held by —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Vanitas · Contemptus Mundi · Vanity of Worldly Things
summary: A reflective lyric on the frail twigs and props we cling to in life's swift river, seen as pitifully scant by everlasting light against the things that truly are.

title: 1087. We miss a Kinsman more
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the paradox of nearness and absence: a kinsman is missed more when expected and close than when oceans away, exploring distance, separation and longing.

title: 1088. Ended, ere it begun —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric using the book/story metaphor for a love or life cut off before it could unfold, attributing the loss to God's interdict — grief, transience and providence.

title: 1089. Myself can read the Telegrams
author: Dickinson
summary: A wry lyric on reading news of markets and weather — trivial tidings sweeter than silence, touching solitude and the consolation of small communication.

title: 109. By a flower — By a letter —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A lyric on love fastened like a rivet at a forge; flowers and letters as the small tokens by which love is welded fast against labor and weariness.

title: 1090. I am afraid to own a Body —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric meditating on the precarious double inheritance of body and soul as property entailed upon an unsuspecting heir, with God as a frontier — identity, the self and soul, immortality.

title: 1093. Because 'twas Riches I could own,
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on possession and value: earned wealth feels like poverty, while an unattainable, intangible income holds a miser's sweeter charm — wealth, paradox and desire.

title: 1097. Dew — is the Freshet in the Grass —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A nature lyric reading dew and the natural world as a hidden mill and a show whose inner meaning we mistake — the book of nature, wonder and childlike perception.

title: 1099. My Cocoon tightens — Colors tease —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric using the cocoon-to-butterfly metamorphosis as emblem of the soul groping toward transformation, deciphering a divine clue — transformation, faith and immortality.

title: 11. I never told the buried gold
author: Dickinson
summary: A playful pirate-treasure conceit (sunset as buried gold, Captain Kidd, Atropos) weighing secrecy versus disclosure of a precious hidden hoard.

title: 1100. The last Night that She lived
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A deathbed elegy narrating a woman's quiet dying, the heightened perception of the watchers and the awful leisure of faith afterward — mortality, grief and the deathbed scene.

title: 1101. Between the form of Life and Life
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric distinguishing mere form of life from living ecstasy via the figure of liquor kept versus poured — joy, transience and the appearance-versus-reality distinction.

title: 1102. His Bill is clasped — his Eye forsook —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of outrage at a shot songbird, likening its murder to firing on angels squandering miracles of tune — death of nature, grief and the loss of beauty.

title: 1103. The spry Arms of the Wind
author: Dickinson
cluster: Night Journey Vision · Katabasis Descent · Quest Hero
summary: A lyric imagining a swift errand carried on the wind to an adjoining zone to check on a soul and rekindle one's own light — the soul's journey, the afterlife and death.

title: 1104. The Crickets sang
author: Dickinson
summary: A twilight nature lyric in which crickets close the day and a faceless Vastness, Wisdom and Peace arrive as the night comes — nature, the sublime and tranquillity.

title: 1105. Like Men and Women Shadows walk
author: Dickinson
summary: A short nature lyric personifying shadows on the hills as courteous folk in a landscape beyond our smaller human boroughs — nature, light and dark, perception.

title: 1106. We do not know the time we lose —
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric on the unnoticed instant of loss and the illusory solidity of life's appearances whose substance is sand — time, transience and loss.

title: 1107. The Bird did prance — the Bee did play —
author: Dickinson
summary: An ecstatic summer-morning lyric of birds, bees and sun in a 'Republic of Delight,' celebrating natural joy and nearness — nature, joy and the pastoral.

title: 1108. A Diamond on the Hand
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on how familiarity diminishes worth: a diamond grown common loses significance while the unbought gem inflames desire — value, desire and paradox.

title: 1109. I fit for them —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of self-discipline and abstinence undertaken to produce a purer food for others, with reward in the very aim — humility, vocation and self-sacrifice.

title: 111. The Bee is not afraid of me.
author: Dickinson
summary: A joyful nature lyric of communion with bees, butterflies, brooks, and breezes that welcome the speaker; sudden tears at the wonder of a summer's day.

title: 1110. None who saw it ever told it
author: Dickinson
summary: A riddling lyric on a hidden treasure as secret as death, whose value depends on rarity — the inexpressible, secrecy and the relation of value to scarcity.

title: 1112. That this should feel the need of Death
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigram on the irony and audacity that the small, no less than the great, must die — mortality, paradox and the universality of death.

title: 1113. There is strength in proving that it can be borne
author: Dickinson
summary: A fragmentary lyric on endurance: the cordage and cedar feet needed to bear and to walk on seas of suffering — endurance, suffering and fortitude.

title: 1114. The largest Fire ever known
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric figuring the daily sunset as the largest fire, consuming an Occidental Town rebuilt and burned each morning — the sun, cyclical recurrence and transience.

title: 1115. The murmuring of Bees, has ceased
author: Dickinson
summary: An autumnal lyric marking the year's turn as bees fall silent and a prophetic, Biblical revelation of seasonal change replaces them — seasons, transience and nature read as scripture.

title: 1116. There is another Loneliness
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric on a rarer loneliness born of nature or thought that enriches beyond measure — solitude, the inner life and paradoxical wealth.

title: 1117. A Mine there is no Man would own
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on an inward, hoarded mine of wealth — a Potosi of the mind worth more than the Indies in the ground — interior riches, value and the self.

title: 1118. Exhilaration is the Breeze
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric defining exhilaration as a breeze that lifts us to enchanted ground and returns us soberly the wiser — joy, transcendence and the sublime.

title: 1119. Paradise is that old mansion
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: An epigram figuring Paradise as an old mansion briefly tenanted, with bliss made frugal by Adam's bankrupting Fall — the Fall, transience of bliss and providence.

title: 112. Where bells no more affright the morn —
author: Dickinson
summary: A vision of heaven as a town where bells and factories no longer frighten and children sleep through centuries of noon; longing for rest and Bliss, with biblical echoes of Moses on Pisgah.

title: 1120. This slow Day moved along —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric personifying a reluctant, slow-moving day whose axles hate motion, while the speaker and soul play it away — time, the inner self and tedium.

title: 1122. 'Tis my first night beneath the Sun
author: Dickinson
summary: A riddling lyric on distance and expectation beneath the sun, whose delights are confided to those who visit from afar — distance, longing and nature.

title: 1123. A great Hope fell
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of inward, silent catastrophe — a great hope wrecking soundlessly within the mind, foundering as if at sea until the lid is nailed down — despair, grief and concealed suffering.

title: 1125. Oh Sumptuous moment
author: Dickinson
summary: A carpe-diem lyric begging a sumptuous moment to slow, contrasting famine and abundance like a condemned man savoring morning before the gallows — seizing the moment, joy and death.

title: 1126. Shall I take thee, the Poet said
author: Dickinson
summary: An ars-poetica lyric dramatizing the poet's search for the right word, when an unsummoned, revealed word arrives like the Cherubim — the creative act, inspiration and language.

title: 1128. These are the Nights that Beetles love —
author: Dickinson
summary: A wry summer-night lyric on a beetle's intrusion as a small bomb of discreet alarm that keeps the nerves progressive — nature, the grotesque-comic and the value of fear.

title: 1129. Tell all the Truth but tell it slant —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Artist and Society · Truth · Regency Georgian England
summary: An ars-poetica epigram counselling indirection: truth too bright must dazzle gradually like lightning explained, or it blinds — truth, the inexpressible and the art of telling.

title: 113. Our share of night to bear —
author: Dickinson
summary: A compressed lyric on each soul's allotted portion of night and morning, bliss and scorn; stars and mists give way at last to day, an emblem of suffering resolving into light.

title: 1130. That odd old man is dead a year —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: An elegy a year after an odd old man's death, his faded lamp gone out, meditating on a life begun in blood and dully consummated — mortality, memory and the dimming of life.

title: 1131. The Merchant of the Picturesque
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: A lyric figuring nature (or the sky/sunset) as an elusive merchant selling beauty cheaply to children and shy of counterfeits — nature, beauty and childlike vision.

title: 1132. The smouldering embers blush —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on enduring inner fire in the coals of the heart, surviving years with a constancy Prometheus never knew — the heart, fire and endurance, alluding to Prometheus.

title: 1133. The Snow that never drifts —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the transient once-a-year snow, recalling stern winter and arguing that value is bought by contrast and that pang sharpens memory — winter, transience and memory.

title: 1134. The Wind took up the Northern Things
author: Dickinson
summary: A storm lyric personifying the wind as an awful power devouring the four divisions of the earth, after which nature ventures out restored — storm, the sublime and nature's order.

title: 1135. Too cold is this
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a corpse too cold and stiff to warm, the agile kernel of the soul gone from the husk leaving but an asterisk — death, the body and the soul's departure.

title: 1136. The Frost of Death was on the Pane —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric dramatizing a desperate fight against personified Frost/Death for a flower, ending in hatred of both Death and Life and the larger sea of Woe — death personified, grief and the struggle against mortality.

title: 1137. The duties of the Wind are few,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A lyric personifying the Wind, cataloguing its duties, pleasures, kinsmen and limitations; nature as free agent whose mortality remains unknowable.

title: 1140. The Day grew small, surrounded tight
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the shrinking light of a November day, personifying season and night; nature, autumn, and the contraction of daylight toward winter.

title: 1142. The Props assist the House
author: Dickinson
summary: An emblematic lyric: scaffolding withdrawn from a finished house figures the soul's perfected, self-supporting life; identity, soul, growth.

title: 1147. After a hundred years
author: Dickinson
summary: A graveyard lyric on oblivion: after a century a grave's agony is forgotten, weeds and strangers obscure it; transience, memory, the forgotten dead.

title: 1148. After the Sun comes out
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on how sunlight transforms the world into freshness and renewal; nature, sun, dawn-like renewal and the joy of altered perception.

title: 115. What Inn is this
author: Dickinson
summary: The grave figured as a strange, cold inn with a 'Peculiar Traveller' and a Necromancer landlord; death as a comfortless lodging, eerie and uncanny.

title: 1150. How many schemes may die
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A lyric on the unseen contingencies of fate: how plans, escapes, and loves turn on accident; chance, fate, and the unknown course of a day.

title: 1152. Tell as a Marksman — were forgotten
author: Dickinson
cluster: Swords and Weapons · Power and Corruption · Tyrant
summary: A narrative lyric retelling the William Tell legend, his defiance of the tyrant Gessler and the apple-shot trial; tyranny, faith, heroism, and tradition.

title: 1153. Through what transports of Patience
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A grief lyric on the bleak endurance of living without a lost beloved, envying the dead their privilege of dying; loss, suffering, longing for death.

title: 1154. A full fed Rose on meals of Tint
author: Dickinson
cluster: Vanitas · Contemptus Mundi · Vanity of Worldly Things
summary: An emblematic lyric: the fully blossomed rose, food for a bee, becomes an image of bright mortality and the forfeit of beauty; transience and the rose.

title: 1156. Lest any doubt that we are glad that they were born Today
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic birthday tribute: a life celebrated as a dateless holiday like Consciousness or Immortality; gratitude, immortality, friendship.

title: 1159. Great Streets of silence led away
author: Dickinson
summary: A visionary lyric of a placeless realm of silence beyond time, law, and universe; death, eternity, silence, and the suspension of clocks and epochs.

title: 116. I had some things that I called mine —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Short Story · Concealment Hidden Identity · Justice Right and Wrong
summary: A wry legal allegory: God lays a rival claim to the speaker's garden, and she threatens a lawsuit before divine justice; faith and doubt cast as property dispute and litigation.

title: 1160. He is alive, this morning —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A lyric of devotion: nature (birds, blossoms, bees) revives to celebrate a beloved's being alive, leaving the speaker mute with love; love, nature, dawn.

title: 1162. The Life we have is very great.
author: Dickinson
summary: A meditative lyric weighing earthly life against infinite afterlife, where the human heart's extent reduces all dominion to nothing; immortality, soul.

title: 1165. Contained in this short Life
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the soul's nocturnal reach toward infinity within a short life, likened to kept children turning to the sea; transience, soul, infinity.

title: 1166. Of Paul and Silas it is said
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: A devotional lyric invoking the biblical prison-release of Paul and Silas as figure for the mind's optional bonds when an Immortal binds; faith, providence.

title: 1167. Alone and in a Circumstance
author: Dickinson
summary: A wry narrative lyric on a spider usurping the speaker's solitude, framed in legal terms of larceny of time and mind for which no law gives redress; identity, time.

title: 1168. As old as Woe —
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric on the coeval ancientness of woe and bliss, found together yet seldom side by side, inescapable to human nature; melancholy, joy.

title: 117. In rags mysterious as these
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on hidden royalty: shining courtiers (perhaps flowers or souls) veil their purple and ermine in rags and beg for alms; appearance versus reality, humility cloaking glory.

title: 1170. Nature affects to be sedate
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A lyric on nature's deceptive sedateness masking necromancy and conjuring trades, the grand citizen turned juggler; nature, appearance vs reality, wonder.

title: 1171. On the World you colored
author: Dickinson
summary: A grief lyric in which a beloved's wrinkled finger shoves away the rosy dawn, plunging the world's day into midnight's awful pattern; loss, light and dark.

title: 1172. The Clouds their Backs together laid
author: Dickinson
summary: A storm lyric dramatizing thunder, lightning, and a galloping gale, ending in the safe refuge of tombs beyond nature's vengeance; storm, the grave, nature.

title: 1173. The Lightning is a yellow Fork
author: Dickinson
summary: An emblematic lyric figuring lightning as cutlery dropped from celestial tables, revealing the dark mansions of the divine; nature, the sublime, wonder.

title: 1174. There's the Battle of Burgoyne —
author: Dickinson
cluster: War and its Cost · American Civil War · Battlefield
summary: A lyric likening the daily sunset to the solemn war of the Battle of Burgoyne, a majestic recurring conflict; nature, war imagery, the daily cycle.

title: 1175. We like a Hairbreadth 'scape
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A reflective lyric on the lingering thrill of a narrow escape, the breeze of risk reaching divinely to our utmost hair; risk, wind, the value of daring.

title: 1176. We never know how high we are
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric on unrealized heroism: our statures touch the skies when asked to rise, but we warp the cubits for fear of greatness; heroism, identity.

title: 1177. A prompt — executive Bird is the Jay —
author: Dickinson
summary: A character-sketch lyric portraying the blue jay as a brisk official, bailiff, brigadier, and magistrate of March; birds, nature, satirical portraiture.

title: 1178. My God — He sees thee —
author: Dickinson
summary: A hymn-like lyric urging the sun to shine its best before God, who outraces it; faith, the sun, divine omniscience, and praise of creation.

title: 118. My friend attacks my friend!
author: Dickinson
summary: A mock-martial lyric on quarrel between friends escalating to fantasies of shooting the human race; satirical treatment of conflict, friendship, and misanthropy.

title: 1180. "Remember me" implored the Thief!
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: A devotional lyric on the penitent thief's plea and Christ's promise of paradise as the mightiest case of compensated trust and grace; faith, redemption.

title: 1182. Remembrance has a Rear and Front —
author: Dickinson
summary: An emblematic lyric figuring remembrance as a house with garret and deepest cellar, warning to guard against being pursued by its fathoms; memory, mind.

title: 1183. Step lightly on this narrow spot —
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac lyric over a grave whose narrow breast holds a deathless fame carried as far as cannon, flag, and fame export; death, the grave, glory, memory.

title: 1184. The Days that we can spare
author: Dickinson
summary: A meditative lyric on the days we squander, stranded when a function, friend, or nature dies, letting go of time without reckoning; time, loss, transience.

title: 1185. A little Dog that wags his tail
author: Dickinson
summary: A whimsical lyric comparing the speaker to a tail-wagging dog and a gamboling boy, joyful without cause, against a quieted cat; childhood, innocence, joy.

title: 1187. Oh Shadow on the Grass,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: An elusive love lyric addressing a shadow as a hesitant candidate of the heart, who while the speaker delays will consecrate another; love, longing, doubt.

title: 1188. 'Twas fighting for his Life he was —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the single decisive inner combat of vitality, whose ordnance aims, kills, and conquers once in the inscrutable campaign of the interior; death, war.

title: 1189. The Voice that stands for Floods to me
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A love lyric on the subjective worth of the beloved, whose voice and face are sterile to others but the sum of all to the speaker; love, value, perception.

title: 119. Talk with prudence to a Beggar
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric warning against speaking of riches to beggars or freedom to captives; the cruelty of unattainable abundance, deprivation, and 'deadly sweet' longing.

title: 1191. The pungent atom in the Air
author: Dickinson
summary: An autumnal lyric on the indisputable sign in the air that summer has relinquished its estate, weighing departed delight; autumn, seasons, transience.

title: 1194. Somehow myself survived the Night
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on barely surviving a night of anguish, entering day as one commuted yet 'dated with the Dead'; suffering, survival, death, night and dawn.

title: 1195. What we see we know somewhat
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: An epistemological lyric on the partial reach of knowledge and surmise, voting for locked lands and the doubtful dividend patented by Adam; knowledge, the fall.

title: 1196. To make Routine a Stimulus
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric: remembering routine can cease makes it vivid; the capacity to terminate is a grace, torment made fair in retrospect; transience, grace, memory.

title: 1197. I should not dare to be so sad
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A lyric on grief's paradox: a load is impossible only once set down, and the withdrawal of the superhuman support leaves us to perish; grief, suffering, soul.

title: 1198. A soft Sea washed around the House
author: Dickinson
summary: A summery fancy in which a sea of summer air sails the house, captained by butterfly and bee for a delighted universe; nature, summer, the sea, joy.

title: 12. The morns are meeker than they were —
author: Dickinson
summary: A compact autumn lyric noting the meeker mornings, browning nuts and the maple's scarlet gown; the speaker dons a trinket to match nature's turn.

title: 120. If this is "fading"
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric making the autumn leaf's death gorgeous: if this red fading is dying, the speaker would die proudly; death as a splendid, peacock-proud, willing sleep.

title: 1201. So I pull my Stockings off
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: A child's wading and disobedience prompts wry doubts about salvation and biblical justice (Moses, Ananias), mixing childhood, faith and doubt.

title: 1202. The Frost was never seen —
author: Dickinson
summary: Frost as an unseen killing stranger in the garden becomes an emblem of unknowable death and the unprovable secrets of nature.

title: 1204. Whatever it is — she has tried it —
author: Dickinson
summary: A petition to an 'Awful Father of Love' over a dead or suffering woman (the Dove), pleading divine mercy and grief at separation.

title: 1205. Immortal is an ample word
author: Dickinson
summary: Meditation on immortality and the loss of a beloved, with heaven defined by absence and Death's marauding hand.

title: 1207. He preached upon "Breadth" till it argued him narrow —
author: Dickinson
summary: Satire of a hypocritical preacher whose counterfeit piety contrasts simple Jesus; appearance vs reality and critique of religion.

title: 1209. To disappear enhances —
author: Dickinson
summary: Absence and death confer value: the vanished and dead become immortal and unattainable, ecstatic limit of unobtained delight.

title: 121. As Watchers hang upon the East,
author: Dickinson
summary: Heaven figured through watchers awaiting dawn, beggars at a fancied feast, and brooks in deserts; deferred longing for bliss whose reality is uncertain ('Heaven to us, if true').

title: 1210. The Sea said "Come" to the Brook —
author: Dickinson
summary: Allegorical dialogue of Sea and Brook on growth, absorption and identity; the small must be subsumed into the great.

title: 1211. A Sparrow took a Slice of Twig
author: Dickinson
summary: A sparrow feeds and then vanishes into the sky, a small nature vignette touching transience and wonder.

title: 1213. We like March.
author: Dickinson
summary: March personified as a bold new arrival heralding spring, sun and bluebirds; seasonal renewal and joy in nature.

title: 1216. A Deed knocks first at Thought
author: Dickinson
cluster: Guilt · Conscience · Fate and Free Will
summary: The genesis of action through thought and will, with God alone hearing the doom of unacted deeds; conscience and the soul.

title: 1217. Fortitude incarnate
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Elegy for the drowned dead laid in the old sea, preferring the ocean's tumultuous rooms to the tomb.

title: 1219. Now I knew I lost her —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: The estrangement and loss of a beloved through emotional remoteness; grief, love's transmigration and idolatry.

title: 122. A something in a summer's Day
author: Dickinson
summary: An ecstatic lyric on the ineffable transcendence of summer day, noon, and night; the sublime in nature that the speaker can only half-glimpse and cannot name.

title: 1221. Some we see no more, Tenements of Wonder
author: Dickinson
summary: The dead become objects of wonder and conjecture; meditation on death, the tomb, and the sublime mystery of the afterlife.

title: 1223. Who goes to dine must take his Feast
author: Dickinson
summary: The mind's inner pattern must be furnished before the world's banquet can satisfy; identity, imagination and the self.

title: 1224. Like Trains of Cars on Tracks of Plush
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A bee assaulting flowers rendered as chivalric, victorious knight; nature, love as war, and playful conquest of blooms.

title: 1225. Its Hour with itself
author: Dickinson
summary: The soul's hidden subterranean terrors that the countenance never discloses; the self, the soul, and concealed inner depths.

title: 1226. The Popular Heart is a Cannon first —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wine and Drink · Ballad Ballade · Road
summary: Satire of mob enthusiasm: cannon, drum, bells and rum giving way to jail; critique of popular glory and society.

title: 1227. My Triumph lasted till the Drums
author: Dickinson
cluster: War and its Cost · American Civil War · Battlefield
summary: Hollow victory turns to hatred of glory before the war dead; the cost of war and the emptiness of triumph.

title: 1228. So much of Heaven has gone from Earth
author: Dickinson
summary: Wry argument that the saints' departure proves heaven must exist; faith, doubt and proof versus belief.

title: 1229. Because He loves Her
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Adoration of a beloved woman exalted by another's love; the unattainable beloved and love bordering on worship.

title: 1230. It came at last but prompter Death
author: Dickinson
summary: Death arrives before love can; frost as faithful death furnishes the house with metallic peace; grief and missed love.

title: 1231. Somewhere upon the general Earth
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Longing for a consecrating beloved still living somewhere; the speaker would trade all but immortality and prays against curtailed eternity.

title: 1232. The Clover's simple Fame
author: Dickinson
summary: Humble unselfconscious fame of the clover outranks vain renown; humility versus self-regarding ambition.

title: 1235. Like Rain it sounded till it curved
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A mighty wind/storm sweeps the land and rides off like Elijah on a wheel of cloud; nature's power and biblical ascension imagery.

title: 1236. Like Time's insidious wrinkle
author: Dickinson
summary: Time's wrinkle and frost dishevel beauty; aging and mutability make us clutch grace the tighter.

title: 1237. My Heart ran so to thee
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: The heart races ahead of the self toward the beloved's face, with longing reaching toward Bethlehem; romantic and divine love intertwined.

title: 1238. Power is a familiar growth —
author: Dickinson
summary: Death-power as a bland abyss beside us always, escaped only at the final glance of consciousness and clay; mortality and fate.

title: 1239. Risk is the Hair that holds the Tun
author: Dickinson
cluster: Temptation · Good vs Evil · Serpent Snake
summary: Risk as a seductive perilous hair luring its victim like perdition; temptation, fate and the lure of danger.

title: 124. In lands I never saw — they say
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the immortal Alps towering over a myriad daisies; an emblem of the great over the small, vastness and humility, with a riddling question of identity.

title: 1241. The Lilac is an ancient shrub
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: The sunset cosmos as a celestial lilac read as the book of nature; faith, revelation and the sublime over scientific analysis.

title: 1243. Safe Despair it is that raves —
author: Dickinson
summary: True agony is frugal and solitary; despair, suffering and the singular, indivisible nature of love and dying.

title: 1247. To pile like Thunder to its close
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Poetry and love as coeval sublime, fatal as seeing God; ars poetica on the overwhelming power of art and love.

title: 1249. The Stars are old, that stood for me —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Aging stars and worn west frame a paradox of victory in defeat over an unattainable beloved; love as war and loss.

title: 125. For each ecstatic instant
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric on the price of joy: every ecstatic instant must be paid for with anguish in keen ratio; ecstasy and grief as a strict economic exchange.

title: 1252. Like Brooms of Steel
author: Dickinson
summary: Winter snow and wind sweep the street into silence; a stark seasonal nature scene of cold and stillness.

title: 1253. Had this one Day not been.
author: Dickinson
summary: A single cherished day measured against loss; how love values what loss would value more, memory and transience.

title: 1254. Elijah's Wagon knew no thill
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: Elijah's wheel-less fiery chariot as inscrutable divine feat; biblical ascension, faith and miracle.

title: 1255. Longing is like the Seed
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Longing likened to a buried seed wrestling toward the sun; desire, hope and the constancy needed before fulfillment.

title: 1256. Not any higher stands the Grave
author: Dickinson
summary: The grave levels hero and man, beggar and queen; death as the great democrat, memento mori and the equality of mortality.

title: 1257. Dominion lasts until obtained —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Power and possession last only until gained, while the ungrasped belongs eternally; the unattainable and transience of dominion.

title: 1258. Who were "the Father and the Son"
author: Dickinson
summary: Childhood and adult wrestling with the Trinity, belief and shame; faith, doubt and the ineffable miracle of heaven.

title: 1259. A Wind that rose
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: An invisible inner wind beyond nature, a lone delight like separation's swell restored to the invisible; wind as spirit and the sublime.

title: 126. To fight aloud, is very brave —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric exalting the unseen inner battle ('cavalry of woe') above public valor; private heroism and suffering honored by angels in uniforms of snow.

title: 1260. Because that you are going
author: Dickinson
summary: A meditation on a loved one's death, immortality, and whether God will refund the beloved in a redemptive afterlife.

title: 1261. A Word dropped careless on a Page
author: Dickinson
summary: On the lasting, infectious power of written words to transmit despair across centuries; the immortality and danger of writing.

title: 1262. I cannot see my soul but know 'tis there
author: Dickinson
summary: Faith in an unseen God who has invited the soul to dwell; concern over being adequately adorned for a sudden divine feast.

title: 1263. There is no Frigate like a Book
author: Dickinson
summary: Celebrates the book and poetry as frugal vehicles of imaginative travel that bear the human soul.

title: 1264. This is the place they hoped before,
author: Dickinson
summary: Hope curdles into disappointment as the seed of disillusion grows; the way back is closed and an escapeless sea lies ahead.

title: 1265. The most triumphant Bird I ever knew or met
author: Dickinson
summary: A bird's song of pure intimate delight becomes an emblem of transient, accidental glory in nature.

title: 1267. I saw that the Flake was on it
author: Dickinson
summary: A dialogue with Time over change and mutability; the speaker insists on permanence but is corrected to accept alteration for progress.

title: 1269. I worked for chaff and earning Wheat
author: Dickinson
cluster: Artist and Society · Truth · Regency Georgian England
summary: A biblical wheat-and-chaff parable on earning truth and wisdom; wisdom is more becoming viewed at distance than at hand.

title: 127. "Houses" — so the Wise Men tell me —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric meditating on the biblical 'many mansions' of heaven the speaker cannot quite believe in; faith and doubt, longing for a warm refuge, with children who might trudge there tonight.

title: 1271. September's Baccalaureate
author: Dickinson
summary: September's autumnal mood of crickets, crows, and retrospect turns the heart philosophical; seasonal transience and melancholy.

title: 1272. So proud she was to die
author: Dickinson
summary: A woman dies so proudly and satisfied that her survivors' anguish almost turns to jealousy of her heavenward going.

title: 1273. That sacred Closet when you sweep —
author: Dickinson
summary: Memory figured as a sacred dusty closet to be swept reverently; the past can silence the present but cannot be superseded.

title: 1274. The Bone that has no Marrow,
author: Dickinson
summary: The marrowless bone as emblem of a soulless being; invokes Nicodemus' question of how a finished creature can be reborn.

title: 1275. The Spider as an Artist
author: Dickinson
summary: The spider as a neglected son of genius whose artistry goes unemployed; the artist unappreciated by society.

title: 1276. 'Twas later when the summer went
author: Dickinson
summary: The cricket as a pathetic pendulum keeping esoteric seasonal time; the passage of summer into winter as a clock toward death.

title: 1277. While we were fearing it, it came —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Long-dreaded calamity (death) arrives almost gently; the terror of anticipation exceeds the endurance of the thing itself.

title: 1278. The Mountains stood in Haze —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A hazy twilight landscape where evening falls softly and the Invisible feels neighborly; nature touched with the numinous.

title: 1279. The Way to know the Bobolink
author: Dickinson
summary: The bobolink as joyous, impudent, seditious sorcerer of the meadow whose departure nullifies the scene; the bird-poet of nature.

title: 128. Bring me the sunset in a cup,
author: Dickinson
summary: A wonder-filled lyric of impossible questions about who made the sunset, rainbow, robin, and spheres; the speaker as soul shut in a 'little Alban House' longing to fly free.

title: 1280. The harm of Years is on him —
author: Dickinson
summary: Time deposes a man like a fading fashion; the glory of decay is a lesser pageant than the least vitality.

title: 1281. A stagnant pleasure like a Pool
author: Dickinson
summary: Stagnant pleasure choked by its own rushes like a slowed pool, yet revivable when fresh waters (freshets) arrive.

title: 1282. Art thou the thing I wanted?
author: Dickinson
cluster: Greek Mythology · Lust Sexual Desire · Desire
summary: Long-deferred desire dismissed once its object finally appears; the speaker now dines self-sufficient, abjuring food, like God.

title: 1284. Had we our senses
author: Dickinson
summary: Blindness and dulled senses figured as merciful, sparing us from madness and from beholding an unmoved earth.

title: 1285. I know Suspense — it steps so terse
author: Dickinson
summary: Suspense personified as a neighborly figure at the window; the speaker, riding by, declares it no longer needs her.

title: 1286. I thought that nature was enough
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Nature gives way to human nature and then the Divine; capacity expands to the giant room given it.

title: 1288. Lain in Nature — so suffice us
author: Dickinson
summary: The buried dead lain in nature; the maddest heart cannot move the sod the simple summer pastes over the longed-for dead.

title: 129. Cocoon above! Cocoon below!
author: Dickinson
summary: The chrysalis-to-butterfly metamorphosis as an emblem of resurrection and the soul escaping imprisonment to 'know the Universe'; transformation and immortality.

title: 1290. The most pathetic thing I do
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Make-believe of hearing from an absent beloved that the heart almost believes; grief, longing, and self-deception addressed to Goliah.

title: 1291. Until the Desert knows
author: Dickinson
cluster: Greek Mythology · Lust Sexual Desire · Desire
summary: The desert's sands suffice until it suspects water exists; desire and the relativity of want, having, and dreamed-of abundance.

title: 1293. The things we thought that we should do
author: Dickinson
summary: The intended deeds, lands, and heaven never reached; unrealized aspiration and the deferred, illogical hope of paradise.

title: 1294. Two Lengths has every Day —
author: Dickinson
summary: Each day has absolute and subjective length lent by hope or horror; to die is not to depart but to remain as one is on Doom's chart.

title: 1296. Death's Waylaying not the sharpest
author: Dickinson
summary: Death is not Time's sharpest theft; Silence is a sorer robber who supplants the balm of life's consummate cluster.

title: 1297. Go slow, my soul, to feed thyself
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: The soul counseled to approach a rare beloved by stages against competing Death; love as redemption purchased for a kiss.

title: 1298. The Mushroom is the Elf of Plants —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: The mushroom as elf, juggler, and apostate of nature whose whole fleeting career is shorter than a snake's delay; transience in nature.

title: 1299. Delight's Despair at setting
author: Dickinson
summary: Delight at its setting despairs because it is less than the longing that craved it; the enchantment of anticipation over fruition.

title: 13. Sleep is supposed to be
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric redefining sleep and morning as the threshold of eternity and the resurrection dawn 'East of eternity'; death, immortality and faith.

title: 130. These are the days when Birds come back —
author: Dickinson
summary: Indian-summer lyric on the lovely 'fraud' of returning warm days; autumn's deceptive June, rendered as a sacrament and last communion the speaker child longs to join.

title: 1301. I cannot want it more —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Greek Mythology · Lust Sexual Desire · Desire
summary: Human nature's fullest force spent on a longing that is nothing to one who easily owns; the gulf between yearning and possession.

title: 1302. I think that the Root of the Wind is Water —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A fanciful natural cosmology deriving wind from water; a maritime conviction heard in the deep sound of the atmosphere.

title: 1304. Not with a Club, the Heart is broken
author: Dickinson
summary: The heart is broken not by clubs but by an invisible whip; a bird sings unto the stone that kills it, and shame may stand erect.

title: 1305. Recollect the Face of me
author: Dickinson
summary: A plea to be remembered in Paradise by one bound for heaven today; memory, courtesy, and a chivalric paragon.

title: 1307. That short — potential stir
author: Dickinson
summary: The one illustrious bustle each can make but once is the eclat of Death, an unknown renown no beggar would accept.

title: 131. Besides the Autumn poets sing
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the bare prosaic days between haze and snow that poets overlook; seasonal decline and the prayer for a sunny mind to bear God's windy will.

title: 1310. The Notice that is called the Spring
author: Dickinson
summary: Spring is a month away, yet the longest day's salary is nothing but a bier; renewal shadowed by mortality.

title: 1314. When a Lover is a Beggar
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: The reversal of lover from abject beggar to owner; the disparity of love's economy, where Bread of Heaven resents bestowal.

title: 1315. Which is the best — the Moon or the Crescent?
author: Dickinson
summary: The unattained is best; to achieve fruition is to efface the sheen, for transport decomposes once attained.

title: 132. I bring an unaccustomed wine
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: A lyric of charity to the dying: the speaker brings wine to parching lips that grow cold in death, then bears the cup ever after for some thirsty soul; grief, mercy, and hope of awaking.

title: 133. As Children bid the Guest "Good Night"
author: Dickinson
summary: A gentle conceit in which flowers, like children, put on nightgowns at dusk and wake to caper at dawn; sleep and waking as a tender emblem of nature's daily round.

title: 134. Perhaps you'd like to buy a flower,
author: Dickinson
summary: A playful lyric refusing to sell a flower but offering to lend it until spring's daffodils and bees return; flowers, seasons, and the small economy of nature's gifts.

title: 136. Have you got a Brook in your little heart,
author: Dickinson
summary: An allegory of the secret inner life as a hidden brook that can flood in March or run dry in August; the fragile, private stream of feeling and the life of the soul.

title: 137. Flowers — Well — if anybody
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the mingled ecstasy and trouble flowers stir in the humble heart; the inexpressible 'system of aesthetics' of daisies and butterflies surpassing the speaker's own.

title: 138. Pigmy seraphs — gone astray —
author: Dickinson
summary: An exuberant lyric praising bees and a velvety 'damask maid' (a flower) above the finery of Paris, Venice, and earls; nature's humble royalty preferred to worldly rank.

title: 1384. Praise it — 'tis dead —
author: Dickinson
summary: Praise of the dead is futile; an elegiac meditation on death, dust, and posthumous tribute that cannot warm the dead.

title: 1385. "Secrets" is a daily word
author: Dickinson
summary: Secrets locked in the human breast emerge only mutely at the grave; meditation on silence, identity, and death.

title: 1386. Summer — we all have seen —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Summer personified as an indifferent beloved adored from afar; nature, seasons, and unattainable transcendence.

title: 1388. Those cattle smaller than a Bee
author: Dickinson
summary: Flies whimsically reframed as cattle remanded to Nature for judgment; the natural order and observation of small creatures.

title: 139. Soul, Wilt thou toss again?
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: A lyric figuring salvation as a desperate gamble: angels and imps raffle for the soul as it tosses the dice; fate, the wager of damnation and redemption.

title: 1390. These held their Wick above the West —
author: Dickinson
summary: Sunset clouds as wicks that wane indefinably; transience, light fading into dark, the indefinable in nature.

title: 1392. Hope is a strange invention —
author: Dickinson
summary: Hope defined as a tireless 'electric' invention of the heart; abstract definition poem on inner spiritual resource.

title: 1395. After all Birds have been investigated and laid aside —
author: Dickinson
summary: The bluebird as 'Elegy of Integrity,' first at March, last when summer cleaves; nature, seasons, fidelity, birds.

title: 1396. She laid her docile Crescent down
author: Dickinson
summary: A gravestone (Shaft) outlasts the dead it commemorates; death, the grave, memory, mutability, constancy.

title: 1397. It sounded as if the Streets were running
author: Dickinson
summary: A storm/eclipse brings awe then calm renewal; nature's terror and sublimity, storm and the awe of the natural order.

title: 1398. I have no Life but this —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A love lyric collapsing life, death, and the afterlife into the beloved's realm; love elevated to religion.

title: 1399. Perhaps they do not go so far
author: Dickinson
summary: Speculation that the dead, freed of corporeal clothes, come closer; death, immortality, faith and doubt about the afterlife.

title: 14. One Sister have I in our house,
author: Dickinson
summary: A tribute to Sue, the chosen sister 'a hedge away'; a lyric of intimate love, sisterhood, memory and devotion 'forevermore'.

title: 140. An altered look about the hills —
author: Dickinson
summary: A spring catalogue of altered light, color and small creatures, closing on Nicodemus' mystery of rebirth; a lyric of seasonal renewal and resurrection.

title: 1400. What mystery pervades a well!
author: Dickinson
summary: The well and nature as a 'haunted house' whose ghost is never simplified; wonder, the unknowable in nature, water, the uncanny.

title: 1404. March is the Month of Expectation.
author: Dickinson
summary: March as the month of joyful anticipation, betraying us like a boy's first betrothal; spring, seasons, joy of expectation.

title: 1405. Bees are Black, with Gilt Surcingles —
author: Dickinson
summary: Bees as ostentatious 'Buccaneers of Buzz'; playful nature riddle on small creatures and indestructible natural order.

title: 1407. A Field of Stubble, lying sere
author: Dickinson
summary: A sere autumn stubble-field on New England farms, seen but seldom felt; autumn, seasons, rural New England landscape.

title: 1408. The Fact that Earth is Heaven —
author: Dickinson
summary: Skeptical syllogism on whether earth is heaven; faith and doubt about heaven, paradox, the divine and the here.

title: 141. Some, too fragile for winter winds
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegy figuring the grave as a tender nest for children who died young; meditates on death, grief and divine care through nature imagery.

title: 1410. I shall not murmur if at last
author: Dickinson
summary: Posthumous wish that loved ones understand why she shunned them; grief, loss, silence, self withheld, tears over treason.

title: 1412. Shame is the shawl of Pink
author: Dickinson
cluster: Guilt · Conscience · Fate and Free Will
summary: Shame defined as a divine pink veil over the soul; abstract definition of shame, the soul, conscience, clothing as metaphor.

title: 1413. Sweet Skepticism of the Heart —
author: Dickinson
summary: Doubt cherished because certainty would be sere; faith and doubt, truth deferred, the thrill of suspended knowing.

title: 1415. A wild Blue sky abreast of Winds
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: The defiant sun crouches behind a door against threatening winds; nature personified as conflict, wind, sun, sky.

title: 1416. Crisis is sweet and yet the Heart
author: Dickinson
summary: The closing rose prefers its rescinded bud; anticipation sweeter than fulfillment, transience, the rose, paradox of desire.

title: 1417. How Human Nature dotes
author: Dickinson
summary: Human nature dotes on the undetectable; the lure of mystery and the unanswerable question of the afterlife.

title: 1418. How lonesome the Wind must feel Nights —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: The wind personified across night, noon, and morning moods; nature, wind, night, dawn, solitude and grandeur.

title: 1419. It was a quiet seeming Day —
author: Dickinson
summary: A calm day erupts into apocalyptic dissolution at sunset; terror and the sublime, sudden death/destruction, appearance vs reality.

title: 142. Whose are the little beds, I asked
author: Dickinson
summary: A fanciful lyric naming flowers as children tucked into beds by a maternal Nature, awaiting spring's awakening; nature, sleep and renewal.

title: 1420. One Joy of so much anguish
author: Dickinson
summary: Birdsong stabs the spirit with painful joy whose meaning waits for death; joy fused with anguish, birds, music, death's answer.

title: 1422. Summer has two Beginnings —
author: Dickinson
summary: Summer's June and October beginnings; 'Forever is deciduous except to those who die'; seasons, transience, immortality through death.

title: 1424. The Gentian has a parched Corolla —
author: Dickinson
summary: The late gentian aids the aged year to an abundant end; fidelity as gain, flowers, autumn, the natural order, truth.

title: 1425. The inundation of the Spring
author: Dickinson
summary: Spring's flood enlarges and estranges then acclimates the soul; spring, water/flood, the soul, transformation, faith.

title: 1426. The pretty Rain from those sweet Eaves
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: Tears ('Rain from sweet Eaves') as an involuntary crowning of feeling; emotion, eyes, innocence overcome by fervor.

title: 1427. To earn it by disdaining it
author: Dickinson
summary: Fame pursues those who spurn it; gather life's bouquet for honor not shame; ambition, fame, carpe diem, honour.

title: 1428. Water makes many Beds
author: Dickinson
summary: Water as a fathomless bed/grave for the drowned; death by water, the sea, the grave, terror of the boundless.

title: 143. For every Bird a Nest —
author: Dickinson
summary: A bird-fable contrasting the aspiring Wren's pride with the humble Lark's joy; meditates on humility, pride and contentment in nature.

title: 1430. Who never wanted — maddest Joy
author: Dickinson
cluster: Greek Mythology · Lust Sexual Desire · Desire
summary: Unfulfilled desire surpasses the actual, lest realization disenthrall the soul; desire, abstemiousness, joy, the soul.

title: 1431. With Pinions of Disdain
author: Dickinson
summary: The soul flies free of the body toward immortality; soul vs flesh, transcendence, immortality, the self and soul.

title: 1433. How brittle are the Piers
author: Dickinson
summary: Faith as a brittle yet crowded bridge tested and pronounced firm by Christ; faith and doubt, the Bible, providence.

title: 1434. Go not too near a House of Rose —
author: Dickinson
summary: Joy is preserved by insecurity; do not grasp the rose or tie the butterfly; transience, beauty, the rose, desire's distance.

title: 1436. Than Heaven more remote,
author: Dickinson
summary: The dead, 'flitted seed,' are more remote than heaven yet absolute as God; death, immortality, grief, faith.

title: 1437. A Dew sufficed itself —
author: Dickinson
summary: A self-contented dew vanishes by sun's doom; the awful tragedy of transience and the instability of transport.

title: 1438. Behold this little Bane —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Love defined as both bane and boon, woe and wound; abstract definition of love as paradox even in Paradise.

title: 144. She bore it till the simple veins
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegy on a patient woman's suffering, death and translation to a heavenly court of crowns and courtiers; grief, immortality and faith.

title: 1440. The healed Heart shows its shallow scar
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A heart that heals too easily shames true grief; grief and loss, fidelity, the scar, the shallowness of recovery.

title: 1441. These Fevered Days — to take them to the Forest
author: Dickinson
cluster: Ode · Nature vs Civilization · Pastoral Retreat
summary: Fevered days longing for the cool, still forest; nature as retreat and refuge, pastoral stillness and water.

title: 1442. To mend each tattered Faith
author: Dickinson
summary: Short lyric on repairing faith with an invisible, air-threaded needle; themes of faith, doubt and spiritual mending.

title: 1443. A chilly Peace infests the Grass
author: Dickinson
summary: Late-autumn nature lyric where the stilled, frost-touched landscape figures death's universal peace delivering all mankind.

title: 1444. A little Snow was here and there
author: Dickinson
summary: Lyric of aging in which decades and snow touch the hair, yet the rose of summer remains indelible against time and decay.

title: 1445. Death is the supple Suitor
author: Dickinson
summary: Personifies Death as a stealthy wooing suitor who wins at last and bears the soul away to an unknown troth; mortality as courtship.

title: 1446. His Mind like Fabrics of the East
author: Dickinson
summary: A mind displayed like priceless Eastern fabric whose only price is comprehension; meditation on worth, value and the rare understanding eye.

title: 1448. How soft a Caterpillar steps —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Close observation of a caterpillar's soundless velvet travel across the hand; nature, wonder and the self-absorbed indifference of the creature.

title: 1449. I thought the Train would never come —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Anticipation of a lover's arrival; rehearsed speech flies away on his coming, a halcyon misery atoned by happiness — romantic longing.

title: 145. This heart that broke so long —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A brief elegy committing a faithful, long-suffering heart to the dead, safe from pursuit; death, grief and faith watched in vain.

title: 1450. The Road was lit with Moon and star —
author: Dickinson
summary: A moonlit road and a traveller ascending a hill toward an unknown shimmering ultimate; the journey as spiritual ascent.

title: 1452. Your thoughts don't have words every day
author: Dickinson
summary: Rare, wordless thoughts likened to communion wine — sacramental and infrequent; the inexpressible value of inspiration.

title: 1453. A Counterfeit — a Plated Person —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: Refuses to be a counterfeit, plated person; truth as health and safety, the lie as meagre exile — integrity versus deception.

title: 1454. Those not live yet
author: Dickinson
summary: Cryptic meditation on death as the hyphen of the sea and 'costumeless consciousness'; mortality, immortality and bare being.

title: 1459. Belshazzar had a Letter —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: The biblical writing on the wall reread as conscience's immortal letter to all; sin, judgment and revelation.

title: 146. On such a night, or such a night,
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegy on the quiet death of a child figured as slipping asleep, recalling busy little feet now stilled; death, sleep and grief.

title: 1461. "Heavenly Father" — take to thee
author: Dickinson
summary: Ironic apology to God for the sin he himself fashioned, charging the Creator with duplicity; doubt, the fall and theological paradox.

title: 1462. We knew not that we were to live —
author: Dickinson
summary: We wear mortality lightly until God's intrusion makes it known; ignorance as armor, life and death uncertain.

title: 1463. A Route of Evanescence
author: Dickinson
summary: Famed riddle-lyric on the hummingbird as a revolving wheel of emerald and cochineal; transience, fleeting beauty and nature's evanescence.

title: 1464. One thing of it we borrow
author: Dickinson
summary: Experience borrowed and returned, its sweetness paid for by sorrow; the coveted power to forget and the avarice of memory.

title: 1465. Before you thought of Spring
author: Dickinson
summary: The early bird heralds spring, shouting for joy to nobody but its seraphic self; nature, song and the herald of the seasons.

title: 1466. One of the ones that Midas touched
author: Dickinson
summary: The golden oriole celebrated through Midas and Jason's Golden Fleece myth; nature, song, beauty and classical allusion.

title: 1468. A winged spark doth soar about —
author: Dickinson
summary: A firefly-like winged spark perceived only by its absence; transient rapture, light against the dark and elusive joy.

title: 147. Bless God, he went as soldiers,
author: Dickinson
cluster: War and its Cost · American Civil War · Battlefield
summary: A martial prayer for a soldier going bravely to war, the speaker emboldened by faith; war, heroism and faith, with Civil War resonance.

title: 1471. Their Barricade against the Sky
author: Dickinson
summary: Autumn's russet trees rendered as withdrawing armies and a 'Massacre of Air'; seasons, decay and a martial metaphor of nature's dying.

title: 1473. We talked with each other about each other
author: Dickinson
summary: Wordless communion before the hoofs of the clock, time offering arks of reprieve; intimacy, mortality and the pressure of time.

title: 1475. Fame is the one that does not stay —
author: Dickinson
summary: Fame as transient lightning that demands the flame; the fleeting nature of glory and the artist's relation to renown.

title: 1476. His voice decrepit was with Joy —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A lovers' tottering interview where the ancient news of love makes lips elderly with delight, woe or terror; romantic love and its intensity.

title: 1479. The Devil — had he fidelity
author: Dickinson
cluster: Temptation · Good vs Evil · Serpent Snake
summary: Witty epigram: the Devil's ability would make him the best friend were he not faithless; sin, perfidy and theological paradox.

title: 148. All overgrown by cunning moss,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: An elegy for Charlotte Bronte ('Currer Bell') buried at Haworth, her anguish reaching heavenly Eden; death, grief and redemption through suffering.

title: 1480. The fascinating chill that music leaves
author: Dickinson
summary: The chill music leaves as earth's corroboration of ecstasy's impediment, wooing us upward but not to the Creator; music, rapture and faith.

title: 1481. The way Hope builds his House
author: Dickinson
summary: Hope builds a sill-less house of pure pinnacle; an abstract emblem of hope as supreme, groundless edifice.

title: 1482. 'Tis whiter than an Indian Pipe —
author: Dickinson
summary: A pale, fog-like spirit each of us shall become; the limitless hyperbole of the soul, drama or tragedy after death — mortality and the uncanny.

title: 1483. The Robin is a Gabriel
author: Dickinson
summary: The robin domesticated as a humble New England Gabriel of the working classes; nature, birds, the common man and gentle New England satire.

title: 1487. The Savior must have been
author: Dickinson
summary: Christ as a docile gentleman who came far on a cold day for little fellowmen, levelling the road to Bethlehem; faith, grace and the incarnation.

title: 149. She went as quiet as the Dew
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A brief elegy comparing a woman's quiet, irrecoverable death to dew and a fallen star; death, grief and the difficulty of belief.

title: 1490. The Face in evanescence lain
author: Dickinson
summary: The dead face grown more distinct than the living, ours surrendered for its sake; mortality, transience and divine detriment.

title: 1491. The Road to Paradise is plain,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: The plain narrow road to paradise holds scarce one, its belles few; salvation, humility and the hard way of redemption.

title: 1492. "And with what body do they come?" —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: An ecstatic riff on Paul's resurrection question, the soul rejoicing that the dead come with a real face and eyes; faith, immortality and the body's return.

title: 1495. The Thrill came slowly like a Boom for
author: Dickinson
summary: A long-delayed thrill swelling like a flood into ravished holiness; rapture, ecstasy and the slow growth of joy out of desolation.

title: 1496. All that I do
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: All the speaker does reviewed by an enamored omnipresent eye awaiting her as a bride; love, surveillance and the bride motif, devotional or amorous.

title: 1497. Facts by our side are never sudden
author: Dickinson
summary: Death the portentous neighbor whose height we never know till an adieu summons us; mortality, the spectral and our ignorance of resumption.

title: 1498. Glass was the Street — in tinsel Peril
author: Dickinson
summary: An icy street of sleds and merry boys, the past's supreme italic making the present mean; winter, childhood, memory and nostalgia.

title: 1499. How firm Eternity must look
author: Dickinson
summary: Eternity the only adamant estate to crumbling, insecure mortals whose identity coheres only in it; immortality, faith and mortal insecurity.

title: 15. The Guest is gold and crimson —
author: Dickinson
cluster: White and Red · Riddle · Secrecy and Concealment
summary: A riddle-lyric personifying the autumn sunset (or a migrating season) as a richly robed guest stopping at every door; nature, color and transience.

title: 150. She died — this was the way she died.
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A spare elegy narrating a death as a departure toward the sun, spied by angels at the gate; death, immortality and grief.

title: 1500. It came his turn to beg —
author: Dickinson
summary: Begging for life is penury in chief; the speaker grants a smuggled reprieve lest gratitude revive the snake — mercy, power over a life and lurking sin.

title: 1503. More than the Grave is closed to me —
author: Dickinson
summary: Both the grave and its eternity closed to the speaker, who clings to nowhere till falling into the crash of nothing-yet-all; mortality, despair and the void.

title: 1506. Summer is shorter than any one —
author: Dickinson
summary: Summer shorter than anyone, life shorter than summer, seventy years spent like a single dollar; transience, the brevity of life and seasons.

title: 1507. The Pile of Years is not so high
author: Dickinson
summary: A short lyric on the accumulating weight of time and memory after loss; the speaker begs the absent beloved's face to efface the mountain of years and catch her before she falls.

title: 1508. You cannot make Remembrance grow
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric using horticultural imagery to argue that genuine memory is rooted, indestructible (shod with adamant), and cannot be artificially cultivated or cut down.

title: 1509. Mine Enemy is growing old —
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric on revenge and hate as appetite: as the enemy ages, the relish of vengeance fades, for anger fed dies while starvation makes it fat.

title: 1510. How happy is the little Stone
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: A lyric praising the carefree humility and self-sufficiency of a roadside stone, fulfilling absolute Decree in casual simplicity, indifferent to careers and fears.

title: 1511. My country need not change her gown,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nationalism and Patriotism · Democracy · Liberty Political Freedom
summary: A patriotic lyric figuring the American nation as a woman whose triple-suit gown, cut at Lexington, still defies Great Britain's disapproval with its bayonet.

title: 1515. The Things that never can come back, are several —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Ruins the Abbey · Sic Transit Gloria Mundi · Ubi Sunt
summary: A meditative lyric on irrecoverable losses (Childhood, Hope, the Dead), contrasting travelers who return with the spirit's one-way journey to its Native Land.

title: 1519. The Dandelion's pallid tube
author: Dickinson
summary: A nature lyric in which the dandelion's bud and shouting flower proclaim, like a resurrection, that winter's sepulture is over.

title: 152. The Sun kept stooping — stooping — low!
author: Dickinson
