summary: An offer of shared heights and secrets refused by the beloved, then a renunciatory glow; unrequited love and self-revelation.

title: 448. This was a Poet — It is That
author: Dickinson
summary: Definition of the poet who distills amazing sense from ordinary meanings, a fortune exterior to time; on art and immortality.

title: 449. I died for Beauty — but was scarce
author: Dickinson
summary: Two dead, one for beauty one for truth, declare them one and talk until the moss covers their names; beauty, truth and mortality.

title: 45. There's something quieter than sleep
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a corpse laid out in the inner room, quieter than sleep, mourners' euphemisms and the speaker's wry distance; death, grief and periphrasis.

title: 450. Dreams — are well — but Waking's better,
author: Dickinson
summary: Weighs dream against waking, surmised dawn against a solid dawn that leads to no day; a meditation on hope, illusion and disappointment.

title: 451. The Outer — from the Inner
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: The inner self paints the outer life; soul as the unvarying axis of the spinning wheel, appearance deriving from inner reality.

title: 452. The Malay — took the Pearl —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Allegory of unattainable love: the reverent speaker loses the pearl/jewel to a bolder, less worthy diver; desire, daring versus worthiness.

title: 453. Love — thou art high —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Love addressed as a high mountain, deep sea, and veiled mystery reaching toward eternity; love as a divine, near-unattainable sublime.

title: 454. It was given to me by the Gods —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: A childhood gift, named Gold/Riches, guarded jealously; identity, wealth as inward possession and the boldness it confers.

title: 457. Sweet — safe — Houses —
author: Dickinson
summary: The sealed graves/tombs as 'safe houses' where Death and Sickness cannot intrude; an ironic meditation on the security of the dead.

title: 458. Like eyes that looked on Wastes —
author: Dickinson
summary: Two faces mirror each other's desolation; a shared, hopeless yet divine misery of mutual recognition and doomed union.

title: 459. A Tooth upon Our Peace
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: Pain vitalizes grace; heaven needs a hell to signalize itself, every sign gilt with sacrifice; paradox of suffering and redemption.

title: 46. I keep my pledge.
author: Dickinson
summary: A vow-lyric: spared by death, the speaker renews her pledge with a rose, sworn by bee, daisy and bobolink that blossom and soul will come again; faith, fidelity and renewal.

title: 460. I know where Wells grow — Droughtless Wells —
author: Dickinson
summary: An inaccessible inner well of water/faith contrasted with the Bible's promise that people 'thirst no more'; thirst, doubt and the homely over the grand.

title: 461. A Wife — at daybreak I shall be —
author: Dickinson
summary: Marriage figured as death and transfiguration at dawn; passage from maid/child to bride to eternity, meeting the Savior's face.

title: 462. Why make it doubt — it hurts it so —
author: Dickinson
summary: The agony of doubt on a deathbed-like little bed; fear of having offended the beloved Master and being forgotten — misery of uncertainty.

title: 463. I live with Him — I see His face —
author: Dickinson
summary: A spiritual marriage to Him (Christ/beloved) witnessing the certainty of immortality; life as stopless beyond judgment.

title: 464. The power to be true to You,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Fidelity to the beloved until Judgment, valued above heaven itself; love as devotion exceeding divine invitation.

title: 465. I heard a Fly buzz — when I died —
author: Dickinson
summary: Iconic deathbed scene: stillness, the willed keepsakes, the awaited King, and a trivial fly interposing between the light and dying sight.

title: 466. 'Tis little I — could care for Pearls —
author: Dickinson
summary: The speaker disdains gems and gold, owning sea, mines, and a continual diadem; inner/spiritual wealth surpassing material riches.

title: 467. We do not play on Graves —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: A child's perspective on graves and mourners, avoiding the slanted ground where grief might crush their play; childhood facing death.

title: 468. The Manner of its Death
author: Dickinson
summary: The privilege of choosing the manner of one's death, alluding to Major André; dignity and fate when choice of life is past.

title: 469. The Red — Blaze — is the Morning —
author: Dickinson
summary: The colors of a day's arc — red morning, violet noon, yellow falling day — and the unconsumed silver territory of evening sparks; time and light.

title: 47. Heart! We will forget him!
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A lyric addressing the heart, willing the forgetting of a lost beloved; renunciation and the impossibility of forgetting love.

title: 470. I am alive — I guess —
author: Dickinson
summary: Proofs of being alive — warm carmine, breath on glass, not laid out in the parlor — set against death and a twofold life in 'Thee'.

title: 471. A Night — there lay the Days between —
author: Dickinson
summary: A long night that must be watched away grain by grain, dividing identical days; suffering, time, and the slow vigil of darkness.

title: 472. Except the Heaven had come so near —
author: Dickinson
summary: A nearly-granted heaven/grace that departs, afflicting with a double loss; longing, hope raised then withdrawn.

title: 473. I am ashamed — I hide —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: A dowerless girl, unworthy and unadorned, longing for the new grace and raiment of soul to be baptized a bride; humility, marriage, transformation.

title: 474. They put Us far apart —
author: Dickinson
summary: Two lovers/souls separated by guns, dungeons, and death yet seeing each other across all barriers; martyrdom, fidelity, love conquering persecution.

title: 475. Doom is the House without the Door —
author: Dickinson
summary: Doom as a doorless house entered from the sun with the ladder thrown away — irreversible fate, with the free outside world only dreamed of.

title: 476. I meant to have but modest needs —
author: Dickinson
summary: A modest prayer to Jehovah for a small heaven is met with divine smiles and silence; faith, doubt, and the suspicion of being swindled by promise.

title: 477. No Man can compass a Despair —
author: Dickinson
summary: Despair as a goalless road traveled a mile at a time, the sufferer unconscious of its width; pain, endurance, and merciful ignorance.

title: 478. I had no time to Hate —
author: Dickinson
summary: Life too short and the grave too near for hatred; the little toil of love chosen instead — time, death, and the priority of love over enmity.

title: 479. She dealt her pretty words like Blades —
author: Dickinson
summary: Pretty words wielded like glittering blades that wound the nerve and bone; cruelty unaware of itself and the mortal endurance of pain.

title: 48. Once more, my now bewildered Dove
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: Biblical allusion to Noah's dove (the Patriarch's bird) launched over the deep; faith and hope of finding land amid uncertainty.

title: 480. "Why do I love" You, Sir?
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Love justified by analogy to wind on grass, lightning on the eye, sunrise compelling sight — love as instinctive, reasonless natural compulsion.

title: 482. We Cover Thee — Sweet Face —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Covering the dead's sweet face at burial, with belated, augmented love offered too late; grief, mourning, and the regret of withheld affection.

title: 483. A Solemn thing within the Soul
author: Dickinson
summary: The soul ripening like fruit in the Maker's orchard, the Sun perfecting it as harvest (death) draws nearer; spiritual maturation and mortality.

title: 485. To make One's Toilette — after Death
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: The difficulty of adorning oneself once the beloved who admired it is dead and wrenched away by death's commandments; grief, vanity, and loss.

title: 486. I was the slightest in the House —
author: Dickinson
summary: A self-portrait of the smallest, quietest, noteless dweller with her lamp, book, and geranium; humility, withdrawal, and an unnoticed death.

title: 487. You love the Lord — you cannot see —
author: Dickinson
summary: Contrasts loving an unseen Lord through daily notes/letters with the speaker's own beloved whose house is in Heaven; faith, love, and longing.

title: 488. Myself was formed — a Carpenter —
author: Dickinson
summary: The poet as carpenter who, against the Builder's measure, declares 'We Temples build'; the artist's vocation and self-justification, echoing Christ the carpenter.

title: 489. We pray — to Heaven —
author: Dickinson
summary: Questions what and where Heaven is — a place, a sky, a tree? — for the dead there is no geography but state and omnipresence; faith and doubt.

title: 49. I never lost as much but twice,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Grief over deaths (in the sod), addressing God as banker/father in financial imagery; bereavement and a tone of complaint toward providence.

title: 490. To One denied the drink
author: Dickinson
summary: To describe water or lead the thirsty to a well only sharpens the pain of the denied; deprivation, longing, and the cruelty of near-grace.

title: 491. While it is alive
author: Dickinson
summary: Love as inseparable union sharing one air, blood, and sacrament; love outlasting death, fellow of the resurrection raising the dust to live.

title: 492. Civilization — spurns — the Leopard!
author: Dickinson
summary: The exiled leopard's untamable nature spurned by civilization, her memories of Asia's palms unsuppressed; wild nature versus society, the outcast's identity.

title: 493. The World — stands — solemner — to me —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: The world grown solemn since a spiritual wedding to Him; modesty, gratitude, and a dream too beautiful for shape to prove — marriage as transfiguration.

title: 494. Going to Him! Happy letter!
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A love-letter personified as messenger to the beloved, dramatizing the lover's nervous, secret longing and the act of writing.

title: 495. It's thoughts — and just One Heart —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Ode · Nature vs Civilization · Pastoral Retreat
summary: Praises a frugal contentment of small domestic riches — books, a picture, flowers, a bird — approaching but not quite immortality.

title: 496. As far from pity, as complaint —
author: Dickinson
summary: Contrasts the numbness of the dead in the sepulchre with the blazing color and life of butterflies above.

title: 497. He strained my faith —
author: Dickinson
summary: The speaker endures wracking trials of faith yet never doubts the divine tormentor, addressing Jesus as 'little John'.

title: 498. I envy Seas, whereon He rides —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A jealous catalogue of everything that may approach the unattainable beloved, ending in fear of eternal separation.

title: 499. Those fair — fictitious People —
author: Dickinson
summary: Meditates on the dead, imagined as figures in portraits now admitted Home, while the living remain in exile, awaiting death.

title: 5. I have a Bird in spring
author: Dickinson
summary: A consolation lyric on the departure and promised return of a beloved (figured as a bird) held safe in a 'truer Land'; loss, faith and reunion.

title: 50. I haven't told my garden yet —
author: Dickinson
summary: Anticipation of the speaker's own death, kept secret from garden, bee, hills and forests; nature, mortality and the riddle of dying.

title: 500. Within my Garden, rides a Bird
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: A hummingbird in the garden becomes a riddle of perception, blurring inner imagination and outer nature.

title: 501. This World is not Conclusion.
author: Dickinson
summary: Asserts an invisible immortal realm beyond death while dramatizing the restless oscillation of faith and doubt.

title: 502. At least — to pray — is left — is left —
author: Dickinson
summary: A desperate prayer knocking everywhere for an absent Jesus, demanding rescue amid earthquake and maelstrom.

title: 503. Better — than Music! For I — who heard it —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: An ineffable music surpassing all tunes, linked to Eden's brooks and the soul's rehearsal for heaven.

title: 504. You know that Portrait in the Moon —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: The beloved's face glimpsed in the moon's changing phases, an image of longing across separation.

title: 505. I would not paint — a picture —
author: Dickinson
summary: An ars poetica preferring to be the awed recipient of art's power rather than its maker, exploring imagination and the sublime.

title: 506. He touched me, so I live to know
author: Dickinson
cluster: Greek Mythology · Lust Sexual Desire · Desire
summary: A transfiguring touch from the beloved that ennobles and transforms the speaker, framed in religious and pilgrimage imagery.

title: 507. She sights a Bird — she chuckles —
author: Dickinson
summary: A cat stalking a robin that escapes, a vivid emblem of predatory nature and frustrated hope.

title: 508. I'm ceded — I've stopped being Theirs —
author: Dickinson
summary: A self-baptism of conscious choice, the speaker crowning herself a queen of her own identity, rejecting an inherited name.

title: 509. If anybody's friend be dead
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Grief that fixes on remembered living details of the dead, who have become a grand, estranged thing in the sepulchre.

title: 51. I often passed the village
author: Dickinson
summary: The village is the graveyard; the speaker foresees her early death and offers consoling comfort from beneath the mould.

title: 510. It was not Death, for I stood up,
author: Dickinson
summary: A famous anatomy of despair by negation, naming a chaos-like inner state worse than death, night, frost, or fire.

title: 511. If you were coming in the Fall,
author: Dickinson
summary: Conditional waiting for a beloved across seasons and eternity, tormented by the uncertainty of time's length.

title: 512. The Soul has Bandaged moments —
author: Dickinson
summary: Charts the soul's oscillation between terror, ecstatic escape, and recapture, with goblin and felon imagery of psychic horror.

title: 513. Like Flowers, that heard the news of Dews,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: Heaven arrives unexpectedly to those who never presumed to hope for it, figured through flowers, bees, and arctic creatures.

title: 514. Her smile was shaped like other smiles —
author: Dickinson
summary: A wounded bird hoisting itself to sing despite a remembered shot embodies concealed pain behind an ordinary smile.

title: 515. No Crowd that has occurred
author: Dickinson
summary: Imagines the General Resurrection as the vastest assembly, dust reconnecting to life, each consciousness facing its individual doom.

title: 516. Beauty — be not caused — It Is —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: An aphoristic claim that beauty cannot be pursued or caused but only exists, ungraspable as wind on a meadow.

title: 517. He parts Himself — like Leaves —
author: Dickinson
summary: Traces a butterfly's playful flight through flowers and its mysterious transformation, ending in cocoon, sepulchre, and abbey imagery.

title: 518. Her sweet Weight on my Heart a Night
author: Dickinson
summary: A beloved bride present for a night then vanishing, blurring dream, reality, and faith in a fiction more real than belief.

title: 519. 'Twas warm — at first — like Us —
author: Dickinson
summary: A clinical depiction of a body cooling into death, chilling and stiffening until lowered like a weight into the grave.

title: 52. Whether my bark went down at sea —
author: Dickinson
summary: The soul/ship as bark at sea, wondering where it is moored now; the sea as figure for death and the uncertain afterlife.

title: 520. I started Early — Took my Dog —
author: Dickinson
summary: A walk to the sea where the tide pursues the speaker like a courtly, threatening lover before withdrawing, fusing desire and death.

title: 521. Endow the Living — with the Tears —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: An admonition to cherish the living rather than squander tears on the dead, who scorn such belated care.

title: 522. Had I presumed to hope —
author: Dickinson
summary: A meditation on renounced hope as 'Confident Despair' that becomes an honor justified only by death.

title: 523. Sweet — You forgot — but I remembered
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: The faithful remembering lover, figured as a beggar spending guineas of devotion, shut out by the forgetful beloved.

title: 524. Departed — to the Judgment —
author: Dickinson
summary: Stages the soul's departure to Last Judgment as a cosmic theatre, the flesh cancelled and the soul left alone.

title: 525. I think the Hemlock likes to stand
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: The hemlock thriving on cold and northern winds becomes an emblem of austere temperament and the awe of wilderness.

title: 526. To hear an Oriole sing
author: Dickinson
summary: Argues that the meaning of birdsong lies in the perceiving ear, not the bird — beauty and divinity are 'within Thee'.

title: 527. To put this World down, like a Bundle —
author: Dickinson
summary: Renunciation of the world figured as the 'Scarlet way' of Christ's crucifixion, with Pilate, Barabbas, and the Eucharistic cup.

title: 528. Mine — by the Right of the White Election!
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: A triumphant assertion of possession by divine election and royal seal, claiming a right confirmed beyond the grave.

title: 529. I'm sorry for the Dead — Today —
author: Dickinson
summary: Pities the dead for being shut out of the homely rural pleasures of haying season, imagining their lonesome homesickness.

title: 53. Taken from men — this morning —
author: Dickinson
summary: Death of a child taken to Eden, met by the gods with banners; elegy imagining heaven as a kingdom of courtiers.

title: 530. You cannot put a Fire out —
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphorism on the irrepressible nature of vital forces — fire and flood — that cannot be contained or hidden away.

title: 531. We dream — it is good we are dreaming —
author: Dickinson
summary: Treats life as a protective dream or drama, safer than the granite reality of death waiting beyond waking.

title: 532. I tried to think a lonelier Thing
author: Dickinson
summary: Seeks comfort by imagining a doppelganger of equal loneliness, a mutual pity across the partition of separate cells of horror.

title: 533. Two butterflies went out at Noon —
author: Dickinson
summary: Two butterflies dance off into the firmament and a shining ether-sea, vanishing without trace into infinity.

title: 534. We see — Comparatively —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Ruins the Abbey · Sic Transit Gloria Mundi · Ubi Sunt
summary: Loss reframes perspective: what loomed towering is reduced once relinquished to God's firmament, treating anguish as kindly preparation.

title: 535. She's happy, with a new Content —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A woman's joyful new vocation felt as sacrament, a humble blessed fate of ministering, fusing love and religion.

title: 536. The Heart asks Pleasure — first —
author: Dickinson
summary: A descending sequence of the heart's diminishing requests ending in the liberty to die, granted by its 'Inquisitor.'

title: 537. Me prove it now — Whoever doubt
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Drowning rising-water imagery as the ultimate proof of love, testing devotion through death.

title: 538. 'Tis true — They shut me in the Cold —
author: Dickinson
summary: Speaker forgives those who wronged her, asking God's mercy on them, conditioning her own pardon on theirs.

title: 539. The Province of the Saved
author: Dickinson
summary: Only one who has endured dissolution in himself can qualify others' despair; salvation as a hard-won science of the grave.

title: 54. If I should die,
author: Dickinson
summary: The world's commerce and nature continue indifferently after one's death; an ironic meditation on mortality and the persistence of ordinary life.

title: 540. I took my Power in my Hand —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Swords and Weapons · Power and Corruption · Tyrant
summary: David-and-Goliath defiance: the speaker goes against the World, but it is she who falls, questioning her own smallness.

title: 541. Some such Butterfly be seen
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief noon-licensed beauty of butterfly and spice, transient and seizable only for a moment, like stars turned foreign by morning.

title: 542. I had no Cause to be awake —
author: Dickinson
summary: After loved ones die in sleep, the speaker yearns to share their circumstance and finally struggles through to join them in death.

title: 543. I fear a Man of frugal Speech —
author: Dickinson
summary: The silent, weighing man is feared as potentially Grand, while the talkative are easily managed; silence as power.

title: 544. The Martyr Poets — did not tell —
author: Dickinson
summary: Martyr poets and painters transmute their pang into art so that after death their work encourages others; immortality through verse.

title: 545. 'Tis One by One — the Father counts —
author: Dickinson
summary: God as schoolmaster teaching value through ciphers; the Eternal Rule regards each least pupil's sum alike, an allegory of providence.

title: 547. I've seen a Dying Eye
author: Dickinson
summary: Close observation of a dying eye searching, clouding with fog, and soldered down without disclosing what it saw.

title: 548. Death is potential to that Man
author: Dickinson
summary: Death matters chiefly to the dying man and his friend; God remembers the friend longest, who dissolves into God.

title: 549. That I did always love
author: Dickinson
summary: Love as proof of life, life as immortality; the final proof, if doubted, is Calvary — love as religion.

title: 550. I cross till I am weary
author: Dickinson
summary: An inner quest across mountains, seas, and desert toward Grace and Heaven, questioning whether arrival is death or victory.

title: 551. There is a Shame of Nobleness —
author: Dickinson
summary: The fine shame of the noble and brave at sudden ecstasy or acclaim, with full blessing deferred beyond the grave.

title: 552. An ignorance a Sunset
author: Dickinson
summary: A sunset's amber revelation confers awe and a sublime sense of being detected in immortality under Omnipotence's inspection.

title: 553. One Crucifixion is recorded — only —
author: Dickinson
summary: Only one Crucifixion is recorded, yet each person bears a nearer Calvary and Gethsemane within; universalizing Christ's passion.

title: 554. The Black Berry — wears a Thorn in his side —
author: Dickinson
summary: The blackberry bears its thorn-wound silently yet still offers its fruit, a Christ-like figure of uncomplaining suffering reaching to the sky.

title: 555. Trust in the Unexpected —
author: Dickinson
summary: Trust in the unexpected drove Kidd, the alchemist, Columbus, and doubting Thomas; faith and belief over proof.

title: 556. The Brain, within its Groove
author: Dickinson
summary: The mind runs true in its groove, but a single swerving splinter makes derangement as unstoppable as a flood; madness imagery.

title: 557. She hideth Her the last —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A personified nature-figure (the bee/sunset) doing her purple work and laying herself in the sod, inimitable by human craft.

title: 559. It knew no Medicine —
author: Dickinson
summary: A nameless tint replacing bloom on a face, neither sickness nor pain, hinting at a glimpse of Paradise that sickens with awe.

title: 56. If I should cease to bring a Rose
author: Dickinson
summary: Death imagined as Death's finger stopping the lip and the bringing of roses; flowers, festal ritual and mortality.

title: 560. It knew no lapse, nor Diminuation —
author: Dickinson
summary: A serene burning light that fails from men through dissolution, conceived as undiminished planetary force merely exchanging worlds.

title: 561. I measure every Grief I meet
author: Dickinson
summary: The speaker probes others' griefs against her own, finding comfort in passing Calvary to see crosses like her own; an anatomy of sorrow.

title: 562. Conjecturing a Climate
author: Dickinson
summary: Imagining a warmer climate sharpens winter; fancy turns to a fictitious country to palliate cold that cannot be erased.

title: 563. I could not prove the Years had feet —
author: Dickinson
summary: Time's passage proven by symptoms and outgrown selves; yesterday's ample aims now seem an awkward, outgrown fit.

title: 564. My period had come for Prayer —
author: Dickinson
summary: Ascending to find God, the speaker meets only vast empty prairies of air and faceless infinitude, and worships rather than prays.

title: 565. One Anguish — in a Crowd —
author: Dickinson
summary: A single anguish, like a doe before hounds or a small wound to the vitals, is as consummate as legions; suffering measured by relation.

title: 566. A Dying Tiger — moaned for Drink —
author: Dickinson
summary: The speaker fetches water for a dying tiger but arrives too late; neither's fault, only the bare fact of death.

title: 567. He gave away his Life —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A self-sacrificing figure whose gift of life, magnified by fame, bursts hearts and unrolls on the heavens; a Christ-like martyrdom.

title: 568. We learned the Whole of Love —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: Lovers learn love as an alphabet, book, and revelation, yet in each other's eyes find an ignorance diviner than childhood; love's manifold truth.

title: 569. I reckon — when I count it all —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Poet as Prophet · Prophet · Romantic Movement (Sensibility)
summary: Ranking Poets above Sun, Summer, and Heaven; poets comprehend the whole, their art a near-religious immortal grace.

title: 570. I could die — to know —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Mundane city street life — newsboys, carts, brick houses — frames an aching desire to know the beloved's passing nearness.

title: 571. Must be a Woe —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: Woe and loss are the price that bends the eye toward best beauty; our Lord thought a Cross no extravagance to pay.

title: 572. Delight — becomes pictorial —
author: Dickinson
summary: Delight grows more fair when viewed through pain and impossibility, like an amber mountain that flits to sky when approached.

title: 573. The Test of Love — is Death —
author: Dickinson
summary: Death is the test of love, as Christ 'so loved'; the Cross's request asks acceptance of love's most, overlooking the dust.

title: 574. My first well Day — since many ill —
author: Dickinson
summary: Recovering from illness, the speaker watches personified Summer fade into autumn, weighing loss against the ethereal gain of measuring the grave then the sun.

title: 575. "Heaven" has different Signs — to me —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Noon, dawn, orchards, birds, and sunset are read as earthly signs and symbols of paradise; nature as the book of heaven.

title: 576. I prayed, at first, a little Girl,
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric tracing the speaker's evolution from rote childhood prayer to adult doubt and longing for a God strong enough to steady a precarious life. Themes of faith, doubt, and childhood.

title: 577. If I may have it, when it's dead,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: An impassioned address to a dead lover, anticipating reunion beyond the grave and recounting the cold midnight of grief. Themes of grief, love, death, and immortality.

title: 578. The Body grows without —
author: Dickinson
summary: A compact meditation on the body as the soul's faithful temple, sheltering the spirit in solemn honesty. Themes of self and soul, faith, identity.

title: 579. I had been hungry, all the Years —
author: Dickinson
summary: An allegory of long deprivation: when long-craved plenty finally arrives it sickens and dissatisfies, for hunger belongs to those outside the window. Themes of desire, deprivation, and the loss of longing in fulfillment.

title: 58. Delayed till she had ceased to know —
author: Dickinson
summary: Joy arriving an hour too late, after death; loss, the imperial round of Victory, and the dead crowned as a king.

title: 580. I gave myself to Him —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A betrothal cast in mercantile terms: the mutual contract of love as a daily, risky, never-fully-paid debt. Themes of romantic love, marriage and fidelity, and exchange.

title: 581. I found the words to every thought
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the inexpressible: the one thought language cannot render, like trying to chalk the sun for races nurtured in the dark. Themes of imagination, the limits of art, and the inexpressible.

title: 582. Inconceivably solemn!
author: Dickinson
summary: A meditation on pageantry, flags, and music whose very brilliance pierces and pains the sensitive eye and ear. Themes of beauty, pain, and the sublime.

title: 583. A Toad, can die of Light —
author: Dickinson
summary: A leveling epigram: death is the common right of toad and man, earl and midge, so why swagger? Life alone differs in worth. Themes of mortality, the leveling of death, and humility.

title: 584. It ceased to hurt me, though so slow
author: Dickinson
summary: A retrospective on grief's imperceptible fading into something almost peace, recognized only by looking back. Themes of grief, pain, healing, and memory.

title: 585. I like to see it lap the Miles —
author: Dickinson
summary: A riddling personification of the railway train as a docile yet omnipotent animal lapping miles and neighing like Boanerges. Themes of nature versus the machine, wonder, and the natural order.

title: 586. We talked as Girls do —
author: Dickinson
summary: Two girls speculate on their futures and avoid the subject of the grave, until Heaven makes their parting contract impossible before another night. Themes of friendship, mortality, and lost futures.

title: 587. Empty my Heart, of Thee —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A lyric arguing that to subtract the beloved is to annihilate the self, the heavens, and eternity itself. Themes of romantic love, identity, and self defined by the beloved.

title: 588. I cried at Pity — not at Pain —
author: Dickinson
summary: A speaker, accustomed to deprivation, is undone not by pain but by a stranger's pity, and dreads being mourned as dead. Themes of pity, poverty, alienation, and grief.

title: 589. The Night was wide, and furnished scant
author: Dickinson
summary: A bleak November night scene of wind, sleet, and a solitary star, with a housewife drawing close to the fire and longing for an absent companion. Themes of loneliness, longing, and winter desolation.

title: 59. A little East of Jordan,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: Retelling of Jacob wrestling the angel at Peniel; biblical narrative of striving with God and winning a blessing.

title: 590. Did you ever stand in a Cavern's Mouth —
author: Dickinson
summary: An interrogation of dread: the goblin horror of a cavern and the face of a cannon, likening loneliness and the question of death to extreme terror. Themes of terror, loneliness, and the threat of death.

title: 591. To interrupt His Yellow Plan
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: The sun pursues his majestic plan unperturbed by snow or weather, while humans presume their own busyness greater. Themes of the natural order, providence, and human self-importance.

title: 592. What care the Dead, for Chanticleer —
author: Dickinson
summary: A grim catalogue of the dead's indifference to cockcrow, sunrise, summer, winter, and birdsong. Themes of death, oblivion, and the insensibility of the grave.

title: 593. I think I was enchanted
author: Dickinson
summary: A tribute to reading a 'Foreign Lady' (Barrett Browning) as a conversion of the mind, a divine insanity that transfigured all nature into magic. Themes of imagination, poetic conversion, and the witchcraft of art.

title: 594. The Battle fought between the Soul
author: Dickinson
summary: The greatest of all battles is the invisible, unrecorded inner campaign of the soul against itself. Themes of the inner life, self and soul, and unseen spiritual struggle.

title: 595. Like Mighty Foot Lights — burned the Red
author: Dickinson
summary: A sunset rendered as theatrical footlights applauded by the universe, with God distinguished as chief of the crowd. Themes of nature as spectacle, the sublime, and wonder.

title: 596. When I was small, a Woman died —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: An elegy for a Civil War soldier killed on the Potomac, reunited in vision with his dead mother, with reflections on pride and bravery in Paradise. Themes of war and its cost, heroism, death, and grief.

title: 597. It always felt to me — a wrong
author: Dickinson
summary: A protest at God's treatment of Moses, allowed to see Canaan but not enter, dwelling on divine injustice and tantalizing play. Themes of justice, faith and doubt, and quarrel with providence.

title: 598. Three times — we parted — Breath — and I —
author: Dickinson
summary: A near-drowning narrated as three partings with breath, ending in survival as the sunrise kisses the speaker's chrysalis back to life. Themes of mortality, survival, and rebirth.

title: 599. There is a pain — so utter —
author: Dickinson
summary: A definition of pain so total it swallows substance and covers the abyss with trance so memory can cross it safely. Themes of pain, suffering, and psychic survival.

title: 6. Frequently the woods are pink
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A brief riddling lyric on the seasonal turning of the woods and the wonder of the earth's rotation through the twelve months.

title: 60. Like her the Saints retire,
author: Dickinson
summary: Flowers (aster, daffodil) and sunset compared to departed saints; nature, death as 'gathering away,' and intimations of immortality.

title: 600. It troubled me as once I was —
author: Dickinson
summary: From childhood the speaker is troubled by how the heavens hold without a bolt, a metaphysical puzzle to be solved only above. Themes of doubt, wonder, and the riddle of the cosmic order.

title: 601. A still — Volcano — Life —
author: Dickinson
summary: An interior life imaged as a still volcano whose hidden, torrid power could make cities ooze away. Themes of repressed passion, the hidden self, and latent destructive force.

title: 602. Of Brussels — it was not —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A riddle naming autumn's fallen leaves as a carpet the winds bought of the woods, with the wind as upholsterer of pines and pond. Themes of nature, the seasons, and humble beauty.

title: 603. He found my Being — set it up —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lover or God sets up the speaker's being, carves his name, and bids it stay faithful until his return with equipage of amber. Themes of devotion, fidelity, and faithful waiting.

title: 604. Unto my Books — so good to turn —
author: Dickinson
summary: A grateful celebration of books as kinsmen of the shelf, a holiday that excludes the night and turns pain to praise. Themes of reading, imagination, and consolation through art.

title: 605. The Spider holds a Silver Ball
author: Dickinson
summary: The spider as silent artist spinning continents of light in an hour, only to be swept away and his boundaries forgotten. Themes of the artist's labor, transience, and unrewarded creation.

title: 606. The Trees like Tassels — hit — and swung —
author: Dickinson
summary: An ecstatic catalogue of a summer day's creatures, sun, birds, snake, and flowers, declared beyond mention compared to Vandyke's painting. Themes of nature, wonder, and the inexpressible beauty of creation.

title: 607. Of nearness to her sundered Things
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: The soul's special times when the buried dead seem to dwell near, the grave yielding back its robberies as bright apparitions. Themes of grief, memory, and the felt presence of the dead.

title: 608. Afraid! Of whom am I afraid?
author: Dickinson
summary: A defiant catechism dismissing fear of Death, Life, and Resurrection through trust in the Father's lodge. Themes of faith, fearlessness before death, and assured immortality.

title: 609. I Years had been from Home
author: Dickinson
summary: A returning exile dreads to enter the old home, finally fleeing in terror like a thief from a door he cannot open. Themes of return, dread, alienation, and the irrecoverable past.

title: 610. You'll find — it when you try to die —
author: Dickinson
summary: Dying grows easier because the remembered dead draw one onward, the former love growing distincter and superseding the fresh. Themes of death, grief, and the pull of the beloved dead.

title: 611. I see thee better — in the Dark —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Love makes the beloved most visible in darkness and even in the grave, the dark surpassing the sun at meridian. Themes of love, paradox, and devotion beyond death.

title: 612. It would have starved a Gnat —
author: Dickinson
summary: The speaker's starved, confined existence is less free than a gnat's, denied even the gnat's power to fly off or end itself. Themes of deprivation, confinement, and helpless suffering.

title: 613. They shut me up in Prose —
author: Dickinson
summary: A declaration of imaginative freedom: shut up in prose like a girl in a closet, the mind, like a caged bird or a star, abolishes captivity at will. Themes of imagination, female confinement, and artistic liberty.

title: 614. In falling Timbers buried —
author: Dickinson
summary: A man buried under fallen timbers is dug out only to die, the rescue ironically becoming death, named the grace of death. Themes of mortality, suffering, futility, and death as deliverance.

title: 615. Our journey had advanced —
author: Dickinson
summary: Life's journey reaches the fork into Eternity, with the Forest of the Dead between, no retreat, and God at every gate. Themes of mortality, the soul's journey, and the threshold of eternity.

title: 616. I rose — because He sank —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric in which the speaker tends and uplifts a dying man with hymns and faith, promising worlds where 'Emperors grew'; meditates on death, the soul, and immortality. Form: lyric.

title: 617. Don't put up my Thread and Needle —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: An invalid/dying speaker promises to sew fine stitches when strong again, dreaming of stitching in sleep; figures illness, will, and the persistence of consciousness. Form: lyric.

title: 618. At leisure is the Soul
author: Dickinson
summary: A short lyric on the soul stunned by a 'Staggering Blow' of grief, begging for humble work to fill its vacant hands. Themes: grief, the soul, suffering. Form: lyric.

title: 619. Glee — The great storm is over —
author: Dickinson
summary: A ballad-like lyric of a shipwreck: four saved, forty drowned; ringing and tolling, then silence as children ask after the lost. Themes: death, grief, the sea. Form: ballad/lyric.

title: 62. "Sown in dishonor"!
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: Witty challenge to Paul's 1 Corinthians 15 on the resurrection body 'sown in dishonor / corruption'; faith, doubt and bodily resurrection.

title: 620. It makes no difference abroad —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Nature continues indifferent to human suffering, judgment and Calvary; the bee's only misery is parting from his rose. Themes: nature's indifference, transience, faith. Form: lyric.

title: 621. I asked no other thing —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: The speaker offers her whole Being to a 'mighty merchant' for one thing and is dismissed; an allegory of denied desire and bargaining with God/fate. Form: lyric/allegory.

title: 622. To know just how He suffered — would be dear —
author: Dickinson
summary: An anxious meditation imagining the last moments and consciousness of a dying beloved, his thoughts of home and God. Themes: death, grief, faith, immortality. Form: lyric.

title: 623. It was too late for Man —
author: Dickinson
summary: When human help fails, prayer and God remain; heaven is most welcome when earth cannot be had. Themes: faith, providence, prayer. Form: lyric/hymn.

title: 624. Forever — is composed of Nows —
author: Dickinson
summary: A philosophical lyric arguing eternity is made of present moments; time and infinity collapsed into the now. Themes: time, immortality, eternity. Form: lyric.

title: 625. 'Twas a long Parting — but the time
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Two 'Fleshless Lovers' reunite before the Judgment Seat of God in a heavenly bridal; love consummated in eternity. Themes: love, immortality, resurrection. Form: lyric.

title: 626. Only God — detect the Sorrow —
author: Dickinson
summary: A terse lyric: only the Trinity perceives and keeps secret the speaker's sorrow. Themes: grief, divine confidence, the soul. Form: lyric.

title: 627. The Tint I cannot take — is best —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: On the inexpressible beauty in nature and sky that eludes capture, leaving the soul in exquisite discontent until the grave offers 'another way to see'. Themes: beauty, the sublime, inexpressibility. Form: lyric.

title: 628. They called me to the Window, for
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A sunset transforms into a jewelled vision of farm, sea and ships that the 'Showman' then rubs away; nature as fleeting illusion and spectacle. Themes: transience, imagination, beauty. Form: lyric.

title: 629. I watched the Moon around the House
author: Dickinson
summary: The speaker watches the moon as a serene stranger free of the cares of life and death, then vaulting beyond reach into the sky. Themes: nature, transcendence, mortality. Form: lyric.

title: 63. If pain for peace prepares
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: Conditional argument that suffering and night prepare for blazing noon; redemption through pain, hope and spiritual blaze.

title: 630. The Lightning playeth — all the while —
author: Dickinson
summary: Lightning/thunder as an awesome power we approach warily with insulators; the sublime terror of an unseen God. Themes: the sublime, awe, faith and doubt. Form: lyric.

title: 631. Ourselves were wed one summer — dear —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: An elegiac address to a dead beloved 'wed one summer'; the survivor's frost-sown garden against the other's sunlit cottage. Themes: love, grief, death, the seasons. Form: lyric/elegy.

title: 632. The Brain — is wider than the Sky —
author: Dickinson
summary: A celebrated lyric measuring the mind against sky, sea and God; the imagination's boundless containing power. Themes: imagination, the self/soul, the divine. Form: lyric.

title: 634. You'll know Her — by Her Foot —
author: Dickinson
summary: A riddling portrait of a bird (the robin) by foot, vest, cap and spring voice; close observation of nature. Themes: nature, birds, spring. Form: lyric/riddle.

title: 635. I think the longest Hour of all
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: The agonized waiting of an hour stretched by anticipated joy, time blocking the clock's hands. Themes: time, longing, anticipation. Form: lyric.

title: 636. The Way I read a Letter's — this —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A secretive ritual of locking the door to read a love letter in private; intimacy, longing, and a heaven of one's own. Themes: love, secrecy, longing. Form: lyric.

title: 637. The Child's faith is new —
author: Dickinson
summary: The child's whole, doubtless faith and sovereign trust contrasted with the sorrowful skill of grown men who anticipate loss. Themes: innocence and experience, faith and doubt, childhood. Form: lyric.

title: 638. To my small Hearth His fire came —
author: Dickinson
summary: A beloved's coming floods the speaker's house with sunrise-like, deathless light; love as eternal day without decay. Themes: love, joy, immortality. Form: lyric.

title: 639. My Portion is Defeat — today —
author: Dickinson
cluster: War and its Cost · American Civil War · Battlefield
summary: A battlefield scene of defeat, bone, blank boyish eyes and stamped death, contrasted with the trumpets of victory. Themes: war and its cost, death, defeat. Form: lyric.

title: 64. Some Rainbow — coming from the Fair!
author: Dickinson
summary: Exuberant vision of spring's return rendered as military regiments of bees, robins and flowers; nature renewed, wonder and the cycle of seasons.

title: 640. I cannot live with You —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A major lyric on impossible love: cannot live, die, rise or be judged together; the lovers meet apart with the door of despair ajar. Themes: unrequited/impossible love, death, faith, despair. Form: lyric.

title: 641. Size circumscribes — it has no room
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric: true greatness ignores petty calumny as a giant tolerates no gnat. Themes: greatness, pride, the self. Form: epigram/lyric.

title: 642. Me from Myself — to banish —
author: Dickinson
summary: The divided self at war with itself; peace only by abdicating consciousness, 'Me — of Me'. Themes: the self and soul, identity, inner conflict. Form: lyric.

title: 643. I could suffice for Him, I knew —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Two souls face infinity, nature and God before a decisive union likened to sea answering the moon's tides. Themes: love, the self, the divine, fate. Form: lyric.

title: 644. You left me — Sire — two Legacies —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A bequest of love and a boundless legacy of pain left by a departed one. Themes: love, grief and loss, suffering, eternity. Form: lyric.

title: 645. Bereavement in their death to feel
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Grieving those never met yet vital to thought; the soul absconds when such immortal friends die. Themes: grief and loss, death, the soul, kinship. Form: lyric.

title: 646. I think to Live — may be a Bliss
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A vision of a life of perfect bliss and midsummer certainty in the mind, dreamed so vividly the real seems fictitious. Themes: joy, imagination, longing, the self. Form: lyric.

title: 647. A little Road — not made of Man —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A tiny road traveled only by bee and butterfly that no human vehicle can take; nature's hidden ways and the speaker's longing. Themes: nature, the journey, longing. Form: lyric.

title: 648. Promise This — When You be Dying —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: The speaker asks to be summoned at the beloved's death, to close his eyes and guard his grave, devotion outlasting denial. Themes: death, devoted love, grief, faith. Form: lyric.

title: 649. Her Sweet turn to leave the Homestead
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A young woman's death figured as a bride leaving home, with carriages, kinsmen and garland; suitor must achieve Paradise to win her. Themes: death, the bride, grief, immortality. Form: lyric/elegy.

title: 65. I can't tell you — but you feel it —
author: Dickinson
summary: The ineffable felt holiness of an April day that cannot be told, only reverenced; inexpressibility, nature and the sublime.

title: 650. Pain — has an Element of Blank —
author: Dickinson
summary: A celebrated lyric on pain as a timeless blank that contains its own past and infinite future. Themes: suffering, time, melancholy. Form: lyric.

title: 651. So much Summer
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: The speaker's small but ample 'summer' set against the rich Lady with the guinea; a robin's larder of contentment. Themes: nature, humility, contentment vs wealth. Form: lyric.

title: 652. A Prison gets to be a friend —
author: Dickinson
summary: Long meditation on how confinement becomes familiar and even beloved, hope exchanged for content; liberty avoided like a dream. Themes: confinement, the self, resignation, freedom. Form: lyric.

title: 653. Of Being is a Bird
author: Dickinson
summary: Being likened to a bird/down soaring with music and ecstasy; pure existence as buoyant joy. Themes: being, nature, joy, the soul. Form: lyric.

title: 654. A long — long Sleep — A famous — Sleep —
author: Dickinson
summary: Death as an endless, idle sleep on a bank of stone, basking the centuries away without waking. Themes: death, sleep, the grave, eternity. Form: lyric.

title: 655. Without this — there is nought —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Without the one beloved/whole all riches are nothing; a wish to subdivide the heart only to magnify gratitude. Themes: love, gratitude, the whole vs the part. Form: lyric.

title: 656. The name — of it — is "Autumn" —
author: Dickinson
summary: Autumn rendered as a vivid bloodshed of scarlet rain, arteries and vermilion wheels across the hills. Themes: autumn, the seasons, blood, mortality. Form: lyric.

title: 657. I dwell in Possibility —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric celebrating poetry ('Possibility') as a house superior to prose, with imagination opening onto infinity and paradise. Central themes: imagination, the poet's vocation, immortality of art.

title: 658. Whole Gulfs — of Red, and Fleets — of Red —
author: Dickinson
cluster: White and Red · Riddle · Secrecy and Concealment
summary: A lyric depicting a red sunset as a martial pageant that performs like a drama and then vanishes. Central themes: nature spectacle, transience, theatre of the world.

title: 659. That first Day, when you praised Me, Sweet,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A love lyric in which a day of praise from the beloved glows central like a jewel among lesser days. Central themes: love, memory, the worth of a single moment.

title: 66. So from the mould
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Bulbs from mould and worms from cocoon as figures of resurrection from the grave; nature, transformation and wonder at hidden renewal.

title: 660. 'Tis good — the looking back on Grief —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A meditative lyric on revisiting past grief now overgrown by summer grass, and on the equivalence of all sorrows. Central themes: grief, memory, transience, consolation.

title: 661. Could I but ride indefinite
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric fantasy of being a free meadow bee roving where it likes, ending with captives' longing for liberty. Central themes: freedom, escape, nature, confinement.

title: 663. Again — his voice is at the door —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A love lyric narrating the agitated reunion with the beloved at the door, the world shrinking to his face. Central themes: love, longing, the single beloved presence.

title: 664. Of all the Souls that stand create —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A lyric of election: one chosen soul will remain when flesh and subterfuge fall away at death. Central themes: love, soul, immortality, death as unveiling.

title: 665. Dropped into the Ether Acre —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A lyric figuring burial as a bride's journey, the dead 'riding to meet the Earl' in sod gown and frozen brooch. Central themes: death, the grave, immortality, marriage imagery.

title: 666. Ah, Teneriffe!
author: Dickinson
summary: An apostrophe to the unreachable mountain Teneriffe, clad in ice and steel, indifferent to sunset's homage. Central themes: the sublime, nature's grandeur, awe, the unattainable.

title: 667. Bloom upon the Mountain — stated —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the sunset's anonymous, recurring bloom over the mountain, the impassive face of nature. Central themes: nature, transience, the sublime, anonymity of natural beauty.

title: 668. "Nature" is what we see —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A definition-lyric cataloguing nature as sight, sound, harmony and knowledge beyond art's expression. Central themes: nature, inexpressibility, wonder, the limits of wisdom.

title: 67. Success is counted sweetest
author: Dickinson
cluster: War and its Cost · American Civil War · Battlefield
summary: Paradox that only the defeated and dying truly comprehend victory; need, loss and the cost of triumph rendered through battle imagery.

title: 670. One need not be a Chamber — to be Haunted —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric arguing the mind's interior is more haunted and terrifying than any external ghost or assassin. Central themes: the self, terror, the uncanny, the divided mind.

title: 671. She dwelleth in the Ground —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the buried beloved among daffodils, longing to pluck and fetch her grace. Central themes: death, the grave, grief, longing.

title: 672. The Future — never spoke —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Guilt · Conscience · Fate and Free Will
summary: A lyric personifying the Future as a dumb agent who executes Fate's telegram without warning. Central themes: fate, time, futurity, powerlessness before destiny.

title: 673. The Love a Life can show Below
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A lyric that earthly love is but a filament of a diviner love pervading noon, music and the sunset. Central themes: divine love, the sublime, transcendence, beauty.

title: 674. The Soul that hath a Guest
author: Dickinson
summary: A brief lyric: a soul hosting a divine guest needs no outward society. Central themes: the self and soul, divine presence, inwardness.

title: 675. Essential Oils — are wrung —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on attar wrung from the rose by 'Screws' surviving the lady's death — art distilled through suffering. Central themes: immortality of art, suffering, transience, the rose.

title: 677. To be alive — is Power —
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric exalting mere existence and will as godlike omnipotence. Central themes: existence, the self, power, vitality.

title: 678. Wolfe demanded during dying
author: Dickinson
summary: A miniature dramatic anecdote of the dying Generals Wolfe and Montcalm at Quebec, exchanging words on victory and surrender. Central themes: heroism, death, war, honour.

title: 679. Conscious am I in my Chamber,
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the felt presence of a 'shapeless friend' the speaker's instinct esteems as Immortality. Central themes: immortality, faith, the unseen presence, intuition.

title: 680. Each Life Converges to some Centre —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on every life striving toward an unreachable goal, attained, if ever, only in eternity. Central themes: aspiration, the unattainable, immortality, perseverance.

title: 682. 'Twould ease — a Butterfly —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric preferring the blossom's fading moment to the bee's eternity, content to fade into divinity. Central themes: transience, mortality, contentment, divine attention.

title: 683. The Soul unto itself
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the soul as both imperial friend and agonizing spy to itself, its own sovereign. Central themes: the self and soul, identity, inner conflict, self-knowledge.

title: 686. They say that "Time assuages" —
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric denying that time heals; real suffering strengthens with age. Central themes: grief, time, suffering, consolation refused.

title: 687. I'll send the feather from my Hat!
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: A short lyric hoping a small token will soften a Sovereign's adamant heart. Central themes: supplication, memory, tenderness, divine mercy.

title: 689. The Zeroes — taught us — Phosphorous —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on knowledge through opposites: cold teaches fire, paralysis teaches vitality. Central themes: paradox, suffering as instruction, opposites, vitality.

title: 69. Low at my problem bending,
author: Dickinson
summary: Earthly arithmetic interrupted by the larger, serener 'problem' of death/eternity; mortality reframed as a baffling sum.

title: 690. Victory comes late —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric protesting that victory and God's bounty arrive too late and too high for the small and starving. Central themes: deprivation, doubt, God's economy, poverty.

title: 691. Would you like summer? Taste of ours.
author: Dickinson
summary: A playful lyric offering nature's wares as remedies for every ill, even death. Central themes: nature, summer, healing, joy.

title: 692. The Sun kept setting — setting — still
author: Dickinson
summary: A first-person death lyric in which the dying speaker watches the light fail and calmly recognizes 'Tis Dying — I am doing.' Central themes: death, dying consciousness, light and dark, fearlessness.

title: 693. Shells from the Coast mistaking —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on mistaking shells for all until a pearl arrives, dialoguing with belated need. Central themes: longing, the sea, value, fulfilment delayed.

title: 694. The Heaven vests for Each
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on each soul's chosen small deity worshipped until faint tabernacles drop into eternity. Central themes: faith, worship, immortality, the sublime.

title: 695. As if the Sea should part
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric imaging eternity as endless seas opening upon further seas. Central themes: eternity, the sea, infinity, the sublime.

title: 696. Their Height in Heaven comforts not —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of doubt preferring finite earthly evidence to heaven's uncertain glory, ending 'I don't know.' Central themes: doubt, faith and doubt, the finite, uncertainty.

title: 697. I could bring You Jewels — had I a mind to —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A love lyric preferring a humble meadow blaze (a bird/flower) over exotic jewels as a gift. Central themes: love, nature over riches, the gift, humble beauty.

title: 698. Life — is what we make of it —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric trusting Christ, who has traversed death first as 'Tender Pioneer,' to make death safe. Central themes: faith, death, Christ, immortality.

title: 699. The Judge is like the Owl —
author: Dickinson
summary: A whimsical lyric likening the Judge to an owl, offering an amber sill as a house in exchange for a midnight tune. Central themes: nature, whimsy, exchange, the rural world.

title: 7. The feet of people walking home
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric figuring death as a homeward journey and resurrection, with peasants as angels and faith adoring the dark; immortality and the hereafter.

title: 70. "Arcturus" is his other name —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Ode · Nature vs Civilization · Pastoral Retreat
summary: Satire of cold science classifying stars, worms and flowers, displacing childlike wonder and heaven; faith, doubt and nature vs. analysis.

title: 700. You've seen Balloons set — Haven't You?
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric narrating a balloon's stately ascent, failure and fatal fall, met by the crowd's indifference. Central themes: aspiration and fall, transience, death, indifference of the world.

title: 701. A Thought went up my mind today —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a half-recognized recurring thought the speaker cannot fully name. Central themes: memory, the mind, the elusive, inexpressibility.

title: 702. A first Mute Coming —
author: Dickinson
summary: A compressed lyric tracing a first silent coming and going in a stranger's house, exhibited to faith alone. Central themes: faith, threshold, mystery, the unseen.

title: 703. Out of sight? What of that?
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric urging bold pursuit of the unseen like a soaring bird, since bashful Heaven hides from earth. Central themes: aspiration, faith, the unattainable, courage.

title: 704. No matter — now — Sweet —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of posthumous/future fame in which the slighted 'dull Girl' imagines becoming an 'Earl' crowned with crests and ermine; themes of fame, vindication, unrequited love and aristocratic self-fashioning.

title: 705. Suspense — is Hostiler than Death —
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric arguing suspense is crueler than death because it never concludes, dying and reviving endlessly; meditates on mortality, immortality and psychic anguish.

title: 706. Life, and Death, and Giants —
author: Dickinson
summary: A terse lyric contrasting great abstractions (Life, Death, Giants) that stay silent with small noisy things (a fife, a beetle) that proclaim themselves; on greatness, fame and accidental noise.

title: 708. I sometimes drop it, for a Quick —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on how the thought of being alive consoles monstrous woe; delirium, the scaffold and a shipwreck image dramatize pain, numbness and the approach of death.

title: 709. Publication — is the Auction
author: Dickinson
summary: A famous ars-poetica lyric condemning publication as selling the mind; the poet keeps her 'Snow' white for the 'White Creator' rather than reduce spirit to a price; on art, integrity and the artist and society.

title: 71. A throe upon the features —
author: Dickinson
summary: Clinical anatomy of the moment of death and the anguish of parting; mortality, grief and eventual reunion with one's own.

title: 710. The Sunrise runs for Both —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric in which sunrise, noon, night and stars equally serve two separated lovers across hemispheres; cosmic nature imagery as a figure for love, distance and union.

title: 711. Strong Draughts of Their Refreshing Minds
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric praising the sustaining power of great minds, figured as sealed wine that lets one cross desert and wilderness; on imagination, intellect and inspiration.

title: 712. Because I could not stop for Death —
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson's most famous lyric: Death personified as a courteous suitor drives the speaker by carriage past school, fields and setting sun to the grave and on toward eternity; central meditation on mortality, immortality and time.

title: 713. Fame of Myself, to justify,
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric on self-sufficiency in fame: self-justification makes all other praise superfluous, while lacking one's own approval renders any supreme name a 'futile Diadem'; on identity, integrity and fame.

title: 715. The World — feels Dusty
author: Dickinson
summary: A deathbed lyric: as we die honors taste dry and flags vex, but a friend's small ministering kindness (dew, a fan) cools like rain; on mortality, thirst, consolation and tender service.

title: 716. The Day undressed — Herself —
author: Dickinson
summary: A sunset lyric personifying Day as a woman undressing in gold and purple, the 'Lady of the Occident' retiring; nature imagery, light and a serene nearness to God.

title: 717. The Beggar Lad — dies early —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of social protest and pity: a beggar boy dies of cold and hunger ignored by the 'Cruel — smiling — bowing World,' then is received among the redeemed; on poverty, social injustice, death and grace.

title: 718. I meant to find Her when I came —
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac lyric: the speaker came to find the beloved but Death had the same design and won; left to wander in restless grief and memory. On death, loss and bereavement.

title: 719. A South Wind — has a pathos
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the wind's plaintive voice, like an emigrant's address hinting at distant ports and peoples; on longing, the foreign and the beauty of distance.

title: 72. Glowing is her Bonnet,
author: Dickinson
summary: A dead woman figured as a glowing flower/daisy vanishing unrecorded, mourned only by sunrise and rill; death, nature and quiet elegy.

title: 721. Behind Me — dips Eternity —
author: Dickinson
summary: A metaphysical lyric placing the self as the term between eternity behind and immortality before, with death as a brief gray dawn; meditation on time, immortality, the divine and the soul's position.

title: 722. Sweet Mountains — Ye tell Me no lie —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A lyric in which the mountains become 'Strong Madonnas,' constant and truthful objects of worship for the 'Wayward Nun'; nature as substitute faith, on doubt, devotion and constancy.

title: 723. It tossed — and tossed —
author: Dickinson
summary: A shipwreck lyric: a little brig overtaken by a storm spins, trips and sinks while the calm blue ocean refuses to grieve; an allegory of death, struggle and nature's indifference.

title: 724. It's easy to invent a Life —
author: Dickinson
summary: A theological lyric on God's casual creation and effacement of lives, the 'thrifty Deity' working a 'Perturbless Plan'; on providence, mortality and divine indifference.

title: 725. Where Thou art — that — is Home —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A love lyric: the beloved's presence makes any place home (Cashmere or Calvary) and any hardship sweet, absence makes all woe; love as religion, on devotion and the beloved.

title: 726. We thirst at first — 'tis Nature's Act —
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric: natural thirst in life and the dying's last call for water intimate a finer thirst whose only supply is the 'Great Water in the West,' immortality; on mortality and immortality.

title: 727. Precious to Me — She still shall be —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A lyric of humble devotion: the beloved (figured through meadow flowers and the bee) remains precious though she forget the speaker; on love, memory and self-effacement.

title: 728. Let Us play Yesterday —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: A lyric recalling childhood schooldays and the dawn of consciousness through images of egg, shell, bird and manacles; a prayer to the 'God of the Manacle' not to take liberty; on innocence, growth, freedom and bondage.

title: 73. Who never lost, are unprepared
author: Dickinson
cluster: War and its Cost · American Civil War · Battlefield
summary: Only those who suffer loss and conquest earn the crown; spiritual reward through hardship cast in conquest and soldier imagery.

title: 731. "I want" — it pleaded — All its life —
author: Dickinson
summary: A deathbed lyric on a soul that pleaded 'I want' all its life, its last steadfast sigh placed like a 'Please' toward eternity; on desire, death and longing.

title: 732. She rose to His Requirement — dropt
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A lyric on a woman renouncing the 'Playthings' of her life for the honorable work of wife; whatever amplitude she lost lies unmentioned like pearl in the sea. On marriage, gender, sacrifice and the hidden self.

title: 733. The Spirit is the Conscious Ear.
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric distinguishing the spirit's true inner hearing from the smaller outward physical ear; on perception, soul and consciousness.

title: 734. If He were living — dare I ask —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A lyric dramatizing the dread of asking whether an absent person is dead, circling cautiously around graves until the blunt 'Buried!' lands; on death, fear, grief and suspense.

title: 735. Upon Concluded Lives
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on how nothing is colder to the dying than life's sweet calculations, with bells and palls making a lacerating tune both 'Coronal and Funeral'; on mortality and the contrast of life's sweetness against death.

title: 736. Have any like Myself
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of seasonal wonder: in March the speaker descries new houses, a church and steeple visible only then, conjecturing heavenly occupants near God; on nature, faith, the seasons and imagination.

title: 737. The Moon was but a Chin of Gold
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric personifying the waxing moon as a regal lady with amber lips, the firmament her bonnet and stars her trinkets; rich celestial nature imagery and wonder.

title: 738. You said that I "was Great" — one Day —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A love lyric of radical self-abnegation: the speaker will be any size, stag or wren, queen or page, 'or nought,' so long as she suits the beloved; on love, identity and self-effacement.

title: 739. I many times thought Peace had come
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric likening repeated false hopes of peace to wrecked men sighting fictitious shores mid-ocean; on hope, despair and disillusionment.

title: 74. A Lady red — amid the Hill
author: Dickinson
summary: Red and white flowers sleeping in the hills as figures of seasonal resurrection; nature's quiet annual rebirth treated with playful awe.

title: 740. You taught me Waiting with Myself —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of devotion and faith: the beloved taught patience, fortitude of fate and the 'Altitude of Death,' and the speaker hopes to be unashamed before Christ; on death, love, faith and self-discipline.

title: 741. Drama's Vitallest Expression is the Common Day
author: Dickinson
summary: An ars-poetica lyric arguing the truest drama is ordinary life enacted in the human heart, needing no Shakespeare or recorded theatre; invokes Hamlet and Romeo. On art, the theatrum mundi and the common day.

title: 742. Four Trees — upon a solitary Acre —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A stark lyric on four trees standing without apparent design or order, their deed to general nature unknown; a meditation on nature, purpose, randomness and the inscrutability of the natural order.

title: 743. The Birds reported from the South —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric in which the grieving speaker rebuffs spring's birds, flowers and summer grace until autumn, a fellow mourner, draws away austere and wins her sympathy; on grief, nature, the seasons and mourning.

title: 744. Remorse — is Memory — awake —
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric defining remorse as awakened memory, a cureless disease and 'complement of hell' instituted by God; on guilt, conscience, memory and suffering.

title: 745. Renunciation — is a piercing Virtue —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A meditative lyric defining renunciation as choosing against oneself, the painful 'putting out of Eyes' at sunrise for a larger expectation; on sacrifice, self-denial and spiritual choice.

title: 746. Never for Society
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric praising self-acquaintance and inner companionship over society; one who cultivates the 'Man within' never lacks company. On solitude, self and identity.

title: 747. It dropped so low — in my Regard —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: A lyric on disillusionment: something prized falls and shatters in the mind, and the speaker blames herself for keeping 'Plated Wares' on her 'Silver Shelf'; on misjudgment, value, self-reproach and appearance vs reality.

title: 748. Autumn — overlooked my Knitting —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A playful lyric in which Autumn, master of dyes, offers colors: the speaker chooses cochineal to resemble the beloved and a dusker border for herself; on the seasons, nature, color and love.

title: 749. All but Death, can be Adjusted —
author: Dickinson
summary: A compact lyric arguing that everything in life and history is mutable and repairable except death, which alone is exempt from change. Themes: mortality, transience, the unique finality of death.

title: 75. She died at play,
author: Dickinson
summary: A child/flower-like figure dies mid-play and lingers as a gentle ghost; childhood, death and the soft persistence of the dead.

title: 750. Growth of Man — like Growth of Nature —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A meditative lyric on inward self-development: like nature, the soul must achieve its ideal through solitary effort, patience, and belief, unaided by any audience. Themes: identity, self-reliance, growth.

title: 751. My Worthiness is all my Doubt —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: A devotional lyric of unworthiness before a divine Beloved, framing the soul as a church offering its sacrament. Themes: faith and doubt, humility, divine love, self and soul.

title: 752. So the Eyes accost — and sunder
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: A brief lyric on a fleeting glance between strangers, a countenance met and lost in an instant. Themes: transience, alienation, the fugitive moment of recognition.

title: 753. My Soul — accused me — And I quailed —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on inner conscience: the soul's accusation outweighs all external blame, and its disdain for worldly artifice becomes the truest friendship. Themes: conscience, self and soul, integrity.

title: 754. My Life had stood — a Loaded Gun —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Swords and Weapons · Power and Corruption · Tyrant
summary: Dickinson's enigmatic masterpiece: the speaker as a loaded gun claimed and wielded by a Master/Owner, exploring agency, power, lethal force, and the paradox of power to kill without power to die. Themes: power, identity, self and soul, the riddle of mortality and service.

title: 755. No Bobolink — reverse His Singing
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the bobolink who keeps singing even when his tree is felled and his future cut off, music his only anodyne. Themes: resilience, loss, song as solace, dispossession.

title: 756. One Blessing had I than the rest
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a single supreme blessing so satisfying it becomes a paralyzing bliss, an earthly heaven obscuring judgment. Themes: joy, satisfaction, earthly paradise, the limits of bliss.

title: 757. The Mountains — grow unnoticed —
author: Dickinson
summary: A nature lyric celebrating the mountains' quiet, unapplauded grandeur and the sun's golden fellowship with their eternal faces. Themes: nature, sublimity, humble grandeur, the natural order.

title: 758. These — saw Visions —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: An elegiac lyric tenderly addressing the eyes, mouth, and hands of a dead woman now received into Paradise. Themes: death, grief and loss, the body, the dead beloved.

title: 759. He fought like those Who've nought to lose —
author: Dickinson
cluster: War and its Cost · American Civil War · Battlefield
summary: A war lyric on a soldier who courts death recklessly yet is left alive because death is coy of those who crave it. Themes: war and its cost, death-wish, the paradox of survival, despair.

title: 76. Exultation is the going
author: Dickinson
summary: The inland soul's ecstatic launch into the sea of eternity; the sea as death/immortality and the divine intoxication of release.

title: 760. Most she touched me by her muteness —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
