title: To Mr. and Mrs. J. L. Jenkins, Mrs. Hanson Read, Mrs. W. A. Stearns, Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, Mrs. J. S. Cooper, Mrs. A. B. H. Davis, Mrs. H. F. Hills, Mrs. Jameson, Mr. F. F. Emerson, Maggie Maher, Mr. and Mrs. George Montague, Mrs. W. F. Stearns, Mr. J. K. Chickering, Mrs. Joseph Sweetser, Mr. Thomas, Niles, Mrs. Carmichael, Dr. and Mrs. Thomas P. Field, Mr. Theodore Holland, “H. H.,” Miss Eugenia Hall, Mrs. E. P. Crowell, and Mrs. J. C. Greenough, Christmas, 1874
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson describes a beautiful Christmas at home with the hens, cats, and horse cared for, a gift of roses, and asks what made the child remember her.

title: To Mr. and Mrs. J. L. Jenkins, Mrs. Hanson Read, Mrs. W. A. Stearns, Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, Mrs. J. S. Cooper, Mrs. A. B. H. Davis, Mrs. H. F. Hills, Mrs. Jameson, Mr. F. F. Emerson, Maggie Maher, Mr. and Mrs. George Montague, Mrs. W. F. Stearns, Mr. J. K. Chickering, Mrs. Joseph Sweetser, Mr. Thomas, Niles, Mrs. Carmichael, Dr. and Mrs. Thomas P. Field, Mr. Theodore Holland, “H. H.,” Miss Eugenia Hall, Mrs. E. P. Crowell, and Mrs. J. C. Greenough
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: An editorial note introducing a letter Dickinson wrote to a niece of her father who had sent roses for his grave.

title: To Mr. and Mrs. J. L. Jenkins, Mrs. Hanson Read, Mrs. W. A. Stearns, Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, Mrs. J. S. Cooper, Mrs. A. B. H. Davis, Mrs. H. F. Hills, Mrs. Jameson, Mr. F. F. Emerson, Maggie Maher, Mr. and Mrs. George Montague, Mrs. W. F. Stearns, Mr. J. K. Chickering, Mrs. Joseph Sweetser, Mr. Thomas, Niles, Mrs. Carmichael, Dr. and Mrs. Thomas P. Field, Mr. Theodore Holland, “H. H.,” Miss Eugenia Hall, Mrs. E. P. Crowell, and Mrs. J. C. Greenough, December, 1874
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson notes that her late father, who scorned Santa Claus, must have become as a little child before a Christmas gift could be dared for him.

title: To Mr. and Mrs. J. L. Jenkins, Mrs. Hanson Read, Mrs. W. A. Stearns, Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, Mrs. J. S. Cooper, Mrs. A. B. H. Davis, Mrs. H. F. Hills, Mrs. Jameson, Mr. F. F. Emerson, Maggie Maher, Mr. and Mrs. George Montague, Mrs. W. F. Stearns, Mr. J. K. Chickering, Mrs. Joseph Sweetser, Mr. Thomas, Niles, Mrs. Carmichael, Dr. and Mrs. Thomas P. Field, Mr. Theodore Holland, “H. H.,” Miss Eugenia Hall, Mrs. E. P. Crowell, and Mrs. J. C. Greenough, 1872?
author: Dickinson
summary: A playful note to the boys Did and Mac urging them never to grow up or improve because they are perfect now.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note that this was Dickinson's last known letter to Clark, followed by her two-word message to her cousins, 'Called back.'

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark
author: Dickinson
summary: Todd's closing account of Dickinson's death and burial at Amherst, the reading of Emily Bronte's Last Lines, and an appraisal of the epigrammatic quality of her verse.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark
author: Dickinson
summary: An editorial note stating that the final letter to Mr. Clark was written a year later and appears in the last chapter.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, April 15, 1886
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Letter to C. H. Clark reporting her slow recovery and recalling his brother, the scholarly stranger who 'went home,' as a vision and an aborigine of the sky.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, April 18, 1883
author: Dickinson
summary: Short letter inquiring after the health of C. H. Clark's ailing brother and of Clark himself.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, April 21, 1884
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson offers sympathy for Clark's ailing father, notes the loss of another friend, and questions whether reunion with the dead could be borne.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, April 21, 1885
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson encloses flowers chosen for the dead brother's sake, imagining he watches over them, and wishes health for Clark and his frail father.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, April 22, 1883
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Letter of sympathy on grave news of Clark's brother, sending sorrowing thoughts and asking to take the brother's hand.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, April 22, 1884
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson encloses a poem meditating on whether the spirit persists apart from the body, comparing soul and flesh to music and touch, and tide and sea.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, April 5, 1886
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter to C. H. Clark asking after his father and home, reporting her long illness and recalling his cherished brother and the flower sacred to him.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, Enclosing pressed flowers, February 22, 1884
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson sends Clark the flower that was her final ministry to his dying brother, along with her first blossoms of the season.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, January 18, 1885
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson sends New Year wishes to Clark and his father, recalls his dead brother whenever the Northampton bells ring, and asks after his blossoms and books.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, January 4, 1884
author: Dickinson
summary: Recovering from illness, Dickinson thanks Clark for his kindness and calls him the only tie between the vanished and the enduring Heaven, wishing to speak of his dead brother.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, July 9, 1883
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson thanks Clark for a photograph of his late brother, offers condolence, and reflects on her doubt of a face in the afterlife and on memory as consolation.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, June 16, 1883
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter mourning the brother's death, comparing sibling bonds, and voicing doubt whether there is another life.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, June 7, 1883
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter mourning the death of Clark's brother, whom she had met but once, and asking for details of his final days.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, May 1, 1883
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter refraining from too-frequent inquiry into the brother's illness and wishing peace on a May morning.

title: To Mr. C. H. Clark, May 21, 1883
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter expressing anxiety over the brother's illness and the absence of news, amid the spring birds.

title: To Mr. F. D. Clark
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note stating this is the last letter to Mr. F. D. Clark, after whose illness Dickinson wrote to his brother.

title: To Mr. F. D. Clark, 1882
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Letter eulogizing a reserved late friend, with a poem on Christ's own expanse bearing him from the tomb.

title: To Mr. F. D. Clark, 1883
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Letter thanking Clark for gifts more precious than birds, quoting Scripture, and offering sorrow over the death of a president.

title: To Mr. F. D. Clark, Late Autumn, 1882
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter of mutual condolence recounting her mother's death, describing grief as many kinds of cold, and calling a letter a form of immortality.

title: To Mr. F. D. Clark, March, 1883
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter hoping for Clark's recovery with the coming spring, describing hyacinths and beauty as timidity, and grieving her late mother.

title: To Mr. Perez D. Cowan, Miss Maria Whitney, Mr. Bowles, Mr. F. D. Clark, and Mr. C. H. Clark
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note identifying Perez Cowan as Dickinson's favorite cousin 'Peter,' with the first letter occasioned by his marriage.

title: TO MR. PYE
author: Coleridge
summary: A literary-satirical epigram mocking the Laureate Pye's 'Carmen Seculare' as eternal because incomprehensible and 'without head or tail.'

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: A short autumn verse on hillside asters and covenant gentians setting their everlasting fashions.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson sends Bowles a verse offering the rose, thanks him beyond words, and reflects that the heaviest-laden heart does not always show its grief in speech or tears.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: A verse defending Dickinson's stooping by likening it to Christ stooping to the grave in love, closing with lines on stealing flowers from a bee.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: An editorial note that many other verses sent to the Bowleses, already published elsewhere, are not reprinted here.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson writes to Mrs. Bowles that, lacking a flower, she encloses her half-broken heart, likens Mrs. Bowles's flowers to heaven, and sends a silver tear of thanks.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: Enclosed poem stating that Nature and God know the speaker while the speaker keeps a secret as secure as Herschel's or Mercury's affair.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: Short poem promising the recipient a perennial bloom untouched by wilderness, desert noon, or coming frost.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: Verses sent with flowers on remembering, missing, and mourning, opening with the paradox that a death-blow is a life-blow to some.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: Enclosed verses on Christ choosing his followers at Bethlehem, with a daisy sharing in his dishonor.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: Two enclosed poems, a plea to an unyielding God of flint and a nature verse on the everlasting-singing whippoorwill, sent with a spray of white pine.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks Mrs. Bowles for a green-and-gold gift book, apologizes for writing so often, and describes winter frost-flowers, snow, and the awaited spring while sending New Year greetings.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: A one-sentence note on parting from the river at its flood, recalling shared play in the same waters.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: A single-sentence note that the only response to the recipient's exquisite act is the humility that grace confers.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: A quatrain on the crushing hidden weight carried by a single delivered syllable.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter contemplating death and enclosing an elegiac tribute to the constancy of Mr. Bowles, done with grief.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note recording Mr. Bowles's death in January 1878 and the irreparable loss felt by his friends and the readers of The Republican.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note dating a letter to the famous 'Yellow Day' of September 6, 1881.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: A short verse Dickinson named herself, sent to Mrs. Bowles, imagining the newborn learning to speak the name Emily.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A one-line note conveying Vinnie's love to the Bowleses.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson sends Bowles the epigram Faith is a fine invention, muses on the East and the mountain road, reflects on death beneath the grass, and encloses a rose for Mary.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: An enclosed verse on how deprivation, the zeros, teaches vitality, sent with a word so as not to let Austin's note go alone.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: An editorial note that Dickinson sent a consoling message to Springfield after Mr. Bowles sailed for Europe.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A brief note telling Bowles that his safe return alive means more than summer or any birdsong.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: A short verse on how a friend's presence is weighed lightly but his departure leaves the heavier emptiness.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles
author: Dickinson
summary: A letter to the Bowleses valuing friends as her estate, inquiring after their health, and musing on resurrection and seeing God.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, 'MARCHIONESS'
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson relays Austin's disappointment at missing Bowles before his sea voyage and Austin's haunted grief over the killing of Frazer in the war, noting Mary's gift of flowers.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, 1863
author: Dickinson
summary: Friendship letter to the ailing Bowles pledging to remember him including in immortality, offering flowers and seasonal remedies and prayers, with several enclosed verses.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, 1865?
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter accepting a book from Bowles and enclosing a poem declaring him the speaker's whole reason for living.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, 1868?
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter praising Bowles's noble letters, reflecting on the law of the flood and on resurrection, and urging him to keep coming.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, 1869?
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief letter on Bowles's triumphant face and on a religion that doubts as fervently as it believes, amid images of burial and dust.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, 1873
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Letter delighting in Bowles's rare visit, comparing him to a peach out of season and to the Arabian Nights, and closing 'Near, but remote.'

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, 1874
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter enclosing the father's portrait with a poem on summer slipping into autumn as a figure for evading the decline of years.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, 1879
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter of remembrance and consolation invoking flowers, dew, ivy, and Nature as eldest mother to shield the grieving recipient.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, 1881
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter to Mary on a photograph of Bowles's child, finding his memorial likeness in the eyes, with allusions to Gabriel and Christ's temporary absence.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, April, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter to Mary recalling her father feeding frightened birds in a late-April snowstorm, with biblical allusion to David and Absalom and reflection on immortality within the family.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, August, 1861
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: Dickinson writes to Mary Bowles about her faith and doubt in their friendship, describes her summer garden and hummingbirds, resolves to forgo winter for the soldiers, and offers consolation to a grieving Mary.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, August, 1862
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson writes to Bowles abroad of the household's longing, marks the seasons and ripening fruit by which they reckon his return, and mentions a soldier who asked for a nosegay to carry to battle.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Autumn, 1861
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson regrets missing Mr. Bowles's visit, keeps wine and a flower for his return, and praises friends as rare gems while apologizing for writing so often.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Early Summer, 1862
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson consoles Mary Bowles in her husband's absence, declaring the heart wants what it wants, and offers herself as steady support amid summer flowers and singing frogs.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Early Winter,
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson expresses gratitude for Bowles's recovery, warns him not to overwork since his rare life is owed to many friends, and reflects on the gain earned by measuring the grave then the sun.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, January, 1862
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson writes to the ailing Bowles of her homesickness and worry over his long illness, evoking the moon over a topaz town and hoping her Amherst sympathy might comfort him.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, January, 1878
author: Dickinson
summary: Condolence letter to Mary Bowles on her husband's death, offering the consolations of love, faith, work, and his nearness in memory.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Late Autumn, 1862
author: Dickinson
summary: A verse on how grief and joy grow so similar that an optician could not tell them apart.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, March, 1862
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson explains she stayed away because the ailing Bowles needed rest, says she prays for his health each morning, and offers her small remedies of breeze and dandelion.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Monday Eve
author: Dickinson
summary: A winter letter to Mrs. Bowles thanking her for flowers, describing snowy Amherst, her graves-dotted garden, and longing to gather loved ones together.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Saturday
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief note conveying the mother's gift of a barrel of sweet apples to Mr. Bowles, with a Baldwin set aside for Mary and the squirrels.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Spring, 1862
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson describes the household's aching disappointment when the expected Mr. Bowles failed to arrive, and pleads that his absence not rob them of spring and summer.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Spring, 1878
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: Second condolence letter to Mary identifying Bowles with Eden and now with heaven, consoling her with faith and Christ's sacrifice.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Summer, 1863
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson tells the Bowleses she is sorry they came only to leave, wishes they would stay, describes a Jerusalem-like evening sky and a morning ride with Austin among mountains and singing brooks.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Sunday Night
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson anxiously asks Mary Bowles whether an errand she requested of Mr. Bowles before his Washington trip caused trouble, and sends a rose for the baby Charlie.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, To Mr. Bowles, June, 1862
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson writes to Bowles in Europe urging him to remember Amherst and come home, evoking unchanged roses and robins, the Bible on life's brevity, and asking him to touch Mrs. Browning's grave for her.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Tuesday
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter to Mary on a dark morning, thanking her, asking for her child's picture, and reassuring her with the sparrow's providence that she is not forgotten.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Wednesday
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A short note welcoming Mr. Bowles's letter, likened to a blossom, that arrived at night.

title: To Mr. Samuel Bowlers and Mrs. Bowles, Written in 1861, on the birth of a son
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson congratulates Mary Bowles on the birth of a son, urges her to return from New York to Massachusetts, and asks that the baby be named Robert.

title: To Mr. Theodore Holland
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Editorial note about Dickinson's lost letters to Helen Hunt Jackson (H.H.), presumed accidentally destroyed, and the discovery of a discarded draft letter among Dickinson's own papers.

title: To Mr. Theodore Holland
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Dickinson thanks Holland for a book, comparing awe at it to a starlight night, reflecting on the chastisement of beauty from the Maker, and alluding to Peter's walk on the sea.

title: To Mr. Theodore Holland, 1885
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson muses on doubt and courtesy through the image of a shot bird, doubting Thomas, and the silent volcanoes Vesuvius and Aetna whose word made Pompeii hide.

title: To Mr. Theodore Holland, 1885
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson playfully accepts Holland's request to remain sincerely hers, commends his kindred, and comments on a painting of the Soudan with a Scriptural aside.

title: To Mr. Thomas Niles
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: The letter transcribes Dickinson's stanza on the happy little stone that rambles alone, independent as the sun and free of careers.

title: To Mr. Thomas Niles, 1880?
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson sends Niles two poems, My Cricket and The Snow, as a modest return for a book he gave her.

title: To Mr. Thomas Niles, 1883?
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson thanks Niles, expresses regret at knowing no more of an admired woman writer, and offers to send him a pebble she thinks she once gave her.

title: To Mr. Thomas Niles, To the Same, 1885
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson sends Niles three poems and a verse tribute to Marian Evans (George Eliot), praising how gallantly she bore life's empty pack.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Editorial note that her father's death on June 16 'swept away all her landmarks.'

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter describing evening and nature, sending blossoms with a poem, and recalling a childhood funeral where a clergyman's phrase left her with a lasting doubt about immortality.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
summary: An enclosed poem on how a death-blow becomes a life-blow, vitality beginning at death.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note on Dickinson's resistance to publishing despite 'H.H.'s' pleading.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Short letter after a silence, fearing the loss of the friend who 'saved my life' and offering a scholar's prayer for his blessing.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note stating that Higginson received Dickinson's next letter while serving in a Civil War army camp in South Carolina in early 1863.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
summary: Writing to Higginson at war, Dickinson expresses awe and alarm for absent friends, includes verses on gains and losses and on revelation, prays for his safety, and entreats him to avoid death.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note framing a letter, referencing 'The Procession of Flowers,' Higginson's 1863 wounding, Dickinson's eye trouble, her Boston visit for care, and Hawthorne's death.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter apologizing for possibly having offended Higginson, calling herself his 'scholar' and comparing her plea to a thief's request.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A poem enclosed in a letter personifying Death as a steel-faced figure who 'drills his welcome in.'

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Letter longing to see Higginson but doubting a visit, noting her father's objection, entreating him to keep teaching her, and closing with a poem on slow growth and the 'summers of Hesperides.'

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter reflecting that a letter feels like immortality as disembodied mind, thanking Higginson, inviting him to Amherst, recalling a childhood memory of the Lord's Prayer, and crediting him with having saved her life.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial account of Higginson's first visit, quoting Dickinson's remarks on finding ecstasy in living, on truth, and her physical definition of poetry.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson
author: Dickinson
cluster: White and Red · Riddle · Secrecy and Concealment
summary: Dickinson replies to Higginson's corrections, admits she cannot rule herself, defends her wayward irregularity, describes her dog and walks in the woods where she met only angels, and offers her portrait.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, 1875
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Condolence letter on the death of Higginson's brother, with a poem on Heaven's 'marauding hand.'

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, 1875
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter on flowers and books, praising Mrs. Hunt and Mrs. Browning, discussing Browning and Shakespeare, and thanking Higginson for his Atlantic Essays.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, 1877
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Condolence letter after Higginson's bereavement, reflecting that nothing is irrevocable but ourselves and that to be human exceeds being divine.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, 1877
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter of concern for the grieving Higginson, urging him to let redemption find him and affirming that 'Love is its own rescue.'

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, 1877
author: Dickinson
summary: New Year letter thanking Higginson, recalling childhood, and enclosing poems about the bee, the rose, death, and a bird that sang.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks Higginson for advice on the charity request, explaining she hesitated because it invoked aiding children.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson asks Higginson's advice about three hymns she has promised to a charity and seeks his approval before giving them.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, 1884
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson offers to send Higginson the forthcoming biography of George Eliot by her husband and remarks that emblem surpasses fulfilment.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, Acknowledging a photograph, 1876
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Letter thanking Higginson for his photograph, comparing it to his living face, referencing Browning, Judge Lord's remark on joy, and Mrs. Jackson, closing with a summer poem.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, April 16, 1862
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson's first letter to Higginson asks whether her verse is alive, enclosing her name and requesting his honest judgment.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, April 26, 1862
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson answers Higginson's questions about her age, reading, companions and family, describing a terror since September, her dead tutor who taught her Immortality, and her solitary life among hills and books.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, August, 1870
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter musing on sufficiency and Revelations, recounting turning to Macbeth after his visit, humbly asking forgiveness for her ignorance, and requesting where to find Mrs. Lowell's poems and his article on a 'Latch.'

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, August, 1870
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief note welcoming Higginson's planned visit on the 15th and remarking that 'the incredible never surprises us.'

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, August, 1874
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter on her father's lonely life and death and its 'redress' in immortality, recalling an early friend's promise to come to Amherst living or dead.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, Authors, 1879
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks Higginson for a gift of books and gives her opinions on authors including Poe, Hawthorne, Howells, and James.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, Autumn, 1876
author: Dickinson
summary: Autumn letter thanking Higginson, reporting her brother's recovery, recalling his words on the majesty of art and a line from Enobarbus, and a childhood comfort from Hitchcock's book on flowers.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, Early in 1876
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter asking Higginson to write a note declaring her unfit to publish so she can decline Helen Hunt Jackson's request to contribute writing.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, Early Summer, 1880
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: Dickinson describes an Indian woman and her baby at her kitchen door amid a prairie of flowers, recalling a dead child and quoting Vaughan.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, January, 1878
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson writes to Higginson on the day of Samuel Bowles's burial, recalling a hymn as the last song she heard.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, July, 1862
author: Dickinson
summary: In place of a photograph Dickinson sends Higginson a verbal self-portrait, declares herself his scholar, asks him to correct her faults, and says her business is circumference.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, July, 1874
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter recounting the last afternoon and death of her father, expressing faith in immortality, and thanking Higginson for his 'prophetic' hymn.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, June 8, 1862
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson responds to Higginson's praise and advice, dismisses the idea of publishing, recalls her dying tutor's wish, and asks him to be her preceptor and friend, enclosing a poem.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, June, 1875
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Brief note telling Higginson that her mother was paralyzed on the anniversary of her father's death.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, March, 1876
author: Dickinson
summary: Spring letter quoting Revelation, praising his papers on Lowell and Emerson, discussing George Eliot's Daniel Deronda, and enclosing a poem on disappearance and immortality.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, Summer, 1864
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter asking after wounded Higginson's health, noting Hawthorne's death, describing her illness and physician's care in Boston that keeps her working 'in prison,' and reporting news from 'Immortality.'

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, Summer, 1878
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson urges Higginson to visit in November, mourns Bowles's death, reflects on faith and immortality, and asks about his travels and meeting George Eliot.

title: To Mr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, Winter, 1871
author: Dickinson
summary: Winter letter thanking Higginson for his Amherst visit, glad of his safe travels, describing the frozen meadow, and remarking how the year's changes 'hurt almost like music.'

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson
author: Dickinson
summary: An editorial note stating that the next letter was written three years later and sent to Boston.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson
author: Dickinson
summary: A short note anticipating Austin's Saturday visit and lamenting how quickly Sunday and the hour of parting arrive.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson
author: Dickinson
summary: A brief note that mother sends her love and Austin's waistcoat.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson
author: Dickinson
summary: An editorial note stating that several subsequent letters dealing entirely with family matters and personal subjects have been omitted.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note stating Edward Dickinson was in Baltimore at the Whig Convention that unsuccessfully sought Daniel Webster's presidential nomination.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note on the new Palmer-to-Amherst railroad's opening and June celebration, noting Emily's growing distaste for mingling in a social crowd.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note on Emily's disinclination for travel, quoting their father's letter about her joining the family's Washington trip, which she eventually did.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily describes a Germanians concert on exhibition day, comparing the players' sounds to brazen robins in broadcloth wings that flew away when it ended.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson
author: Dickinson
summary: A short note enclosing a South Hadley Seminary dinner bill of fare, joking that the menu is fit to set before a king.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Friday Morning
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson describes Austin's deserted, dusty, spider-haunted room and her half-fearful fancies, the arrival of severe autumn frost on the fading flowers and leaves, and closes with a verse inviting him into an unfading garden and another sky.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Friday Morning
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily writes an answer to a letter she has not yet received, describes their father's delight in re-reading Austin's letters aloud, and urges him to write often.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Friday Morning
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson urges Austin to leave his tiresome Boston schoolboys for the bright autumn at home, describes the crimson trees and singing crickets, and dwells on the shared future they imagine together.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Friday, Afternoon
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily notes that some of their exchanged letters have gone missing in the mail, praises one their father brought her, and looks forward with happiness to Austin's homecoming.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Friday, Morning
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson reports the town's jubilant celebration of the railroad decision, with cannon and rejoicing, calling it a fairy-tale event, and wishes Austin were present to share the excitement.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, June 14, 1853
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily gives her impressions of Alexander Smith's poems, quotes Burns, describes the growing grove and singing landscape, and anticipates crowded Commencement and reunion with Austin and Vinnie.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, March 17, 1854
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Emily describes unearthly mild weather, birds, lightning and northern lights giving way to a returning winter wind, and a married-people's party from which her celibacy excludes her.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Monday Morn
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson reports that Miss Whitman denied her request to go home for the Sabbath under the seminary rules, and resigns herself to waiting out the final weeks of the term.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Monday Morning
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson explains she delayed writing to reach a cheerful mood, describes a solemn snowy morning and cold, longs for sleigh-rides with Austin, and reflects on how the family misses him and on her father's insistence that life is real rather than poetry.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Monday Morning
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily recounts the New London railroad-celebration day with their father as chief marshal, and how she watched the train from the woods and slipped home to avoid being seen.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Monday Morning
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks Austin for his welcome letter and describes a powerful sermon by Professor Park to a hushed, awestruck congregation, wishing Austin had heard it.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Monday Morning, 5 o'c.
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Emily describes the season's first thunder-shower at home and contrasts her refreshing rural morning with the dust and din of Austin's city.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Saturday Morn
author: Dickinson
summary: With Austin gone, Emily reflects on loving and weeping for absent kin, describes a radiant blossoming spring day, and reminds him that at home they are now but four.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Saturday Morn
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson writes of her distorted sense of time since Austin left, her loneliness on a gray day, and calls home a holy thing, a bit of Eden, wishing she could send him its fragrant autumn air.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Saturday Noon
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily jokes about resuming her essays to Austin and recounts their father scolding her over Uncle Tom, Dickens and modern writers, closing with the family's constant thought of him.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Saturday, P.M.
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson reports finishing her Euclid examination and her current studies, comments on Austin reading the Arabian Nights and advises balancing imagination with other faculties, and notes her birthday.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Sunday Afternoon
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: Dickinson recounts a stormy, mishap-ridden carriage journey to the Jenny Lind concert, her mixed impressions of the singer's exile-touched manner, and the family's amusement, and the church revival that morning.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Sunday Afternoon
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson praises Austin's long funny letter and mock-promises a simpler style, then describes setting an extra place at table and brushing away a tear in memory of her absent brother, and the ripening cherries.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Sunday Afternoon
author: Dickinson
summary: Home from meeting on a cold snowy day, Dickinson recalls Austin's seat of the previous Sunday, looks forward to the full Thanksgiving circle, and wishes she could give him courage and bring him home for good.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Sunday Afternoon
author: Dickinson
summary: On a cold windy day Emily describes the growing grove and the pines' music, the cat's rambles, and her longing to walk there with Austin when he returns.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Sunday Afternoon
author: Dickinson
summary: On a bright afternoon Dickinson wishes Austin were home rather than in muddy, rattling Boston, and fixes her hopes on his promised return in early April.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Sunday Evening
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks Austin for his letter, endorses his skeptical opinion of the singer Jenny Lind, asks about his life in Boston, and reports on senior levees at Amherst.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Sunday Evening
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson describes missing Austin's presence, whistling like a boy in a graveyard past his empty room, planning to set out crickets against the gloom, and reports there is no news in town.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Sunday Evening
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson imagines Austin as a schoolmaster-king disciplining his little pupils, recounts Vinnie's echoing question of where Austin is, and describes the lonely summer at home with ripening apples.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Sunday Evening
author: Dickinson
summary: On a cold windy Sunday with Vinnie ill, Emily reports going to meeting alone, praises Mr. Dwight's sermons, and tells the comic story of their father mistaking a box of maple sugar for Quaker soap.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Sunday Evening
author: Dickinson
summary: After Austin's departure Dickinson describes the crestfallen household during a northeast storm, Vinnie at the instrument, and her reluctance to expose her feelings of loss.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Sunday Morning
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily relays news of her absent father's letters and enjoyment away, and of lively college levees and receptions at Amherst ahead of Austin's return.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Sunday Night
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Emily teasingly scolds Austin for not writing, reports the family's preparations for his return, and describes a barn fire on the street fought by the men and their thanks for the narrow escape.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Thursday Evening
author: Dickinson
summary: Feeling lonely at home while Austin and Vinnie are together, Emily quotes a Beatitude, puzzles over a cryptic note from Austin, and asks him to write.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Thursday Evening
author: Dickinson
summary: Writing on a rainy evening amid the family circle, Dickinson keeps a diary of her thoughts of Austin, recounts a snowstorm and her disappointment at receiving no letter, and grieves that two young women will spend Thanksgiving among the dead.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Thursday Morn
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Writing from seminary, Dickinson describes her loneliness and homesickness after a visit home, recounts the forbidden valentine episode among the students, and longs for the term to end.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Thursday Night
author: Dickinson
summary: A brief note in which Dickinson mentions reading the novel Ellen Middleton and thanks Austin warmly for the pleasures he gives her.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Thursday Noon
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily writes to her brother Austin from the Seminary about how his visit cheered her, a travelling menagerie, her fondness for the teachers, and a dream of the family's ruin that she asks him to interpret.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Tuesday Evening
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily welcomes Austin home, jokes about his forgotten slippers and franking them through Congress, and mocks Congress and the family's callers.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Tuesday Evening
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Dickinson describes returning home after visiting Austin, weighing home and parents against city life shared with her brother, and recounts the sparse train journey back.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Tuesday Noon
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily writes of missing Austin, wishing they could remain children, an Aeolian harp a cousin made, and reassures him his letters are always welcome.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Tuesday Noon
author: Dickinson
summary: Writing from Mount Holyoke seminary, Dickinson answers Austin's letter, reports on her studies and the required account-keeping, and anticipates going home in three weeks.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Wednesday Morn
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily tells Austin of a late-spring snowstorm at home and their joyful anticipation of his return, with news of a sick neighbor.

title: To Mr. William Austin Dickinson, Wednesday Noon
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson urges Austin not to resign his share of the ripe peaches and grapes and struggles to find a traveller to carry them, reports a neighbor's death and a striking red sky phenomenon that alarmed the town.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong
author: Dickinson
summary: An affectionate letter recalling the first time she saw Abiah bedecked with dandelions, linking her friend to spring flowers, and musing on how a revived flower resembles resurrection.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong
author: Dickinson
summary: A long letter to Abiah about her music lessons, the eleven-week school term, her anxiety over the coming examination, her garden, local births, and the piano pieces she is learning.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong
author: Dickinson
summary: A short note sending a pressed flower as a memento, describing a converted Jew's lectures and a returned missionary in town, and her daily music practice.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong
author: Dickinson
summary: Postscripts about a deadly heat wave in Boston, nostalgic memories of a former teacher, her brother Austin entering college, and how she has grown.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily writes about her spring-term studies, an affectionate description of her new preceptress, her teacher Miss Adams leaving to be married, and Abiah's Christmas celebration.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong
author: Dickinson
summary: A brief postscript noting that her school section has begun reading and writing compositions.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong
author: Dickinson
summary: A brief postscript listing her studies of astronomy and rhetoric and her reduced music practice.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily thanks Abiah for her letter with reflections on colds, human weakness and the Fall, and mentions visiting cousins.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: An editorial note recording the sudden death in November 1850 of Emily's friend Leonard Humphrey, an admired scholar, and the grief it caused among his friends.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong
author: Dickinson
summary: A brief postscript asking Abiah to send a copy of a romance she had been writing at Amherst.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, AMHERST, Feb. 23, 1845
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily writes to Abiah about the mild winter weather, keeping her friend's lock of hair as a treasure, local news, her needlework and singing lessons, and wishes her a happy New Year.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, AMHERST, Jan. 12, 1846
author: Dickinson
summary: A New Year's letter to Abiah reflecting on the flight of the old year and broken resolutions, describing her German lessons, Christmas gifts, a funeral she witnessed, and playful Biblical allusions to Eve and Adam.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, AMHERST, Jan. 29, 1850
author: Dickinson
summary: An imaginative, playful letter describing Emily's solitude at home, a trinity of God, her friend, and herself, an elaborate personification of her head-cold, meditations on snakes, and her longing for her absent friend.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, AMHERST, May 7, 1845
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily writes to Abiah about their separation, piano lessons, local marriages, her school studies, and sends a pressed geranium leaf while discussing flowers and herbariums.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, AMHERST, May 7, 1850
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily writes while nursing her mother, who suffers acute neuralgia, describing her new household duties, her struggle to resist a temptation to go riding, and her comparison of it to Christ's temptations.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, BOSTON, Sept. 8, 1846
author: Dickinson
summary: Writing from Boston, Emily describes her health-motivated journey, visits to Mount Auburn cemetery and the Chinese Museum, and reflects on the swift flight of the seasons and the wise use of one's time.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, Friday Eve (summer), 1846
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily apologizes for her delay and announces her plan to enter South Hadley Seminary, describing her eager anticipation of it and the return of a beloved teacher.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, MT. HOLYOKE FEMALE SEMINARY, Jan. 17, 1848
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: Emily recounts her joyful journey home to Amherst for Thanksgiving through a storm, the family celebration, and her return to the Seminary to study chemistry and physiology.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, MT. HOLYOKE FEMALE SEMINARY, May 16, 1848
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily apologizes for her delay, describes being taken home by her brother because of illness and dosed with medicine, her love of spring flowers, and her recent reading.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, MT. HOLYOKE SEMINARY, Nov. 6, 1847
author: Dickinson
summary: A detailed account of her first weeks at Mount Holyoke Seminary: homesickness, the strict examinations, her cousin roommate, her daily schedule and domestic duties, and a surprise visit from her parents.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, Sabbath Eve, 1846
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily reports returning home from Boston in good health, her decision to stay home for the fall term doing sewing and household work, and news of the Seminary's new principal.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, Sunday Evening
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: A Sunday letter dwelling on the sacred bonds of their friendship, imagining herself paddling down the Susquehanna to reach Abiah in Philadelphia, and her disappointment that a snowstorm prevented a final visit.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, Thursday, Sept. 26, 1845
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily writes to Abiah about the swift passing of time, a friend's wedding, learning to make bread, the arrival of autumn, and saving the last flowers of her garden from the frost.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, Tuesday Evening
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily laments their brief, fleeting meetings, describes a moth that taught her to lay up no earthly treasure, praises their mutual friend Sarah, and looks toward reunion in heaven.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, Tuesday Evening
author: Dickinson
summary: Emily thanks Abiah for a note and invitation, describes visiting Abiah's friend, and gently declines to travel, portraying herself as an old-fashioned homebody who never leaves home.

title: To Mrs. A. P. Strong, Tuesday Evening
author: Dickinson
summary: A grieving letter written after the death of her friend Humphrey, meditating on the churchyard, her first bereavement, mortality, growing old, and the soul's passage to eternity.

title: To Mrs. Anthon
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: A letter to Kate Anthon on separation and faith, imagining future reunion amid images of moss, violets, and the deep sea.

title: To Mrs. Anthon
author: Dickinson
summary: An editorial note explaining that the following letters were written to Lavinia Dickinson while Emily received eye treatment in Boston in 1864-1865.

title: To Mrs. Anthon
author: Dickinson
summary: A letter expressing alienation during long illness away from home, grieving over plants left behind and longing to return.

title: To Mrs. Anthon
author: Dickinson
summary: A brief note about the doctor permitting her return home for Thanksgiving, with an allusion to funeral drums.

title: To Mrs. Anthon
author: Dickinson
summary: A short poem welcoming a friend back to health after a serious accident, describing her as half of dust and half of day.

title: To Mrs. Anthon
author: Dickinson
summary: A short farewell poem, sent with an oleander, that avoids a formal goodbye to spare the pain of missing those who have died.

title: To Mrs. Anthon
author: Dickinson
summary: A short poem contrasting two kinds of ripening in nature, one visible and one hidden, disclosed by October frost.

title: To Mrs. Anthon, 1864
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A letter to Lavinia from Boston during eye treatment, expressing homesickness, gratitude for kind friends, and a wish to recover.

title: To Mrs. Anthon, AMHERST, 1859
author: Dickinson
summary: An intense figurative welcome to Kate Anthon, casting her as a rare rose gathered in March and cherished by the writer.

title: To Mrs. Anthon, To the Same, 1860
author: Dickinson
summary: A dense letter to Kate Anthon mixing longing for the departed friend with imagery of poverty, the dead, and seasons parting them.

title: To Mrs. Anthon, To the Same, 1865
author: Dickinson
summary: A chatty letter to Lavinia from Boston about home improvements, flowers, and news of Jefferson Davis's capture.

title: To Mrs. Carmichael, 1882?
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson recounts a gift of candy received by a small delighted household, recalls the Skeels' musical evenings, and relays a comic exchange between Vinnie and Gilbert over a cat.

title: To Mrs. Carmichael, 1884?
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson playfully thanks Mrs. Carmichael and Mrs. Skeel for gifts of honey and a little tub, joking about Diogenes, ocean steamers, and their intercession with Santa Claus.

title: To Mrs. Carmichael, 1885?
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson condoles with Mrs. Carmichael over a great loss, praises her comfort in the family's bereavement, and asks a remembrance in Mrs. Skeel's prayer for the bereaved.

title: To Mrs. Currier, April 10, 1886
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter to her aunt Mrs. Currier on her own illness, the spring crocuses and daffodils, and local news of a hanging, a poisoning, and Shakespeare.

title: To Mrs. E. P. Crowell, March 2, 1885
author: Dickinson
summary: Short note to Mrs. Crowell on love marine, terrene, and celestial, invoking angels' charge.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman
author: Dickinson
summary: Frame noting a box of chocolate caramels accompanying a note to Mrs. Tuckerman.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman
author: Dickinson
summary: Frame noting a poem-note that contained a pressed dandelion tied with scarlet ribbon.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief frame noting yellow flowers sent to Mrs. Tuckerman when the country was drenched in rain.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, 1880
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Poem-note questioning the sages' claim that love is done when love's begun and adjourning truth's boon without day.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: Note asking whether Mrs. Tuckerman's little hands will enfold a daphne, meditating on trust as a shelving word and treasures partly denied us.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, 1881
author: Dickinson
summary: One-line note that finding her sweet friend is harder than blessing her, both slightly possible this afternoon.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, About 1877
author: Dickinson
summary: Note arguing no joy is in vain and that the immortality of flowers must enrich our own, resenting a redemption that excluded them.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, After Professor Root's death, December, 1880
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Condolence note after Professor Root's death, with a quatrain bidding a bright adieu to the Brother of Ophir.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, April, 1884
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Condolence note comparing the friend's hidden grief to Mary's words to Christ over the death of Lazarus.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, April, 1885
author: Dickinson
summary: Easter note lamenting the friend's absence, with morning crows turning her thoughts toward celestial things.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, August, 1878
author: Dickinson
summary: Note that surmise exceeds sight, that magic is a frugal meal, and that cherishing Mrs. Tuckerman is intuitive.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, August, 1883
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Brief verse contrasting the sober dress humans wear in death with summer, which is frilled as for a holiday.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, December, 1881
author: Dickinson
summary: Note that Vinnie sought a message before she ran away, with a poem on knowing without seeing and Eden's innuendo of seraphic fear.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, February, 1884
author: Dickinson
summary: Thank-you note for a gift, weaving biblical and Aesopic fox allusions to praise friendship as a wondrous gift of neither Heaven nor earth.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, January 5, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: Note on the intimidating sweetness of a short letter, invoking a mastiff guarding Eden, with a poem that a lover's conjecture eludes finding out.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, January, 1874
author: Dickinson
summary: Note to Mrs. Tuckerman about a belated congratulation, comparing it to repentance according to Calvin and its durability.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, January, 1879
author: Dickinson
summary: Two-line note calling Mrs. Tuckerman's coming a symptom of summer whose symptom excels the malady.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, January, 1882
author: Dickinson
summary: Thank-you note recalling a friend's visit and a gift of spiced kernels, closing with a short verse addressed to a 'pirate of the heart.'

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, January, 1883
author: Dickinson
summary: Thank-you note praising the friend's presence as a fortune and acknowledging a gift of figs, likening the affected heart to the vast sea.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, January, 1884
author: Dickinson
summary: Verse on the inexpressibility of gratitude and the soul figured as an untamable 'mutineer.'

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, July, 1878
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: Note on subjecting an apparitional interview to a grosser test, citing the Bible on spirit, with a poem warning not to approach a house of rose or tie the butterfly.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, June, 1878
author: Dickinson
summary: Note asking whether words are too small or we too large to thank a friend, concluding it is chiefly both.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, June, 1883
author: Dickinson
summary: Short note on her own frailty and slowness in old age, with a verse on the slow wind and sea.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, March, 1875
author: Dickinson
summary: Note to Mrs. Tuckerman on seeking her with the birds and on home feeling far from home since Dickinson's father died.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, March, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: Poem-note portraying the robin as a Gabriel of the working classes, punctual as a New England farmer, self-denying and covert.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, May, 1875
author: Dickinson
summary: Note sending inland buttercups since outdoor flowers are still at sea, signed Emily.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, May, 1885
author: Dickinson
summary: Note on a friend's recovery from illness, musing that a chastened grace becomes a holiness.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, November 8, 1881
author: Dickinson
summary: Poem-note on the dandelion's tube astonishing the grass and turning winter to an Alas, proclaiming that sepulture is over, with mention of Mr. Root.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, November, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief note thanking Mrs. Tuckerman, reporting recovery, and saying her redemption would otherwise save Dickinson.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, October, 1885
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Consoling letter recalling the October death of her young nephew Gilbert and his last words, invoking the resurrection bugle of Corinthians.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, Saturday
author: Dickinson
summary: Note musing that yesterday was a year ago, with a verse on a departed flower's stem bearing a despatch of pink, thanking her for the lovely love.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, sent her friends at New Year's, with the recipe
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: New Year's note sending a recipe and a scorched biscuit of Love, with canna and blossoms, closing on love that comes and goes without herald.

title: To Mrs. Edward Tuckerman, September, 1879
author: Dickinson
summary: Playful note fretting whether Mrs. Tuckerman does or does not have pears like Dickinson's own.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson sends Mrs. Cooper flowers grown from pinks that Cooper had given her mother in winter, closing with a biblical allusion.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: A one-line note remarking that Nature does not knock and yet does not intrude.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A note contrasting the biblical demand 'Give me thine heart' as too peremptory for earthly courtship though fitting in Heaven.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: A note describing the intimacy between Nature and her children as that of 'comrades in arms.'

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson tells Cooper that thanking her would profane her, and adds verses on stars as asterisks pointing to a human life.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: A one-line note saying that in a world too full of beauty for peace she has met nothing more beautiful than her friend.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A note of sympathy for Cooper's pain, offering to share her sorrow and affirming that grief has a right to express itself.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson offers Cooper flowers 'snatched from the frost' along with more practical trinkets.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
cluster: Guilt · Conscience · Fate and Free Will
summary: Playful note reinterpreting the patriotic hymn 'My country 'tis of thee' as her love of the woods.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: Witty note on wealth versus flowers, alluding to Midas and silver currency, calling the keeper of golden flowers safe from the 'Silver Bill.'

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief note sending an April flower amid February, called the month of fleetest sweetness.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: Note apologizing that a flower meant for the friend wilted overnight and sending a design instead.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Aphoristic note observing that the founders of honey, the bees, have no names.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: Cryptic note calling her circle of the dead a select if dim 'family of apparitions.'

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: Note sending flowers to the friend, adding a 'face' from her own garden.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: Thank-you note deeming some little tumblers forever consecrated by the friend's gesture.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Brief note thanking the friend for remembering the anniversary of her father's death.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper, 1875
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Reflection that having her father's friend within confiding reach eases her fatherlessness.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper, 1876
author: Dickinson
summary: Note conveying her mother's thanks, remarking on the mother's fondness for flowers and for recollection, 'that sweetest flower.'

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief note musing whether sickness is pathos or infamy while sending along a small gift.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper, 1883?
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks Cooper for a glimpse of Vinnie's friends' residence and offers in exchange a view of her own house, painted white by Nature.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper, 1885?
author: Dickinson
summary: A note reflecting that friends' tender resentment at our weakness is more inspiriting than strength itself.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper, After a fire, in 1876
author: Dickinson
summary: Note after a fire consoling the friend that disaster endears beyond fortune.

title: To Mrs. F.S. Cooper, January, 1875
author: Dickinson
summary: Condolence letter affirming, through a verse on the sleeping deep and a steadfast God, that eternity endures beyond loss.

title: To Mrs. Ford
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A brief note thanking a correspondent for a forget-me-not and asking for a companion flower, sending family love.

title: To Mrs. Ford, Sunday Afternoon, 1852
author: Dickinson
summary: A friend longs for absent Mrs. Ford, describing the beauty of the New England spring and imploring her to return home.

title: To Mrs. Ford, Wednesday Eve
author: Dickinson
cluster: Ruins the Abbey · Sic Transit Gloria Mundi · Ubi Sunt
summary: A friend mourns Mrs. Ford's marriage and departure to Connecticut, feeling her loss like a bereavement and recalling the wedding.

title: To Mrs. Gordon L. Ford, Mr. Bowdoin, Mrs. Anthon, and Miss Lavinia Dickinson
author: Dickinson
summary: A friend sends Emily flower buds with her love, apologizing that rosebugs had already devoured the sweetest one.

title: To Mrs. Gordon L. Ford, Mr. Bowdoin, Mrs. Anthon, and Miss Lavinia Dickinson
author: Dickinson
summary: A postscript in which the friend describes running past the corner and wayside houses as her own gate flies open to welcome her home.

title: To Mrs. Gordon L. Ford, Mr. Bowdoin, Mrs. Anthon, and Miss Lavinia Dickinson
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note explaining that the following undated letters to Emily from a friend span 1848 to 1853, arranged in order by Mrs. Ford.

title: To Mrs. Gordon L. Ford, Mr. Bowdoin, Mrs. Anthon, and Miss Lavinia Dickinson, 1848
author: Dickinson
summary: A friend sends Emily a lock of hair as a keepsake against the day their hair turns gray, invoking Burns's 'John Anderson my Jo,' and asks for a lock of Emily's in return.

title: To Mrs. Gordon L. Ford, Mr. Bowdoin, Mrs. Anthon, and Miss Lavinia Dickinson, 1852
author: Dickinson
summary: A comic macaronic valentine studded with Latin tags and historical names, playing on mortality, immortality, and mock-heroic themes.

title: To Mrs. Gordon L. Ford, Mr. Bowdoin, Mrs. Anthon, and Miss Lavinia Dickinson, December, 1849
author: Dickinson
summary: A playful note returning Jane Eyre, wishing in mock-religious terms that its author Currer Bell might be saved.

title: To Mrs. Gordon L. Ford, Mr. Bowdoin, Mrs. Anthon, and Miss Lavinia Dickinson, Saturday Morn
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A friend apologizes for not visiting Emily during a snowy week and sends flowers in her stead as a message of love.

title: To Mrs. Gordon L. Ford, Mr. Bowdoin, Mrs. Anthon, and Miss Lavinia Dickinson, Thursday Morn
author: Dickinson
summary: Too cold to enter, a friend rings Emily's doorbell and leaves a note, resisting the temptation to come in lest she grow so happy she would never go home.

title: To Mrs. Gordon L. Ford, Mr. Bowdoin, Mrs. Anthon, and Miss Lavinia Dickinson, Thursday Morning
author: Dickinson
summary: A friend reflects on the preciousness of youthful friendship and jokes that Emily will one day be married and taken away.

title: To Mrs. Gordon L. Ford, Mr. Bowdoin, Mrs. Anthon, and Miss Lavinia Dickinson, Thursday Morning
author: Dickinson
summary: On a dark snowy day a friend sends Emily comfort, imagining a distant summer of gardens and singing robins and a heavenly home where sorrow cannot come, quoting the Beatitudes from Vinnie's Testament.

title: To Mrs. Gordon L. Ford, Mr. Bowdoin, Mrs. Anthon, and Miss Lavinia Dickinson, Tuesday Morn
author: Dickinson
summary: A friend writes that she visits Emily in spirit many times a day without her body, sitting and chatting by her side undisturbed even by a king.

title: To Mrs. Gordon L. Ford, Mr. Bowdoin, Mrs. Anthon, and Miss Lavinia Dickinson, Valentine Week, 1850
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A valentine poem arguing that all creation pairs and marries, urging a solitary bachelor to court and win a bride.

title: To Mrs. Greenough, After her Mother's Death, October, 1885
author: Dickinson
summary: Condolence to Mrs. Greenough on her mother's death, comparing it to the death of Dickinson's own mother and the first snow on her grave.

title: To Mrs. Hanson Read, December 27, 1873
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson sends Mrs. Read flowers recalling her martyrs and, on a later anniversary, writes of thinking of her while leaving her alone with a thronged Heaven.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills
author: Dickinson
summary: Thanks for heavenly flowers brought to her room after a wakeful, gale-tossed night, wishing her friend may wake in Eden.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills
author: Dickinson
summary: A note trying to requite the remembered gift of Sabbath-morning blossoms.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills
author: Dickinson
summary: A note of thanks accompanying a little dish prepared too late to give in person.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills
author: Dickinson
summary: A note affirming that speechless cherishing is as warm a form of remembrance as spoken words.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills
author: Dickinson
summary: A brief note telling Mrs. Henry Hills that even the simplest consolation, offered with loving intent, has a heavenly quality.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills
author: Dickinson
summary: Thanks for a gift of a cross and sacred flowers, with allusions to Gethsemane and Cana as a still-travelled route.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, 1880
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A note assuring grieving friends that Dickinson is near them in their sorrowful hours.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, 1881
author: Dickinson
summary: A note sending a kiss and a flower, one of which will endure.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, 1881
author: Dickinson
summary: A note thanking Mrs. Hills for exotic delicacies, likening them to the Arabian Nights.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, 1882
author: Dickinson
summary: A one-line note sending a pond lily that Dickinson had cultivated herself.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, Christmas, 1878?
author: Dickinson
summary: A Christmas greeting to the Hills household as 'little brethren and sisters of the mystic tie.'

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, Christmas, 1879
author: Dickinson
summary: A Christmas note musing that Heaven will not surpass earth unless it keeps the power to remember.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, February 23, 1879
author: Dickinson
summary: A note on the child's death, framing it through the biblical 'Come unto me' as a commandment obeyed.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, February, 1879
author: Dickinson
summary: A note on the limits of consolation, suggesting the child's early death before it feared to die may have been a boon.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, February, 1879
author: Dickinson
summary: A note of sympathy for the sufferings of a sick child, sending a flower and calling such children 'on a furlough from Paradise.'

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, January, 1879?
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson explains that she did not know her neighbor was ill or she would have inquired, expressing regret.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, January, 1883
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic note observing that when one truly means the word 'beautiful' nothing more can be said, closing with the phrase 'a dream personified.'

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, March, 1879
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson writes that the only balmless wound is a departed human life we needed, for which even Immortality is a slow solace.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, With Christmas delicacies, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: A Christmas note sending 'little annual creatures' of confectionery and flowers to Mrs. Hills.

title: To Mrs. Henry Hills, With red lilies, Spring, 1883
author: Dickinson
summary: A one-line note accompanying a gift of red lilies to a neighbor, calling them 'Persian hues.'

title: To Mrs. J. C. Greenough
author: Dickinson
summary: Note to Mrs. Greenough on the flower keeping its appointment and Memory ringing her bell.

title: To Mrs. J. C. Greenough
author: Dickinson
summary: Note to Mrs. Greenough sending a flower against the coming of spring at the door.

title: To Mrs. J.S. Cooper
author: Dickinson
summary: Note about her late father, hoping to speak of him and expecting to behold him again after death.

title: To Mrs. J.S. Cooper, June, 1874
author: Dickinson
summary: Thank-you note to a near-stranger for kindness to her family, reflecting that only one who has suffered comprehends suffering.

title: To Mrs. J.S. Cooper, Later Summer, 1874
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Brief grieving note about her late father, whom she still instinctively expects to see.

title: To Mrs. Jameson
author: Dickinson
summary: A playful note about a child, Arthur, forgetting to set a trap for Santa Claus and a mouse stealing the cakes instead.

title: To Mrs. Jameson
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: A consoling note to a neighbor invoking the biblical sparrows and 'the great Logician' (God) against a tear on her cheek.

title: To Mrs. Jameson, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: A note mourning the death of George Eliot, enclosing verse on the tomb and immortality and lamenting the brevity of her life.

title: To Mrs. Joseph Sweetser
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks her aunt for flowers that revive a long-warm memory and returns a kiss and gratitude, likening the flowers to saints and angels.

title: To Mrs. Joseph Sweetser
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson says she has found her grandfather's Bible but will wait for a trusted messenger, thanks her aunt for loving her dead parents, and hopes they are with the Source of love.

title: To Mrs. Joseph Sweetser
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson explains why she could not see her aunt, notes Judge Lord's visit and the death of a Dr. A., calls Death an intimate friend, quotes Shakespeare, and recalls shared memories.

title: To Mrs. Joseph Sweetser, 1884
author: Dickinson
summary: A note thanking Aunt Katie for her account of the lilies, invoking the Bible's 'consider the lilies' and anticipating meeting them in autumn.

title: To Mrs. Joseph Sweetser, 1885
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson praises her aunt's patience, condoles on a recent death recalled through spring flowers, mentions her own mother in the grave, and cites Jesus and Milton.

title: To Mrs. Joseph Sweetser, Autumn, 1879?
author: Dickinson
summary: An autumn letter mourning the fading flowers ('sultans') of the garden, comparing their reluctant death to an evening star, and reporting the mother's ill health.

title: To Mrs. Joseph Sweetser, December, 1881
author: Dickinson
summary: A winter letter recounting the loss of the 'sultan' flowers in the 'Guiteau year' to worm and frost, joking about a treasonous gardener, and describing the snow-storm weather.

title: To Mrs. Joseph Sweetser, November, 1884
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks her aunt Katie for lilies, recalls her mother and her father's death, comments on the aunt's illness, and frames God as both enemy and friend.

title: To Mrs. Todd
author: Dickinson
summary: Note to Mrs. Todd enclosing the hummingbird poem A route of evanescence, with Todd's account of the flower design used for the Poems cover.

title: To Mrs. Todd
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note by Todd introducing a later note that enclosed Dickinson's hummingbird poem.

title: To Mrs. Todd, 1884
author: Dickinson
summary: Note to Mrs. Todd on the martial apology of nature, quoting the deathless of Thermopylae dying in obedience to law, with verses on the brave and the adjourning heart.

title: To Mrs. Todd, March 21, 1885
author: Dickinson
summary: Playful note to Mrs. Todd thanking her for a painting of a trumpet vine, invoking Egypt, the Orient, and Antony's words to Cleopatra.

title: To Mrs. Todd, Mrs. Tuckerman, the Misses——, Mr. Clark, and Mrs. Currier
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial preface by Mabel Loomis Todd introducing the selection of Dickinson's late notes, beginning with a response to a painted panel of Indian pipes.

title: To Mrs. Todd, September, 1885
author: Dickinson
summary: Note to Mrs. Todd on Othello and jealousy, with Todd's recollection of playing music for the reclusive Dickinson and the notes she sent in return.

title: To Mrs. Todd, Winter, 1882
author: Dickinson
summary: Thank-you note to Mrs. Todd for a painting of Indian pipes, recalling childhood wonder at the flower and the mystery of God's creation.

title: To Mrs. Tuckerman
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Editorial transition to a condolence note to Mrs. Tuckerman written after Professor Tuckerman's death in March 1886.

title: To Mrs. W. A. Stearns
author: Dickinson
summary: An editorial note stating that a stanza came to Mrs. Stearns when President Stearns died.

title: To Mrs. W. A. Stearns
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: At Professor Snell's death Dickinson sent his family purple and white flowers with the single line, 'I had a father once.'

title: To Mrs. W. A. Stearns
author: Dickinson
summary: On receiving an Easter card, Dickinson writes that the rising of her lost father would have eclipsed Christ's but for the admonition, recalls his last Sabbath, and encloses a clover verse.

title: To Mrs. W. A. Stearns, 1875
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson writes that a pansy's only pang is its transience, thanks Mrs. Stearns for love, and imagines an angel toiling with its needle beneath the snow.

title: To Mrs. W. A. Stearns, June 8, 1876
author: Dickinson
summary: A short verse on love's stricken 'why', built of a single syllable that breaks the hugest hearts.

title: To Mrs. W. A. Stearns, Spring, 1876
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson sends a gift she likens to the Bible's fabrics beyond rubies, more accessible to the recipient's fingers than to a thief's.

title: To Mrs. W. F. Stearns
author: Dickinson
summary: A recollection preserving one of Emily's destroyed notes, a whimsical passage about Mrs. Nellie arriving with the robins and a 'society for the prevention of wings.'

title: To Mrs. W. F. Stearns, May, 1881
author: Dickinson
summary: A condolence note on the death of the Stearnses' child, invoking the Kingdom of Heaven and confessing her heart breaks.
