title: To Mrs. W. F. Stearns, October, 1882
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A brief note assuring Mrs. Stearns that affection is present and inviting her to demand it to the utmost.

title: TO MY BROTHER GEORGE
author: Keats
summary: Sonnet on the wonders of sea and sky witnessed in a day, made meaningful only by the absent brother's shared thought; nature, the sea and fraternal love.

title: TO MY BROTHER GEORGE
author: Keats
summary: Verse epistle on poetic doubt and inspiration: the trance of the poet who sees visionary knights in the clouds, hopes for poetic immortality, and treasures fraternal love.

title: TO MY BROTHERS
author: Keats
summary: Domestic sonnet for Tom's birthday by the fireside, quietly aware that the 'great voice' of death will one day part the brothers; fraternal love and mortality.

title: TO MY CANDLE
author: Coleridge
summary: A 'farewell epigram' addressed to a candle, whose short pointed flame is itself an image of the epigram; a self-reflexive meditation on light, brevity, and the art of the epigram.

title: TO NATURE
author: Coleridge
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: A sonnet making nature itself a temple: the poet builds an altar in the fields and worships God through leaves and flowers. Themes: nature as worship, piety, the book of nature.

title: To One in Paradise
author: Poe
summary: An elegiac love lyric mourning a dead beloved who was the speaker's whole hope; the light of life is now over, his days mere trances. Themes of grief, lost love, mortality and despair.

title: To One Shortly to Die
author: Whitman
summary: Tender address to a dying person, telling them merciless truth yet congratulating their spiritual escape; the corpse is mere excrement, the soul eternal.

title: TO ONE WHO HAS BEEN LONG IN CITY PENT
author: Keats
cluster: Ode · Nature vs Civilization · Pastoral Retreat
summary: Sonnet on the sweetness of escaping the city into open countryside to read of love; nature versus the city, transience of the happy day.

title: TO ONE WHO PUBLISHED IN PRINT
author: Coleridge
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: A cluster of satirical epigrams (several adapted from Wernicke) attacking a treacherous friend, the spread of scandal and lies, and a sneering miser; themes of betrayed friendship, falsehood, and avarice.

title: To Professor J. K. Chickering
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: Dickinson declines to talk, saying her own words chill and burn her, and encloses a short verse about the human fear of joy and of Heaven.

title: To Professor J. K. Chickering
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson admires the magnanimity of one who does a favor yet feels he has received one, calling it the kingdom of knights.

title: To Professor J. K. Chickering
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Editorial note describing Dickinson's anonymous appearance in the No Name series, the Saxe Holm rumor, and the start of her correspondence with the publisher Thomas Niles.

title: To Professor J. K. Chickering
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson defers a meeting with Chickering, describing grief as a sable but vital introduction and thanking him for his kindness.

title: To Professor J. K. Chickering, 1885
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson praises the Amherst heart, compares her lasting garden to perennial seed, and mourns Chickering's departure, calling the loss a painful fiction.

title: To Professor J. K. Chickering, Autumn, 1882
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks Professor Chickering for his help, saying her sorrow is too deep to measure her indebtedness.

title: To Rich Givers
author: Whitman
cluster: Wine and Drink · Ballad Ballade · Road
summary: The poet cheerfully accepts modest gifts as he rendezvous with his poems, giving in return the entrance to all the gifts of the universe; free-verse on the open road, the poet and gift.

title: TO RICHARD BRINSLEY SHERIDAN, ESQ.
author: Coleridge
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A sonnet praising Sheridan's eloquence and wit, ranging from Petrarchan sweetness to patriot rage that scorches the political apostate; themes of eloquence, satire, and patriotism.

title: TO SIMPLICITY
author: Coleridge
summary: A parodic sonnet satirising the cult of affected 'simplicity' and self-pitying melancholy in contemporary poetry; a satire of poetic fashion in sonnet form.

title: TO SOME LADIES
author: Keats
summary: Light occasional lyric thanking ladies for a sea-shell keepsake; nature, friendship and graceful compliment in moon-lit pastoral imagery.

title: To St. Michael in Time of Peace
author: Chesterton
cluster: Temptation · Good vs Evil · Serpent Snake
summary: A martial hymn invoking the Archangel Michael, who threw down the Dragon, to guard the Word against the soft corruptions of a false peace bought with gold and bribes.

title: TO SUSAN STEELE ON RECEIVING THE PURSE
author: Coleridge
summary: Comic 'extrumpery' lines thanking Susan for a purse the poet has no cash to fill, joking about lost money and a kiss for the purse; light verse on poverty and money.

title: TO T. POOLE: AN INVITATION
author: Coleridge
summary: A boisterous comic dinner invitation in dialect promising meat, potatoes and cabbage and mock-cursing the friend if he stays away; conviviality, feasting, and friendship.

title: TO THE AUTHOR OF POEMS
author: Coleridge
summary: A verse epistle to Joseph Cottle praising his modest verse via an allegory of the Poetic mount, Oblivion's stream, and the impassioned theme Poesy demands; themes of poetry, the artist, and nature.

title: TO THE AUTHOR OF ‘THE ROBBERS’
author: Coleridge
summary: Sonnet to Schiller in awe of the terror and sublimity of his tragedy; the sublime, terror and horror, the artist, and a Gothic dungeon scene.

title: To the East and to the West
author: Whitman
cluster: Comradeship · Union · Hands Hand in Hand
summary: Address across the regions of the States proclaiming a 'superb friendship' latent in all men; comradeship as the purpose of the nation, democracy.

title: TO THE EVENING STAR
author: Coleridge
summary: An apostrophe sonnet hailing the evening star as an emblem of the beloved's serene beauty and of a hope to join her spirit in its kindred orb.

title: To the Garden the World
author: Whitman
summary: Opening of Children of Adam: speaker as new Adam re-ascending to the garden with Eve, celebrating the body and resurrection through love; Edenic, sexual, cyclic.

title: TO THE HONOURABLE MR. ERSKINE
author: Coleridge
cluster: Nationalism and Patriotism · Democracy · Liberty Political Freedom
summary: A sonnet from the 'Sonnets on Eminent Characters' praising Erskine as a 'hireless Priest' defending British Freedom with eloquence; themes of liberty, fame surviving the tomb, and the poet's immortalizing power.

title: To the Indians who Died in Africa
author: Eliot
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: WWII elegy for Indian soldiers who died fighting in Africa; meditates on death, home, exile and the fruit of action known only after the judgment.

title: To the Ladies who Saw Me Crown’d
author: Keats
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: A sonnet weighing the bay wreath against natural beauties and finally bowing to the ladies' sovereign eyes; poetic glory, beauty and gallant compliment.

title: To the Leaven’d Soil They Trod
author: Whitman
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Closing Drum-Taps benediction to the American land that witnessed war and peace, the soil and continent nourishing and ripening the poet's songs.

title: To the Man-of-War-Bird
author: Whitman
summary: An apostrophe to the storm-riding frigate-bird as emblem of soul and freedom over sea and sky; free-verse lyric on birds, the sea, storm and the soul.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: Brief note enclosing the poem 'We send the wave to find the wave,' with mention of old bells that might wake the children.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
summary: Spring letter mocking a church revival, praising the exquisite happiness of spring, and declaring George Eliot and Middlemarch a mortal that has already put on immortality.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter written days after her father's sudden death in June 1874, recounting the arrival of the fatal despatch and her grief, imagining him now living in a new house to which they bring flowers.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks L for an offer of kindness, reports the family well, and imagines a future illness when the cousins would supplement the angels at her deathbed.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks the cousins for the bread recipe, praises the result, mentions Lathrop's poem, reflects on home, and asks them to share both their happiness and their sadness.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
summary: Short note to Frances on gratitude as mute appreciation and willingness unto death in imitation of Christ.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief reflection that sorrow has grown general since the war began, noting Robert Browning's new poem and that life now feels mightier.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial note recording the cousin's remark that the trouble behind the letter has become only a myth, likely some forgotten illness or calamity.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: Brief note expressing overwhelming affection when she thinks of her cousins' little faces.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
summary: Note on the memorial chime of bells for the Amherst students killed in the war, followed by editorial commentary on Dickinson's refusal to publish and her private writing habits.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief note thanking her cousins for a passage and asserting that a word only begins to live on the day it is spoken.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
summary: Whimsical note about a woman coming to visit, describing tidying and straightening the house in preparation for her arrival.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
summary: Reflective letter on absence and affection, observing that love is like unnoticed bread and that a careless word on a page may consecrate an eye after the author lies buried.

title: To the Misses
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial bridging note explaining that Lavinia Dickinson was visiting the cousins when their mother died and that Emily's letter belongs here.

title: To the Misses, 1864
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Letter relaying the many neighbors and relatives who ask after and sympathize with the bereaved cousins, and cataloguing the flowers now blooming in the garden.

title: To the Misses, 1865
author: Dickinson
summary: Short letter closing with a hymn-like poem contrasting the white and green of the year and reflecting that looking back is half of prospect.

title: To the Misses, 1866
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief anxious note wishing heaven's protection over the frail cousins, likening them to a lamb sharing its fleece with a timider one.

title: To the Misses, 1868
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter written ill from bed, enclosing a poem on the limits of anguish, comforting the cousins amid grief, and pointing to the unseen courageous place beyond this world.

title: To the Misses, 1870
author: Dickinson
summary: Domestic note describing her mother carrying pears to settlers and Vinnie protecting flowers from frost, with a remark that life is meant for two, never for a committee.

title: To the Misses, 1870
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Letter of consolation urging her cousins to cast out their pain, affirming that love never dies and citing the Bible on those who shall not see death.

title: To the Misses, 1872
author: Dickinson
cluster: Ruins the Abbey · Sic Transit Gloria Mundi · Ubi Sunt
summary: Letter thanking her cousins for annual candy, reflecting on loving the dead, and mentioning the memorial chime of bells given for Frazer Stearns killed in the war.

title: To the Misses, 1872, or 1873
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter reporting her timid recovery, a poem on hope and disappointment, a minor foot injury, a Rubinstein concert, and concern for her cousin's ailing eye.

title: To the Misses, 1874
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter written during illness recalling a sermon on Jesus's disappointment in Judas, and consoling her cousins in grief by likening a finite life to a garment one might decline to wear.

title: To the Misses, 1874
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter reporting her father's illness and Maggie's fever with allusions to Apollyon and the Devil, and a grim joke about a man wanting a nimble horse to ride to his execution.

title: To the Misses, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson muses on the stars differing in glory, quotes Macbeth's physician and Browning on love, describes the closing of summer, and mentions Vinnie's new black kitten.

title: To the Misses, 1881
author: Dickinson
cluster: Swords and Weapons · Power and Corruption · Tyrant
summary: Recovering from illness, Dickinson recounts another night fire in Phoenix Row, notes the frequency of fire-bells, defines genius as the ignition of affection, and closes with a poem on death.

title: To the Misses, 1881
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson reflects on the power of a written letter to serve as a life- or death-warrant, describes apples being picked and departing birds and insects, and recalls a family visit.

title: To the Misses, 1881
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson describes a robin, Maggie's toy donkeys and fresh clover, a visitor, and a passage from the Bible about an enemy who has yet to make war on them.

title: To the Misses, About July 4, 1879
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson recounts a night fire in Amherst that nearly left the family homeless, describing the bells, the blaze, Vinnie's reassurances that it was only the Fourth of July, and her sleeping mother.

title: To the Misses, About May 30, 1863
author: Dickinson
cluster: Swords and Weapons · Power and Corruption · Tyrant
summary: Letter explaining why nighttime fears kept Emily home, pleading that the cousins attend Commencement, and describing a burial where a hen sought the dead woman's window.

title: To the Misses, After the death of the Misses—–'s father, Jan. 1864
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter of consolation after the cousins' father's death, offering her own parents and home, reflecting that the grief is theirs and the gladness his, and enclosing a poem on dying.

title: To the Misses, April, 1860
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter mourning the death of Aunt Lavinia, expressing grief, uncertainty whether the dead can still see the living, and imagining her borne to heaven.

title: To the Misses, April, 1862
author: Dickinson
summary: Detailed account of Frazer Stearns's death at Newbern by a Minie ball and his funeral at the Amherst church, calling him a brave young crusader.

title: To the Misses, April, 1875
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief April note offering a buttercup for the centennial, styling herself an 'embattled farmer' with little time.

title: To the Misses, August, 1876
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson writes of a summer drought and thunderstorm, Vinnie's new cat, her nightly dreams of her dead father, and the death of Dr. Stearns, reflecting on the unknown.

title: To the Misses, Autumn, 1860
author: Dickinson
summary: Autumn letter of affection to the cousins, joking about drama and dress, recalling their dead mother, and urging that they keep hold of one another.

title: To the Misses, Autumn, 1863
author: Dickinson
summary: Autumn letter longing to see the cousins' faces rather than write, finishing her mother's sack, gathering flowers for winter, and relating homely news.

title: To the Misses, Autumn, 1869
author: Dickinson
summary: Autumn letter rejoicing at Vinnie's and the cousins' return, describing household and garden life, her improving health, and reading Lowell's Winter.

title: To the Misses, Autumn, 1873
author: Dickinson
summary: Autumn letter joking about the 1873 financial panic and Jay Cooke, with domestic news of a bird's nest fitted with a geranium and her father wintering with the cousins.

title: To the Misses, Autumn, 1873
author: Dickinson
summary: Autumn letter picturing her cousins' parlor as a place of peace and books, enclosing the poem 'There is no frigate like a book' on how books carry the soul across the world.

title: To the Misses, December 29, 1861
author: Dickinson
summary: Year-end letter reporting the wartime deaths of Mrs. Adams's two sons and Frazer Stearns's departure, and asking anxiously after the ailing cousin's chills.

title: To the Misses, December, 1861
author: Dickinson
summary: December letter thanking the cousin for a feather, describing bitter cold, her plain dress, the hens and cat, and the snow-covered garden as the year's sad toilet.

title: To the Misses, December, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson reflects on seeing the printed news of George Eliot's death and hopes the novelist, denied the gift of belief in life, receives it in the kingdom of heaven.

title: To the Misses, Early Summer, 1859
author: Dickinson
summary: Playful early-summer note to the Norcross cousins describing a garden vegetable, hay, a tame fly, and budding peonies at the Dickinson home.

title: To the Misses, Early Summer, 1872
author: Dickinson
summary: Early-summer letter of domestic whimsy about crocuses, an injured cousin, a shivering tree she means to clothe, and a coming circus, closing with memory of the late Eliza.

title: To the Misses, February, 1862
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Letter reporting that Vinnie and the household were gravely ill but recovering, amid bitter cold, and longing for the return of spring birds and summer.

title: To the Misses, February, 1865
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter describing her ailing eyes offended by snow-light, her domestic chores and care of her plants, and urging the cousin to take her cure while promising to visit Boston.

title: To the Misses, February, 1881
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson reports that Maggie's brother was killed in a mine and that Maggie wants to die, asking the cousins to send her a note to help her begin mourning.

title: To the Misses, January 14, 1885
author: Dickinson
summary: Prompted by Vinnie's dream of F, Dickinson writes of books she and the cousins are reading, the death of a member of Bowles's group, and the temporary permanence of life.

title: To the Misses, January, 1859
author: Dickinson
summary: Playful winter letter to a young friend on sewing, building castles in the air, longing to be distinguished, and Fanny Kemble's readings.

title: To the Misses, January, 1865
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter written from bed noting the ailing cousin at peace, reading Shakespeare, biblical allusions to Ishmael and Eve, and a dream of bees fighting for pond-lily stamens.

title: To the Misses, January, 1882
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson describes how caring for her ailing mother, reading and fanning her, consumes her days so that morning and night collapse into one another.

title: To the Misses, July 27, 1872
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Letter reporting the death of little Irish Maggie, to be buried at Northampton, then turning to seasonal news of birds, nasturtiums, chestnuts, and the coming autumn.

title: To the Misses, July, 1862?
author: Dickinson
summary: Summer letter recalling the cousins' visit, sweet-peas left to sow themselves, a thundershower, and domestic and garden details at home.

title: To the Misses, July, 1884
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson describes fainting unconscious for the first time while making cake, waking to alarmed family and a physician, and recalls a child laid away, closing with a poem on the unknown world beyond.

title: To the Misses, March, 1859
author: Dickinson
summary: Late-winter letter to a friend on the changing season, garden flowers, robins, and Vinnie's visit.

title: To the Misses, March, 1872
author: Dickinson
summary: March letter thanking her cousins for candy, celebrating the arrival of spring and a bluebird, and enclosing a poem on the soul awaiting a rare approach.

title: To the Misses, March, 1873
author: Dickinson
cluster: Bible · Sin and the Fall · Fall from Innocence
summary: March note imagining God dusting as snow fills her chamber, with wind and a wry reflection that a wilderness comes to each of us in turn.

title: To the Misses, March, 1886
author: Dickinson
cluster: Ode · Nature vs Civilization · Pastoral Retreat
summary: Letter to her cousins describing months of illness in bed since November, asking after their health and reading, quoting Keats's bird.

title: To the Misses, May
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter to her Norcross cousins recalling a keepsake sheet kept in her Shakespeare, thanking them for cooking instructions, and describing a rainy day with Maggie ironing and no birds out.

title: To the Misses, May, 1862
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Letter grieving the sudden death of young Myra, questioning whether suffering has a loving side, and confessing Emily's fear that the cousins may not visit at Commencement.

title: To the Misses, November
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Dickinson thanks the cousins for a gift of witch-hazel that reached her by mail, describing its beauty and enclosing a short poem comparing it to the stars of Genesis.

title: To the Misses, November, 1882
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson tells the cousins of her mother's death, describes her passing and burial beside her father, and reflects on eternity and remembrance.

title: To the Misses, October, 1881
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson asks whether the cousins knew of Dr. Holland's death, relays her mother's wish for their graham-bread recipe, and inquires after their wellbeing in the October sunshine.

title: To the Misses, Saturday
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson explains how a misaddressed note reached them after the postmaster's confusion, mentions Maggie and Vinnie, and reflects on faith and Paul's finishing of the faith.

title: To the Misses, September, 1870
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter wishing her cousins were with her in imagined heavenly mansions, musing on whether such places exist, with news of flowers, a lost cat, and the approach of October.

title: To the Misses, Spring, 1861
author: Dickinson
summary: Spring letter sending flowers and questioning why God denies small wishes, invoking Elizabeth Barrett Browning and George Sand while urging the cousins to take heart.

title: To the Misses, Spring, 1870
author: Dickinson
summary: Spring letter describing bluebirds, deep mud, and arbutus, joking about politics and household figures, and reporting the death of Mrs. J with a Macbeth quotation.

title: To the Misses, Spring, 1871
author: Dickinson
summary: Spring letter recounting how winter's terror unnerved her and her father's serious illness, offering to bear her cousins' sorrow and affirming that love takes care of them.

title: To the Misses, Spring, 1874
author: Dickinson
summary: Spring letter on hearing robins, rivers, and wagons in the distance, reflecting that remoteness is the source of sweetness, with a poem celebrating a triumphant bird.

title: To the Misses, Spring, 1881
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: Dickinson thanks the cousins for a gift, describes spring hurricanes giving way to sunshine, a man planting a garden, and invokes Gabriel, Eden and Genesis.

title: To the Misses, Spring, 1883
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks the cousins for sympathy on the loss of another friend, includes a poem on loss and the tides, and reflects on spring crocuses and Miss W.

title: To the Misses, Summer, 1875
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson sends the Norcross cousins a yearly package of lemon drops and recalls the summers when her father was alive, noting birds frolicking at his grave and quoting Charlotte Bronte on expectation.

title: To the Misses, Wednesday
author: Dickinson
summary: Domestic letter of loneliness after the cousins' departure, describing the dog Carlo, household chores, garden and flowers, and father's devotions.

title: To the Misses, Winter, 1860–61,
author: Dickinson
summary: Winter letter exchanging news of new friends and letters, reflecting on the love of God, and describing snow, trees, and birds at home.

title: To the Misses, Winter, 1873
author: Dickinson
cluster: Guilt · Conscience · Fate and Free Will
summary: Winter letter affirming her deep love for her friends, with a poem about being invited by an unseen host to dwell with him and wondering what raiment would honor him.

title: To the Misses, Written to Milwaukee, just after the Chicago fire, 1871
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Letter written to her cousins in Milwaukee just after the Chicago fire, expressing relief at their safety, grief over the disaster, and admiration for the relief efforts.

title: TO THE MUSE
author: Coleridge
cluster: Artist and Society · Truth · Regency Georgian England
summary: A lyric thanking the Muse for refining the poet's soul, softening sorrow into joy, and teaching pity and gentle satire of fashion and folly.

title: TO THE NIGHTINGALE
author: Coleridge
summary: A lyric addressing the nightingale (Philomel), 'most musical, most melancholy', yet finding the beloved Sara's voice sweeter; themes of poetic melancholy, love, and the bird as symbol.

title: To the Pending Year
author: Whitman
cluster: Swords and Weapons · Power and Corruption · Tyrant
summary: A fierce, self-interrogating address to the coming year, the poet searching for a last weapon-word against affectation and his own rebellious self.

title: To the Rev. F. F. Emerson
author: Dickinson
summary: A note relaying the mother's congratulations that the 'philosopher's stone' lies in making others happy.

title: To the Rev. F. F. Emerson
author: Dickinson
summary: A note saying any gift but spring seems a counterfeit and that the birds rebuke everyone as sweet neighbors.

title: To the Rev. F. F. Emerson
author: Dickinson
summary: A note conveying the mother's thanks for Mrs. Emerson's thoughtfulness and remembrance to Mr. Emerson.

title: To the Rev. F. F. Emerson
author: Dickinson
summary: A note written from her sickbed thanking Emerson for a package she hoards rather than uses, while still weak, sending Vinnie's love and gratitude.

title: To the Rev. F. F. Emerson
author: Dickinson
summary: A note thanking Emerson for a little book and observing that all we secure of beauty is its evanescence.

title: To the Rev. F. F. Emerson
author: Dickinson
summary: A note sending fruit from a stranger and declaring that 'valor in the dark' is the Maker's code.

title: To the Rev. F. F. Emerson, 1880?
author: Dickinson
summary: A one-line note sending a blossom as an introduction whose ultimate recipient none can infer.

title: To the Rev. F. F. Emerson, 1881?
author: Dickinson
summary: A note wishing that, should Mr. Emerson ever fall ill and idle, his clergyman be as thoughtful of him as he has been of the mother.

title: TO THE REV. GEORGE COLERIDGE
author: Coleridge
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · Common Man
summary: A prose dedicatory letter to the poet's brother arguing that mathematics, the quintessence of truth, starves the imagination, and proposing to wed Mathesis to poetic Harmony.

title: TO THE REV. GEORGE COLERIDGE OF OTTERY ST. MARY, DEVON
author: Coleridge
summary: A blank-verse epistle to his brother contrasting George's settled domestic happiness with the poet's restless wandering and alienation; themes of friendship, exile, home and providence.

title: To the Rev. J. L. Jenkins and Mrs. Jenkins
author: Dickinson
summary: A one-line wish that the love that occasioned the first Easter may shelter a few on this bereaved day.

title: To the Rev. J. L. Jenkins and Mrs. Jenkins
author: Dickinson
summary: A one-line note asking whether a flower from home in hand would make the recipient feel more at home.

title: To the Rev. J. L. Jenkins and Mrs. Jenkins, 1875?
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson responds to news of the clergyman's wife suffering, insisting the tiniest ones are mightiest and the wren will prevail, echoing Scripture on being bruised.

title: To the Rev. J. L. Jenkins and Mrs. Jenkins, 1877?
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson mourns the pastor's leaving in May as her father left in June, distinguishes real from counterfeit sorrow, and recalls the bell bidding farewell at the door.

title: To the Rev. J. L. Jenkins and Mrs. Jenkins, Autumn, 187—
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson urges the departed pastor to return, confesses a jealous love, compares Vinnie's wrath to Saul, and reads the fallen autumn leaves as a pledge of summers to come.

title: To the Rev. J. L. Jenkins and Mrs. Jenkins, June, 1878
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson describes the summer town's circus and Commencement crowds by the churchyard, Vinnie's restlessness, and the home left desolate without the absent friends, quoting Tennyson and invoking Othello.

title: To the Rev. Perez D. Cowan
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Editorial note marking a letter written upon receiving an account of little Margie's life and death.

title: To the Rev. Perez D. Cowan
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Dickinson writes to Cowan after long silence, condoles the death of his sister as a gain, and speaks of his preaching.

title: To the Rev. Perez D. Cowan, After the death of Mr. Cowan's little daughter Margie November 8, 1879
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson consoles Cowan after the death of his little daughter Margie, invoking 'Come unto me' and offering tenderness.

title: To the Rev. Perez D. Cowan, October 26, 1870
author: Dickinson
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Dickinson congratulates her cousin Peter Cowan on his marriage and declares that home is the definition of God.

title: To the Rev. Perez D. Cowan, October, 1880
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks Cowan for a memorial book of his dead daughter and meditates on immortality and resurrection, citing Paul and Bethlehem.

title: TO THE REV. W. J. HORT: WHILE TEACHING A YOUNG LADY SOME SONG-TUNES ON HIS FLUTE
author: Coleridge
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A lyric on flute-music waking memory and hope and dreams of retirement with the beloved in Freedom's dell; themes of music, love, and rural retreat.

title: TO THE REV. W. L. BOWLES
author: Coleridge
summary: A sonnet of grateful tribute to the poet Bowles, whose tender verse healed the speaker's melancholy youth; themes of poetry's consolation, sympathy, and the imagination.

title: To the River--
author: Poe
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: A short love lyric making the clear river an emblem of the beloved's beauty and unhidden heart, her image deep in the speaker's trembling heart. Themes of love, beauty, water and reflection.

title: To the States
author: Whitman
cluster: Nationalism and Patriotism · Democracy · Liberty Political Freedom
summary: Aphoristic political lyric: resist much, obey little; warns against enslavement and loss of liberty. Democracy, the rebel, reform.

title: To The States (To Identify the 16th, 17th, or 18th Presidentiad)
author: Whitman
summary: A political lyric of disgust at corrupt antebellum government, prophesying that the sleeping States will awake; a satire of political decay and a call to democratic vigilance.

title: To the Sun-Set Breeze
author: Whitman
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: The sick, aged poet addresses the cooling evening wind through his window as a spiritual, God-sent messenger linking him to nature and the cosmos.

title: TO THE YOUNG ARTIST: KAYSER OF KASERWERTH
author: Coleridge
summary: A complimentary verse-letter to a young portrait artist, praising his genius and skill at making the absent present through art.

title: To Thee Old Cause
author: Whitman
cluster: War and its Cost · American Civil War · Battlefield
summary: Dedication to the deathless cause of liberty for which all wars are fought; the wheel-on-axis image; war, democracy, eternal struggle. Free verse.

title: To Think of Time
author: Whitman
summary: Extended meditation on mortality, burial and time that concludes in defiant affirmation of the eternal soul and universal immortality.

title: To Those Who’ve Fail’d
author: Whitman
summary: A free-verse tribute raising a laurel monument to those cut off by early death before their aspirations were realized; themes of failure, death and heroism.

title: To To Mrs. Stearns
author: Dickinson
summary: Editorial frame noting a box of flowers sent as apology for tardy congratulations on Mrs. Tuckerman's return from Europe.

title: To To Mrs. Stearns
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Short note to Mrs. Stearns sending a faded flower as the gift of one who cared, signed Emily.

title: To To Mrs. Stearns, 1877?
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson thanks Mrs. Stearns for a gift her frail mother received, and speaks of friends' love as the only remnant of a grieved life and of a shared loss binding them.

title: To To Mrs. Stearns, 1878
author: Dickinson
summary: Note to Mrs. Stearns reflecting on the shame generosity causes, devotion, and why a full heart is speechless.

title: To To Mrs. Stearns, 1879?
author: Dickinson
summary: Note to Mrs. Stearns about pond lilies and lotus, comparing water and land and calling the Nile a jealous brook.

title: TO TWO SISTERS: (MARY MORGAN AND CHARLOTTE BRENT)
author: Coleridge
summary: A Wanderer's Farewell thanking two sisters whose kindness recalled his beloved sisters, blending memory, grief and despairing hope. Themes of love, grief, memory and the wanderer's loneliness.

title: To Walter de la Mare
author: Eliot
summary: Tribute poem in terza rima praising de la Mare's art of evoking the supernatural, ghosts, dreams and the uncanny through sound and craft.

title: TO WILLIAM GODWIN
author: Coleridge
cluster: Short Story · Concealment Hidden Identity · Justice Right and Wrong
summary: A sonnet to the author of 'Political Justice', hailing his enlightening reason against oppression; themes of justice, reform, and intellectual liberation.

title: TO WILLIAM WORDSWORTH COMPOSED ON THE NIGHT AFTER HIS RECITATION OF A POEM ON THE GROWTH OF AN INDIVIDUAL MIND
author: Coleridge
cluster: Poet as Prophet · Prophet · Romantic Movement (Sensibility)
summary: Major blank-verse tribute to Wordsworth's recitation of The Prelude, on the growth of mind, hope born of the French Revolution, and the poet's own grief and reawakening. Themes of imagination, memory, the poet as prophet and dejection turning to prayer.

title: To You
author: Whitman
summary: A direct free-verse address to the unknown reader, affirming the divine worth, identity and unrealized soul of every person; democratic intimacy and the self.

title: To Zante
author: Poe
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A sonnet on the Greek isle of Zante, whose flowery shores now wake only memories of a vanished maiden and entombed hopes; the place is cursed by the refrain 'no more'. Themes of grief, lost love, transience and the classical Mediterranean.

title: To —
author: Keats
summary: A tender consolatory lyric urging a weeping beloved not to grieve over a fleeting bliss, proposing a dirge of kisses; transience, love, grief and consolation.

title: To “H. H.”
author: Dickinson
summary: Brief note to friends sending a message by a mouth that cannot speak, with lines on the ecstasy of guessing.

title: To “H. H.”
author: Dickinson
summary: Fragment reflecting on the danger of an accent or punctuation mark and its power over hearts.

title: To “H. H.”
author: Dickinson
summary: Note written after Helen Hunt Jackson's death, contrasting Helen of Troy with Helen of Colorado and recalling Jackson's reply about flying.

title: To “H. H.”, March, 1885
author: Dickinson
summary: Letter to Helen Hunt Jackson sympathizing with her injured foot, enclosing verses on ecstasy and on asking God for forgiveness, and noting she has finished the novel Ramona.

title: To Hilaire Belloc
author: Chesterton
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A dedicatory lyric to Belloc (preface to The Napoleon of Notting Hill), dreaming an epic hour of revolution and battle where streets of earth meet the starry streets that point to God.

title: To-Day and Thee
author: Whitman
summary: The whole heirdom of human history and art converges in the present 'thee', a meditation on time and inheritance.

title: To Frances
author: Chesterton
summary: Whimsical love-letters and a mock-autobiography addressed to his fiancee Frances Blogg; turns ordinary domestic objects sacramental, treats love and death as kindred transformations.

title: Leo Tolstoy
author: Chesterton
cluster: Artist and Society · Truth · Regency Georgian England
summary: A critical essay (with Perris and Garnett) on Tolstoy: his cult of simplification, his realism about war, and Chesterton's argument that logic without mysticism breeds fanaticism and madness.

title: THE TOWERS of TIME
author: Chesterton
cluster: Ruins the Abbey · Sic Transit Gloria Mundi · Ubi Sunt
summary: A visionary lyric on the mutability and fall of empires, thrones and republics, set against the eternal endurance of the Virgin and the City of God outlasting all towers men rear.

title: Translation from a Sonnet of Ronsard
author: Keats
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A translated sonnet on the heavenly-made beauty of Cassandra, whose descent sets the poet's heart afire with sweet burning pain. It treats idealized beauty, romantic love, and Greek myth.

title: TRANSLATION OF A FRAGMENT OF HERACLITUS
author: Coleridge
cluster: Poet as Prophet · Prophet · Romantic Movement (Sensibility)
summary: A verse rendering of Heraclitus on the Sibyl's prophetic voice rolling unadorned truth through a thousand years, plus a couplet on truth and erring fancy.

title: TRANSLATION OF A LATIN INSCRIPTION BY THE REV. W. L. BOWLES IN NETHER-STOWEY CHURCH
author: Coleridge
summary: A short translated funerary epitaph bidding a departed parent go in joy from the world's strife to celestial quiet; themes of mortality, grief, faith and consolation.

title: TRANSLATION OF A PASSAGE IN OTTFRIED’S METRICAL PARAPHRASE OF THE GOSPEL
author: Coleridge
summary: A devotional translation celebrating the Virgin Mother nursing the infant Christ, blending natural maternal imagery with religious mystery and litany-like blessing.

title: TRANSLATION OF THE FIRST STROPHE OF PINDAR’S SECOND OLYMPIC
author: Coleridge
summary: A literal English version of the opening strophe of Pindar's Second Olympic ode (celebrating victor and city) plus a fragment on superstition as the shadow of weak mortality.

title: TRANSLATION OF WRANGHAM’S ‘HENDECASYLLABI AD BRUNTONAM E GRANTA EXITURAM’ (KAL. OCT.MDCCXC)
author: Coleridge
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Beauty · Eyes and Sight
summary: Tribute to the actress Miss Brunton, praising her truth, pity and tragic art (Monimia, Juliet, Euphrasia); art, beauty, theatrical sorrow and Pierian garlands.

title: Transpositions
author: Whitman
summary: Epigrammatic world-upside-down poem reversing judges and criminals, keepers and prisoners; satirical reformist inversion of social order.

title: The Trees of Pride
author: Chesterton
cluster: Short Story · Concealment Hidden Identity · Justice Right and Wrong
summary: A 1922 mystery novella set on the Cornish coast: peasant legends of poisonous 'peacock trees', a squire's disappearance, a faked murder unravelled by a detective doctor; pits rational scepticism against folk wisdom.

title: Tremendous Trifles
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · Common Man
summary: A 1909 collection of familiar essays finding the marvellous in commonplace objects and events; teaches wonder, gratitude and the renewing of perception against habitual blindness.

title: Tribute To Gladstone
author: Chesterton
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: An 1898 elegiac tribute on Gladstone's death, celebrating a strong man who died with his head high and rebuking the grey, sad spirit of the decadent younger generation.

title: Trickle Drops
author: Whitman
summary: Intense Calamus lyric in which 'confession drops' of blood stain every page; blood, confession, shame and the body as the bleeding source of song.

title: TROCHAICS
author: Coleridge
summary: A trochaic metrical experiment on a diviner spirit and unearthly sound making heroic hearts faint; prosodic study with visionary, supernatural imagery.

title: TROILUS AND CRESSIDA
author: Shakespeare
cluster: Order vs Chaos · Historical Novel · Fanaticism
summary: A bitter, philosophical play set during the Trojan War that deflates heroic ideals and dramatizes the betrayal of love by Cressida; a sardonic anatomy of war, lust, time and the frailty of human value.

title: True Conquerors
author: Whitman
cluster: War and its Cost · American Civil War · Battlefield
summary: Old workers, sailors and soldiers who merely survived their struggles are the true conquerors over all the rest.

title: Turn O Libertad
author: Whitman
cluster: Nationalism and Patriotism · Democracy · Liberty Political Freedom
summary: Post-war summons to Liberty to turn from the feudal past of kings and slavery toward a democratic future; patriotism, progress, and the rejection of the old order.

title: On Turnpikes and Medievalism
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · Common Man
summary: A 1933 familiar essay defending the maligned 'medieval' against the cult of modernity, using a turnpike-toll to expose the worship of speed and progress; paradoxical social criticism.

title: TWELFTH NIGHT
author: Shakespeare
summary: A festive romantic comedy of shipwreck, twins, cross-dressing disguise and mistaken identity in Illyria, where tangled love, music and folly resolve in marriage; a comedy turning on appearance versus reality.

title: Twelve Types
author: Chesterton
cluster: Artist and Society · Truth · Regency Georgian England
summary: A 1902 collection of critical-biographical essays on figures such as Bronte, Byron, Pope, St Francis, Carlyle, Tolstoy, Savonarola and Scott; literary criticism probing each subject's character and ideals.

title: The Twelve Men
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · Common Man
summary: An essay on jury service arguing that the ordinary man, not the expert, must judge grave human matters; defends the common man, tragedy as the value of life, and Christian wisdom.

title: Twenty Years
author: Whitman
summary: A sailor returns after twenty years circling the globe to find the place changed and parents dead; a meditation on time and homecoming.

title: Two Kinds of Paradox
author: Chesterton
cluster: Artist and Society · Truth · Regency Georgian England
summary: A 1911 essay distinguishing fruitful, life-giving paradox (Lear, Carroll) from barren, thought-killing epigram (Shaw, Nietzsche imitators); a meditation on nonsense, art and truth.

title: Two or Three
author: Keats
summary: A playful nonsense-verse jingle from a letter to his sister, built on the refrain 'two or three' and ending self-referentially on hatching sonnets; light comic song.

title: Ulalume
author: Poe
summary: An incantatory, hauntingly musical ballad: the speaker, wandering a ghoul-haunted October woodland with his Soul (Psyche), is led to the tomb of his lost beloved Ulalume, exactly a year after burying her. Themes of grief, death, memory and the supernatural night-journey.

title: By the Babe Unborn
author: Chesterton
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: A lyric poem spoken by an unborn child longing to enter the world; its central themes are wonder and gratitude for existence, innocence before experience, and the magic of ordinary life seen as fairyland.

title: Uncle Bernac
author: Conan Doyle
cluster: Historical Novel · War and its Cost · Honour and Chivalry
summary: A young French emigre, Louis de Laval, returns to Napoleonic France at his uncle's invitation, only to be drawn into intrigue, an assassination plot against Napoleon, and family treachery centred on his ancestral estate of Grosbois.

title: Uncollected Short Stories
author: Conan Doyle
cluster: Domestic and Social Fiction · Romantic Love · Class
summary: A gathering of miscellaneous Doyle short stories spanning comic hoaxes, ghostly and supernatural tales, and crime narratives, including the comic 'The Parish Magazine' and the macabre cabman's-eye mystery 'The Cabman's Story', alongside a chronological list of his early uncollected fiction.

title: UNDERWOODS
author: Coleridge
summary: Ben Jonson's 'The Hour-Glass': the dust in the glass is the burnt body of a dead lover, so that even lovers' ashes find no rest; a conceit on time, death and love.

title: UNFINISHED POEMS
author: Eliot
cluster: Spiritual Emptiness · Waste Land (Sterility) · Greek Tragedy
summary: Section file containing Sweeney Agonistes: jazz-rhythm verse drama of birth/copulation/death, murder, dread; spiritual emptiness of the modern waste land.

title: Unfolded out of the Folds
author: Whitman
summary: Litany that man and all his greatness is unfolded out of woman; the great mother, the body, and the generative origin of poems and justice.

title: United States
author: Chesterton
cluster: Artist and Society · Truth · Regency Georgian England
summary: A biographical memoir-preface honouring his brother Cecil, tracing his conversion to Catholicism and Distributism, his exposure of the Marconi corruption, and his death in the First World War fighting Prussianism.

title: The Higher Unity
author: Chesterton
summary: A satirical ballad about a missionary literally devoured by converts, mocking the modern doctrine of religious syncretism and forced unity of faiths; combines comic verse with theological satire.

title: TO the UNKNOWN WARRIOR
author: Chesterton
summary: A lyric poem celebrating the anonymous dead soldier whose nameless heroism defeats vulgar publicity and commercial fame; central themes are war's cost, honour, and the dignity of the unknown.

title: Unnamed Land
author: Whitman
summary: On the countless vanished nations and unrecorded dead who nonetheless still exist; ubi sunt, mortality, immortality of the soul, and memory.

title: Unseen Buds
author: Whitman
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Hidden under snow and ice, infinite germinal buds wait latent throughout earth and cosmos, urging slowly forward in endless unborn becoming.

title: Upon This Rock
author: Chesterton
summary: An apologetics essay expounding Roman Catholicism: the Papacy, the Eucharist, Penance, asceticism, and the cult of the Virgin, defending the Church as guardian of faith against heresies.

title: Utopia of Usurers
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · Common Man
summary: A collection of polemical essays attacking capitalism, plutocracy, and the Servile State, advocating Distributism and warning of a dystopia ruled by usurers; opens with militant verse on the Irish road.

title: V If the lost word is lost, if the spent word is spent
author: Eliot
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: Meditation on the silent unspoken Word (Logos) shining in darkness amid a noisy world, with the Reproaches 'O my people'; the Word, silence, grace, the desert/garden and prayer of the veiled sister.

title: V O Lord, deliver me from the man of excellent intention and impure heart
author: Eliot
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · Bread and Wine Eucharist
summary: Prayer against the deceitful heart amid snakes and dogs; humility, purity, silence, conscience; sin and the watchful labour of faith.

title: V, W, X
author: Eliot
cluster: Spiritual Emptiness · Waste Land (Sterility) · Greek Tragedy
summary: Index-of-first-lines fragment (V–X) listing openings such as 'We are the hollow men', 'Webster was much possessed by death' and 'When Mr. Apollinax visited the United States'; apparatus to the corpus.

title: V. What the Thunder said
author: Eliot
summary: Final section: the waterless rock journey, the hooded figure on the road to Emmaus, the empty chapel, falling cities and the thunder's Datta/Dayadhvam/Damyata; quest, redemption sought, drought and fragments shored against ruin.

title: Varied Types
author: Chesterton
cluster: Artist and Society · Truth · Regency Georgian England
summary: A collection of critical essays on figures such as Charlotte Bronte, William Morris, Byron, Pope, St Francis, Stevenson, Carlyle and Tolstoy; literary criticism that probes the inner truth and creed behind each writer's art.

title: VARIOUS POEMS
author: Shakespeare
summary: A miscellany of short poems attributed to Shakespeare (songs, Passionate Pilgrim pieces, the metaphysical elegy 'The Phoenix and Turtle', and epitaphs) ranging over love, beauty's transience, constancy and mortality.

title: The Logical Vegetarian
author: Chesterton
cluster: Wine and Drink · Ballad Ballade · Road
summary: A comic nonsense song (from The Flying Inn) mocking faddish vegetarianism and abstract logic through a drunkard who calls himself a rigid vegetarian; light satire built on wine, the inn, and paradox.

title: VENUS AND ADONIS
author: Shakespeare
cluster: Greek Mythology · Lust Sexual Desire · Desire
summary: Ovidian erotic narrative poem in sixains: the goddess Venus's failed seduction of the chaste youth Adonis, who is killed by a boar. Central themes: desire and lust, the unattainable beloved, beauty, mortality and transience.

title: VER PERPETUUM
author: Coleridge
summary: A short fragment on transient mortals hoping for a brighter destiny of one perpetual Spring; themes of transience, hope, and immortality.

title: Vera, or The Nihilists
author: Wilde
cluster: Swords and Weapons · Power and Corruption · Tyrant
summary: Wilde's first play, a melodramatic political tragedy set in Tsarist Russia about nihilist revolutionaries plotting to assassinate the Czar; Vera's sworn oath to renounce love and pity collides with her love for the Czarevitch, ending in self-sacrifice. Central themes: tyranny and revolution, love versus duty, oath and betrayal, martyrdom.

title: Verses
author: Belloc
summary: A collection of Belloc's verse (introduced by Joyce Kilmer) mixing serious lyric and devotional poems with rollicking drinking songs and light satirical ballads. Recurrent notes are Catholic faith, the South Country landscape of Sussex, comradeship and the friends of youth, wine, and the Boer War ('To the Balliol Men Still in Africa').

title: VERSES: ADDRESSED TO J. HORNE TOOKE AND THE COMPANY WHO MET ON JUNE 28TH, 1796,
author: Coleridge
cluster: Nationalism and Patriotism · Democracy · Liberty Political Freedom
summary: A political celebratory poem hailing Horne Tooke and the dawn of Freedom against Corruption, citing his persecution and Roman tyrannicide; themes of liberty, reform, and political injustice.

title: Verses and Sonnets
author: Belloc
summary: Belloc's first collection of verse, gathering lyrics, sonnets, epigrams and a sequence of Sonnets of the Twelve Months. The poems move between devotional and nocturnal moods, love and honour, satirical epigrams on actors and dons, and seasonal landscapes of England and France.

title: VERSES TRIVOCULAR
author: Coleridge
summary: A nonsense jeu d'esprit built on a chain of '-ocular' rhymes about unilocular hearts, roquelaures and periwinkles; comic verbal play and wit for its own sake.

title: VI Although I do not hope to turn again
author: Eliot
summary: Closing section of Ash-Wednesday: penitential prayer poised between birth and dying, sea imagery, surrender to God's will. Religious conversion and faith-doubt tension.

title: VI It is hard for those who have never known persecution
author: Eliot
summary: Chorus on complacent comfort and persecution, why men should love the Church which speaks of Evil and Sin; faith, doubt, sin, satire of society.

title: The Victorian Age in Literature
author: Chesterton
cluster: Artist and Society · Truth · Regency Georgian England
summary: A book-length critical survey of Victorian literature, treating the Victorian Compromise, its great novelists and poets, and the breakup of that compromise; argues that a writer's creed and moral attitude are inseparable from his art.

title: Vigil Strange I Kept on the Field One Night
author: Whitman
summary: A soldier keeps an all-night vigil over the body of a fallen comrade-son and buries him at dawn; an elegy of comradeship, death and love.

title: VII In the beginning god created the world
author: Eliot
summary: History of religion from Genesis chaos to the Incarnation, a moment in and out of time; faith, the bible, light and dark, the ages of the world.

title: VIII O Father we welcome your words
author: Eliot
summary: Chorus on the Crusades and Peter the Hermit, mixed motives of glory, greed and faith; the bible, the Crusades, faith, martyrdom and moral corruption.

title: Villette
author: Bronte
summary: Charlotte Bronte's first-person psychological bildungsroman: the isolated Lucy Snowe teaches at Mme Beck's school in the foreign city of Villette, enduring repression, surveillance, unrequited love and the spectral nun. Central themes are loneliness, self-suppression, Protestant/Catholic conflict and the ambiguous, storm-shadowed close.

title: Virginia--The West
author: Whitman
cluster: War and its Cost · American Civil War · Battlefield
summary: An allegory in which the rebellious South lifts a knife against the Mother of All while the loyal West (drest in blue) rushes to her rescue; the Union defended.

title: Vocalism
author: Whitman
summary: On the hard-won divine power to speak words and the magnetic right voice that all things obey; the body, the artist, identity, and song.

title: Von Kempelen and his Discovery
author: Poe
summary: A pseudo-scientific hoax-tale presenting Von Kempelen's alchemical discovery of turning lead into gold and its economic consequences. Themes of gold, science, satire and appearance vs reality.

title: W. L. BOWLES
author: Coleridge
summary: A meditative lyric (1793) in the manner of Bowles, mourning misspent youth and longing that all who silently mourn might hear joy, accepting man's mixed lot of pleasure, toil and pain by God's will.

title: Wandering at Morn
author: Whitman
summary: Morning meditation in which a singing thrush, transmuting grubs and worms into song, becomes a hopeful emblem for the troubled Union's future.

title: Warble for Lilac-Time
author: Whitman
summary: Joyous spring catalog of returning lilac-time and birds rousing the restless soul to fly forth; spring, flowers, birds, nature, and the soul's longing.

title: Washington’s Monument February, 1885
author: Whitman
summary: Washington's true monument is not marble but the worldwide spirit of freedom, courage and patriotism.

title: WATER BALLAD
author: Coleridge
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A song translated from the French in which a river-crossing becomes a courtship; the boat becomes the lovers' home, blending the journey-over-water with love and marriage.

title: Waterloo
author: Conan Doyle
summary: A one-act play, written for Henry Irving, in which the aged Corporal Gregory Brewster, a veteran who fought at Hougoumont in 1815, is visited by soldiers and a colonel who honour him, while his grand-niece Norah cares for him in his failing final days, his mind wandering between past glory and present frailty.

title: We Two Boys Together Clinging
author: Whitman
cluster: Comradeship · Union · Hands Hand in Hand
summary: Exuberant catalogue of two inseparable comrades roaming, mocking statutes and owning no law but themselves; comradeship, the open road, rebellion and the body.

title: We Two, How Long We Were Fool’d
author: Whitman
summary: Two lovers transmuted into all of nature, returning home to freedom and joy; love, nature, eternal return, cosmic identity.

title: Weave in, My Hardy Life
author: Whitman
summary: A free-verse lyric using the weaving metaphor to urge ceaseless labor of life in campaigns of peace and war; themes of the soldier, work and life-as-struggle.

title: The Well and the Shallows
author: Chesterton
summary: A late collection of controversial Catholic essays (1935) defending the Church against modern materialism, sex reform, and the Reformation legacy; argues conversion is a return to the deep well of tradition rather than the modern shallows.

title: WESTPHALIAN SONG
author: Coleridge
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A literal translation of a Westphalian folk-song, a wry lover's message turning on a feigned report of death and a promise of return tomorrow.

title: What Am I After All
author: Whitman
summary: Tiny lyric on the self as a child pleased with the sound of its own name; identity, the self, childhood, and language.

title: What Best I See in Thee
author: Whitman
cluster: Nationalism and Patriotism · Democracy · Liberty Political Freedom
summary: A free-verse tribute to U. S. Grant whose real greatness lies in carrying the common Western people with him among kings; themes of the common man and democracy.

title: WHAT IS LIFE?
author: Coleridge
summary: Philosophical riddle-poem questioning the nature of life as a war-embrace of life and death and of consciousness. Metaphysical meditation on existence and mortality.

title: What Is Right with the World
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · Common Man
summary: A philosophical essay arguing that existence is fundamentally good at its origin (not merely at some progressive end), attacking facile optimism, Meliorism, and the modern cult of unity; celebrates wonder, variety and the dignity of the common life.

title: What Place Is Besieged?
author: Whitman
summary: Brief martial allegory: to a besieged place the poet sends an immortal commander with artillery; war imagery, the poet-hero, weapons.

title: What Ship Puzzled at Sea
author: Whitman
summary: Quatrain offering the soul, as a perfect pilot rowing out in a little boat, to guide the puzzled ship of the self into the true channel.

title: What the Thrush Said
author: Keats
summary: An unrhymed sonnet-letter spoken as the thrush's counsel, urging trust in instinctive song over anxious pursuit of knowledge, set against winter passing into spring. Central to it are negative capability, the seasons, and the value of receptive idleness.

title: What Think You I Take My Pen in Hand?
author: Whitman
cluster: Comradeship · Union · Hands Hand in Hand
summary: Poet records not the battle-ship or great city but two men kissing in parting on a pier; comradely love privileged over public grandeur.

title: What I Saw in America
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · Common Man
summary: A book of travel essays reflecting on American democracy, Prohibition, business, Lincoln and the spirit of the nation; meditates on the rights of man, the creed of equality, and the contrast between America and England.

title: What's Wrong with the World
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · Common Man
summary: Chesterton's 1910 book-length work of social criticism arguing that modern society misdiagnoses its ills; it defends the family, property and tradition against industrialism, imperialism, feminism and mechanical schooling, and advances his distributist programme.

title: When I Heard at the Close of the Day
author: Whitman
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Calamus poem contrasting empty public fame with the happiness of lying beside the sleeping beloved by the sea; love, the body, the sea, dawn and autumn imagery.

title: When I Heard the Learn’d Astronomer
author: Whitman
summary: Wearied by the lecturer's charts, the poet wanders out to look in silence at the stars; a free-verse lyric contrasting dry science with mystical wonder, on stars, night and nature.

title: When I Peruse the Conquer’d Fame
author: Whitman
cluster: Comradeship · Union · Hands Hand in Hand
summary: Poet envies not generals or presidents but the 'brotherhood of lovers'; comradeship and faithful love exalted over heroism and worldly fame.

title: When I Read the Book
author: Whitman
summary: Skeptical lyric on the impossibility of biography truly knowing a life, including one's own; identity, memory, the book and writing.

title: When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d
author: Whitman
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: Whitman's great pastoral elegy for the assassinated Lincoln, built on the trinity of lilac, fallen western star, and hermit thrush, culminating in a hymn of reconciliation to 'lovely and soothing death.'

title: When the Full-Grown Poet Came
author: Whitman
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: An ars-poetica parable of the poet as reconciler standing between Nature and the Soul of man, joining their hands and blending them into one.

title: When the World Screamed
author: Conan Doyle
cluster: Science Fiction · Discovery · Reason vs the Supernatural
summary: A Professor Challenger short story in which the irascible scientist, funded by a vast bequest, drills an eight-mile shaft to the earth's crust to prove his theory that the planet is a living organism, and enlists an Artesian engineer to drive a drill into its sensitive inner tissue so the earth may 'scream' and prove his point.

title: While Not the Past Forgetting
author: Whitman
summary: Reconciliation poem laying wreaths on the graves of all dead soldiers, North and South, for peace and brotherhood.

title: Whispers of Heavenly Death
author: Whitman
summary: Hushed nocturnal lyric in which murmurs, unseen rivers and a dimmed star intimate a soul passing over as a solemn immortal birth.

title: Whispers of Immortality
author: Eliot
summary: Quatrain poem setting Webster and Donne's metaphysical obsession with death and the skull against the fleshly modern Grishkin; mortality, the body, desire and metaphysical wit.

title: Who Learns My Lesson Complete?
author: Whitman
summary: Free-verse catalogue addressing all classes of people; meditates on the wonder of the cosmos and the speaker's own immortality, finding ordinary existence equally marvelous.

title: Whoever You Are Holding Me Now in Hand
author: Whitman
cluster: Comradeship · Union · Hands Hand in Hand
summary: Calamus opening poem warning the reader-lover about the cost of comradely love; free-verse meditation on intimacy, elusive identity, and the demanding 'novitiate' of love between comrades.

title: WhoGoesHome
author: Chesterton
cluster: War and its Cost · American Civil War · Battlefield
summary: A short, martial lyric on the city, parliament and the call 'Who goes home?', turning a civic cry into a meditation on blood, liberty, victory and the soul's homecoming after death.

title: Why the Little Frenchman Wears his Hand in a Sling
author: Poe
summary: A broad dialect comedy narrated in thick Irish brogue by a vain 'Barronitt' courting a widow, who is duped in a hand-holding ruse with a French rival. Themes of farcical satire, vanity and deception.

title: The Wisdom of Father Brown
author: Chesterton
cluster: Short Story · Concealment Hidden Identity · Justice Right and Wrong
summary: A collection of detective short stories in which the unassuming priest Father Brown solves crimes through moral and psychological insight rather than science, exploring appearance versus reality, sin, and the human heart.

title: Wild Ducks
author: Chesterton
summary: A posthumous collection of Chesterton's journalistic essays on manners, culture, civilization, travel and everyday wonders; paradoxical, satirical prose celebrating the common life and gratitude while criticizing modern society and progress.

title: William Cobbett
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · Common Man
summary: Chesterton's critical biography of the radical pamphleteer and rural reformer William Cobbett, championing him as a self-made patriot and prophet of the common Englishman against industrialism, and a forerunner of distributist ideals.

title: William Wilson
author: Poe
summary: A doppelganger tale: the dissolute narrator is shadowed all his life by a double bearing his own name who thwarts his every vice, until he kills him and destroys himself; the double is his conscience. Themes of the double, conscience, guilt and identity.

title: With All Thy Gifts
author: Whitman
cluster: Nationalism and Patriotism · Democracy · Liberty Political Freedom
summary: Apostrophe to a powerful, wealthy America asking whether it lacks the one gift of perfect women and mothers fit for it.

title: With Antecedents
author: Whitman
summary: The present America as the heir and centre of all past ages and civilizations; free-verse on history, time, the common man and self as the meeting point of past and future.

title: WITH FIELDING’S ‘AMELIA’
author: Coleridge
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A complimentary sonnet presented with Fielding's novel Amelia, praising its portrayal of wifely and social virtue and wishing a mother's daughters to resemble Amelia.

title: With Husky-Haughty Lips, O Sea!
author: Whitman
cluster: Nature · Book of Nature · Natural Order
summary: Apostrophe to the sea as a chained, striving kindred soul telling the cosmic tale of elemental passion.

title: WORK WITHOUT HOPE
author: Coleridge
summary: A sonnet contrasting busy springtime Nature with the poet, 'the sole unbusy thing', concluding that work without hope draws nectar in a sieve. Themes: despair, creative sterility, transience, melancholy.

title: World Take Good Notice
author: Whitman
cluster: Poet as Prophet · Prophet · Romantic Movement (Sensibility)
summary: A compressed emblem-lyric of the national flag (thirty-eight stars, scarlet stripes) flaunting a warning to the world; patriotic emblem of the Union and the flag.

title: WRITTEN AFTER A WALK BEFORE SUPPER
author: Coleridge
summary: A comic verse-epistle searching for a simile to describe a grotesquely mismatched fat wife and thin husband, settling on an ape chained to a she-bear.

title: WRITTEN IN AN ALBUM
author: Coleridge
summary: A self-deprecating album epigram comparing Parry's polar quest to the poet's quest for rhymes, joking that the public little knows and the publisher knows too much of his works; satire of authorship.

title: WRITTEN ON THE DAY THAT MR. LEIGH HUNT LEFT PRISON
author: Keats
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: Political sonnet celebrating the imprisoned Leigh Hunt's freedom of spirit (roaming with Spenser and Milton); liberty, friendship and the immortality of genius.

title: Wuthering Heights
author: Bronte
summary: Emily Bronte's frame-narrated Gothic novel of the destructive passion between Catherine Earnshaw and the outcast Heathcliff on the Yorkshire moors. Central themes are obsessive love, revenge, social outsiderhood, the supernatural and the bond between the living and the dead.

title: X You have seen the house built, you have seen it adorned
author: Eliot
cluster: Temptation · Good vs Evil · Serpent Snake
summary: Closing chorus: the dedicated church as light on a hill, the great snake/serpent of iniquity, the hymn 'O Light Invisible'; faith, light, good vs evil.

title: X-Ing a Paragrab
author: Poe
summary: A comic literary squib: a feud between rival newspaper editors over the letter 'o' ends with a typesetter X-ing out a vowel-laden paragraph into nonsense. Themes of satire of letters, language and folly.

title: Y, Z
author: Eliot
cluster: Artist and Society · Truth · Regency Georgian England
summary: Index tail (Y–Z) with Practical Cats lines plus a short biographical note on T. S. Eliot (1888–1965, Nobel 1948); index apparatus and brief author biography.

title: Year of Meteors (1859-60
author: Whitman
summary: A retrospective chant of a portentous year — John Brown's execution, ships, comets and meteors — the poet himself a transient meteor; free-verse on history, mortality and the nation.

title: Year That Trembled and Reel’d Beneath Me
author: Whitman
cluster: Grief and Loss · Elegy · Clothing and Costume
summary: A brief lyric of the poet shaken by a year of defeat, asking whether he must now chant cold dirges and hymns of defeat; war, grief and the poet's vocation.

title: Years of the Modern
author: Whitman
cluster: Nationalism and Patriotism · Democracy · Liberty Political Freedom
summary: A visionary free-verse prophecy of a coming democratic world-era, solidarity of races and falling thrones, staged as theatrum mundi; themes of democracy and the new era.

title: Yet, Yet, Ye Downcast Hours
author: Whitman
summary: Poem of dark downcast hours and the dread that matter is conqueror; the dying voices cry out for their destination as the speaker prepares to sail.

title: Yonnondio
author: Whitman
cluster: Ruins the Abbey · Sic Transit Gloria Mundi · Ubi Sunt
summary: A dirge for vanished Native American races who pass like ghosts and disappear unrecorded, a lament of transience.

title: You Felons on Trial in Courts
author: Whitman
summary: Confessional identification of the poet with felons, convicts, and prostitutes, refusing to deny the lusts and wickedness in himself; the outcast, guilt, the body, and social compassion.

title: You Lingering Sparse Leaves of Me
author: Whitman
summary: The poet likens himself to a well-shorn tree's last sparse leaves on winter-nearing boughs, the hardiest and last.

title: You Say You Love
author: Keats
cluster: Unrequited Frustrated Love · Unattainable Beloved · Petrarchan Sonnet
summary: A refrain-song reproaching a cold, nun-like beloved whose professions of love lack warmth; plea for true passion against a statue-like reserve.

title: YOUTH AND AGE
author: Coleridge
summary: A lyric on the passage from youth to age, Youth imagined as a bold masker now departed, with the body a 'breathing house' grown burdensome. Themes: transience, ageing, nostalgia, melancholy.

title: Youth, Day, Old Age and Night
author: Whitman
summary: A short free-verse epigram pairing youth/age and day/night, affirming that old age and the restoring night follow with equal grace.

title: ZAPOLYA A CHRISTMAS TALE IN TWO PARTS
author: Coleridge
summary: Coleridge's romance verse-drama in blank verse, modelled on Shakespeare's Winter's Tale: a usurper (Emerick) seizes the throne of Illyria, the rightful queen and infant heir are driven into exile, and after twenty years legitimacy is restored. Central themes are kingship and legitimacy, usurpation, fate and providence, exile, and the restoration of the natural order.
